properties.method: Subtraction of the city count from the county count at each census, both from Census publications this corpus already holds and cites. Not a published figure: no source states it, and it is tagged as this corpus's inference throughout. The `value` above is the series maximum. Boundaries are as reported at each census and are known to have moved in 1902, 1903, 1905, 1906, 1944 and between 1980 and 1990 — twice out of the city and four times into it. [inference]
properties.parameter: county population less the city of Lima, decennial

blocks.text: The county's population with [Lima](../place/lima.yml) taken out of it, at fourteen censuses. [inference] — subtraction performed here; every input is a Census count already held by this corpus.

Written out: **the county outside Lima held 24,663 people in 1890, 26,253 in 1900, 26,072 in 1910, 26,877 in 1920, 27,132 in 1930, 28,592 in 1940, 37,937 in 1950, 52,654 in 1960, 57,410 in 1970, 64,414 in 1980, 64,206 in 1990, 68,157 in 2000, 67,560 in 2010 and 66,627 in 2020.** [inference] — same subtraction. County figures from [1940–1990](allen-county-population-1940-1990.yml), [2000](allen-county-population-2000.yml), [2010](allen-county-population-2010.yml) and [the 2020 census count](allen-county-population-2020-census.yml), with 1930 from [the 1950 townships table](allen-county-townships-1930-1950.yml) and 1890 to 1910 from [the 1910 one](allen-county-townships-1890-1910.yml); Lima from [1850–1960](lima-population-1850-1960.yml), [1970–1990](lima-population-1970-1990.yml), [2000](lima-population-2000.yml), [2010](lima-population-2010.yml) and [2020](lima-population-2020-census.yml). The 2020 pair is census-to-census; the estimates base gives 102,217 and 35,531 for the same date and would put this series' last term at 66,686.

**Four of the fourteen terms are measured as well as derived.** The townships in [the 1950 volume's Table 6](allen-county-townships-1930-1950.yml) sum to 27,132 for 1930 and 28,592 for 1940, and the twelve outside Ottawa in [the 1910 supplement](allen-county-townships-1890-1910.yml) sum to 24,657 for 1890 and 26,072 for 1910 — the same numbers this subtraction produces, from sources that never perform it. [verified] — those tables. The 1890 pair differs by six, and correctly: the twelve exclude Ottawa Township, which held six people outside Lima city that year and none afterwards.

**The first fifty years of this series are almost flat, and that is the finding.** From 24,663 in 1890 to 28,592 in 1940 the county outside Lima grew 16 per cent, while the county grew 80 per cent and Lima 180. [inference] — computed here. Then it reversed: the balance is up 133 per cent since 1940 and the city is down a third since 1970. **Lima's share of the county peaked in 1940 at 61.0 per cent, having been 39.3 in 1890 and 34.8 in 2020** — a rise and a fall of almost exactly the same size, hinged on one census. [inference]

**This answers a question [depopulation](../period/depopulation.yml) left open.** That node said the ring around Lima grew while the city emptied, and that "when the ring turned is not established here". **It turned between 2000 and 2010.** The county outside Lima grew at every census from 1910 to 2000 except one, and has fallen at the two since. It fell once before that too, between 1900 and 1910. [inference]

**So the county has three peaks and they are thirty years apart.** Lima peaked in 1970, the county as a whole in 1980, and the county outside Lima in 2000. [inference] — from the three series above. A single line labelled "Allen County" hides all of this: from 1970 to 2000 the county was falling and two thirds of it was growing.

**The exception is the decade the boundary moved, and it moves the right way.** Between 1980 and 1990 the balance fell by 208 — the only fall before 2000 — and it is the one decade in which Lima is known to have annexed, from American, Bath and Shawnee townships. [verified] — [1990 Census, Population and Housing Unit Counts, Ohio](../../catalog/census-cph-2-37-ohio.md), Geographic Change Notes. Annexation moves people from the balance into the city without anybody moving house, so it pushes this series down and the city's up. The 1980s fall is therefore an upper bound on a decline and may be no decline at all. [inference]

**Lima's share of the county rose at every census from 1890 to 1940 and has fallen at every one since, including the three at which the city grew.** 39.3% in 1890 to 61.0% in 1940, then down to 34.8% in 2020, through a decade in which the city gained 5,535 people and still lost four points of share. [inference] — computed above. The county was redistributing before it was declining, and the two processes are seventy years out of phase.

**What the corroboration reaches and does not.** Between 2000 and 2010 the Census Bureau's own "balance of county" — everything outside *every* incorporated place, a narrower base than this one — fell from 50,809 to 50,048. [verified] — [Census Intercensal Estimates, 2000–2010](../../catalog/census-intercensal-2000-2010.md). Same direction, different denominator: the difference between the two is Delphos, Bluffton, Spencerville, Elida and the smaller villages, which this series keeps and that one removes.

properties.method: Decennial census counts as compiled in 1906 from published returns, with the 1906 figure an estimate by the compilers. Not read from a Census Bureau publication. [verified]
properties.parameter: total resident population, decennial

blocks.text: The county's decennial census counts for its first seventy years. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md), both scans agreeing figure for figure.

**The oil decade is visible in it.** The largest gain of the seven is 1880 to 1890, **9,330 people or 29.7 per cent**, and the 1906 compilers attribute it without hesitation: "the marked increase in the decade preceding 1890 is accounted for by the discovery of oil in 1885. During this decade the city of Lima doubled her population." [verified] — same source. That is the demographic signature of [the strike](../event/lima-oil-strike.yml), from men who watched it happen.

**The series is not continuous across 1848 and the corpus will not smooth it.** The first two figures describe a county that included eight townships now in Auglaize County and excluded four that are in Allen today, and the [reorganization of February 28, 1848](../event/reorganization-of-1848.yml) cost it a net 138 square miles. So 578 and 9,079 count different ground from everything after them. [inference]

properties.method: Read from Table 3 by counting column positions against the header printed earlier in the document, and checked against the 1970 count this corpus already held from a different Census product. The `value` above is the series maximum, not its last term. [verified]
properties.parameter: total resident population, decennial

blocks.text: The county's decennial counts for the six censuses this corpus was missing. [verified] — [1990 Census, Population and Housing Unit Counts, Ohio](../../catalog/census-cph-2-37-ohio.md), Table 3.

**The county's peak is 1980, not 1970, and the corpus has been saying 1970 since genesis.** 112,241 against 111,144 — a rise of 1,097 across the decade the corpus described as the start of a decline. [verified] — same source. Every figure this corpus held began at 1970 or later, so the sentence "no reversal at any measured point" in [depopulation](../period/depopulation.yml) was true of the data and false of the county. See [that node](../period/depopulation.yml), which now says so.

**The 1970 figure matches an unrelated source exactly**, which is how the reading of these columns was checked: 111,144 here and 111,144 in the [1970–1979 county estimates](../../catalog/census-county-estimates-1970s.md), from a different Census product. [verified]

**Housing grew when population did not.** Between 1970 and 1990 the county gained 7,281 housing units and lost 1,389 people. [inference] — computed from the figures above. Household size fell across the United States over those decades, so this is not peculiar to Allen County; what it does mean is that the county's building stock and its population stopped moving together around 1970, and the corpus's account of decline has until now been a population account only.

**1930 is no longer a gap: 69,419.** [verified] — [1950 Census, Number of Inhabitants, Ohio](../../catalog/census-1950-number-of-inhabitants-ohio.md), Tables 5 and 6, which give it twice. So the county ran 68,203 in 1920, **69,419 in 1930** and 73,303 in 1940 — a gain of 1,216 in the 1920s and 3,884 in the 1930s. [inference] — computed here; the source prints the second as 5.6 per cent and this corpus's arithmetic agrees. The county grew three times faster through the Depression decade than through the boom before it, which is the opposite of the shape the decades' reputations suggest and is [true of Lima too](lima-population-1850-1960.yml), at 2.3 per cent then 5.7.

**And 1910 is closed too: 56,580.** [verified] — [Abstract of the Thirteenth Census, Supplement for Ohio](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md); see [the 1890–1910 divisions](allen-county-townships-1890-1910.yml). **The county now has a count for every decennial census from 1830 to 2020 and an estimate for 2024, with no gaps.** Twenty-one observations, every one from a published table. [verified] The two figures that were open when this node was written are both closed, one phase apart, and both by volumes older than the one this node is named for.

properties.method: Decennial enumeration, unrounded. The estimate columns in the same file are rounded to hundreds; this column is not. [verified]
properties.parameter: total resident population

blocks.text: The 1970 decennial census count for Allen County. [verified] — [Preliminary Estimates of the Intercensal Population of Counties, 1970–1979](../../catalog/census-county-estimates-1970s.md), first block, column headed `Census 1970`, FIPS 39003.

This is the earliest population figure in the corpus and the anchor the [depopulation](../period/depopulation.yml) claim rests on. Against the [2024 estimate](allen-county-population-2024.yml) of 100,866 the county has lost 10,278 people, or 9.2%, over 54 years. [inference] — arithmetic this corpus's; both figures verified.

properties.method: Decennial enumeration as revised for the intercensal series. [verified]
properties.parameter: total resident population

blocks.text: The April 1, 2000 estimates base for Allen County. [verified] — [Census Intercensal Estimates, 2000–2010](../../catalog/census-intercensal-2000-2010.md), county file, field `ESTIMATESBASE2000`.
An intercensal series is fitted between two known censuses rather than projected from one, so this figure is the 2000 enumeration as revised with the 2010 count in hand. [verified]

properties.method: Decennial enumeration. [verified]
properties.parameter: total resident population

blocks.text: The April 1, 2010 decennial census count for Allen County. [verified] — [Census Intercensal Estimates, 2000–2010](../../catalog/census-intercensal-2000-2010.md), field `CENSUS2010POP`.

The same value appears in the Vintage 2020 county file, a separate release built for a different purpose. [verified] Two files agreeing on a census count is weak confirmation — they rest on the same enumeration — but a disagreement would have been strong evidence of a transcription error, and there was none.

properties.method: Sum of block-level `POP100` from the 2020 Census redistricting file, as served by TIGERweb. Not a modelled figure and not subject to later revision. [verified]
properties.parameter: total resident population

blocks.text: The 2020 decennial enumeration for Allen County as published for redistricting, obtained by summing `POP100` over all 3,552 census blocks in the county. [verified] — [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md), 2020 vintage block layer.

The figure is a sum and not a published total, so it carries the sum's own check: the Allen County portions of the twelve school districts covering the county also sum to 102,206, from a different partition of the same blocks. [verified] — [2020 Census Block Assignment Files](../../catalog/census-block-assignment-2020.md).

properties.method: Decennial enumeration as revised for the Vintage 2024 estimates base. A later vintage may revise it again. [verified]
properties.parameter: total resident population

blocks.text: The Census Bureau's April 1, 2020 estimates base for Allen County. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates, Vintage 2024](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), county file, field `ESTIMATESBASE2020`.

This is the 2020 enumeration as subsequently revised, not a modeled estimate — which is why it is the right figure to anchor a series on and the wrong one to describe as "the 2020 census count" without qualification. That caution is now measured: [the enumeration itself](allen-county-population-2020-census.yml) is 102,206, eleven fewer. [verified] — [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md), summed over the county's 3,552 blocks.

properties.method: Modeled postcensal estimate, not an enumeration. Comparing it to the 2020 base compares a model output to a revised count. [verified]
properties.parameter: total resident population

blocks.text: The Vintage 2024 estimate for Allen County. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates, Vintage 2024](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), county file, field `POPESTIMATE2024`.

Against the [2020 base](allen-county-population-2020.yml) of 102,217 this is a fall of 1,351, or about 1.3% over four years. [inference] — the arithmetic is this corpus's; both figures are verified. The intervening years in the same file run 102,137 / 101,800 / 101,086 / 100,851, so the 2024 figure is a slight rise on 2023 rather than a continuation of the fall.

properties.method: Summed by candidate over the county's 88 precincts. The 2016 file carries no registered-voter or ballots-cast column, so no turnout rate is derivable from it. [verified]
properties.parameter: presidential votes cast

blocks.text: Of 45,815 presidential votes cast in the county, **30,487 for Trump and 13,294 for Clinton** — 66.5 per cent against 29.0, with 1,486 for Johnson and 323 for Stein. [verified] — [OpenElections](../../catalog/openelections-ohio.md), summed over the county's 88 precincts.

**Thirteen precincts went to Clinton**, twelve of them in [Lima](../place/lima.yml) and the thirteenth `AMERICAN D`, in the township wrapped around the city. Four years later [eleven went to Biden](allen-county-presidential-vote-2020.yml): `LIMA 1A` and `LIMA 1C` crossed over and nothing crossed the other way. [verified] — same source.

The 1,486 votes for Johnson are the largest third-party showing in the three elections this corpus holds — three times Jorgensen's 590 in 2020 on a similar total vote. [verified] — same source. What that means is not recorded here; it is the kind of thing two data points cannot carry.

properties.method: Summed by candidate over the county's 88 precincts. The total is 360 fewer than the 48,353 ballots cast — an undervote of 0.7 per cent. [verified]
properties.parameter: presidential votes cast

blocks.text: Of 47,993 presidential votes cast in the county, **33,116 for Trump and Pence and 14,149 for Biden and Harris** — 69.0 per cent against 29.5, with 590 for Jorgensen and Cohen and 138 for Hawkins and Walker. [verified] — [OpenElections](../../catalog/openelections-ohio.md).

**Eleven of the county's 88 precincts went to Biden, and ten of them are in Lima.** The eleventh is `AMERICAN D`, in the township wrapped around the city's west and north. Every other precinct in the county — all twelve townships' rural ground, both cities' outer wards, every village — went the other way. [verified] — same source. The most Republican precinct is `MONROE E` at 90.6 per cent; the most Democratic is `LIMA 6C` at 87.9. A county that votes 69–29 contains precincts ninety points apart.

**It is the third of three, and the county is drifting.** Republican share of the top-of-ticket vote ran 66.5 per cent in [2016](allen-county-presidential-vote-2016.yml), 67.3 in [2018](allen-county-governor-vote-2018.yml) and 69.0 here — a move of 2.5 points across two presidential elections, against a median precinct move of 1.5. [verified] — same source.

**Every precinct Clinton won in 2016 moved toward the Republicans**, all thirteen of them, by a mean of 4.5 points; `LIMA 1A` and `LIMA 1C` crossed over entirely. Across the 88 the correlation between 2016 Republican share and the 2016–2020 swing is **−0.39**: the more Democratic a precinct was, the harder it moved. [verified] — computed here from the three [OpenElections](../../catalog/openelections-ohio.md) files.
Down-ballot in 2020, Jim Jordan took 33,201 to 13,080, Matt Huffman 34,303 to 12,645, and Bob Cupp ran unopposed with 38,882. [verified] — same source.

nodes.label: Allen County population by race, 2023

properties.method: 2023 five-year estimates. Race categories are "alone" except the two-or-more column; Hispanic origin is asked separately and overlaps every race column, so the rows do not sum to 100. The twelve townships and Lima partition the county: 2,515 plus 8,290 is 10,805, the county row. [verified]
properties.parameter: population by race (B02001) and Hispanic origin (B03003)
properties.unit: residents identifying as Black or African American alone, Allen County

blocks.text: Race and Hispanic origin for the county, its thirteen civil subdivisions, the state and the nation. [verified] — [American Community Survey](../../catalog/census-acs-summary-file.md), 2023 five-year estimates.

**Lima holds a third of the county's people and three quarters of its Black residents.** 8,290 of 10,805, or 76.7 per cent ± 4.6, against a 34.7 per cent share of the population. [verified] — same source. The twelve townships hold the other 2,515, and the two sum exactly to the county's figure.

**Eight of the twelve townships have fewer than a hundred Black residents**, and two report none. [verified] Outside Lima and the two townships that adjoin it — American at 10.1 per cent and Shawnee at 4.1 — the county is between 90 and 97 per cent white. [verified]

refusals: This does not establish why the county is distributed this way.

nodes.label: Children in poverty in Allen County's school districts, 2023

properties.method: Joined on the five-digit LEA code prefixed with the state FIPS, matching the `fips_code` these district nodes carry. [verified] Rates are computed here as the poverty count over the 5-to-17 population; the file publishes neither the rate nor an interval.
properties.parameter: children aged 5 to 17 in poverty, by school district
properties.unit: children in poverty across the twelve districts

blocks.text: The modelled number of children aged 5 to 17 in poverty in each district holding ground in Allen County, with the district's whole population. [verified] — [SAIPE school district estimates](../../catalog/census-saipe-school-districts.md), 2023.

**Lima City Schools is 31.7 per cent child poverty and Bluffton is 5.6.** Lima holds a quarter of the twelve districts' school-age children and very nearly half of their poor ones — 1,626 of 3,368. [verified] — same source, and computed here.

**This is the same sorting the corpus has already measured, arriving through a third instrument.** Lima is 34.7 per cent of the county's people, 64.1 per cent of its poor, 46.4 per cent owner-occupied where every township is above 72, and its median house is worth 46 per cent of Shawnee Township's. [verified] — [race](allen-county-race-2023.yml), [income](allen-county-income-and-poverty-2023.yml) and [housing](allen-county-housing-stock-2023.yml). A survey, a model and a finance return describe one shape. [inference]

**Perry is the district that does not fit either story.** 22.1 per cent child poverty on 602 children — the county's second-highest rate — in a township whose median household income the margins would not let this corpus call lower than Lima's. [verified] The district and the township are not the same ground: Perry Local reaches into Lima. [inference]

**These twelve are not the county and their sum is not a county figure.** 117,057 people against the county's 101,685, because five of the districts hold ground in Putnam, Auglaize, Van Wert or Hancock. The 16.5 per cent in the last row is a rate for twelve districts, not for Allen County. [verified]

refusals: This does not establish a rate that can be ranked against another district.

nodes.label: Enrolment in Allen County's twelve school districts, 2010-2023

properties.method: `ENROLL` from the annual survey, read by column name across three column layouts and joined on `NCESID`, which is the `fips_code` these district nodes already carry. [verified] Twelve of twelve matched in all fourteen years. Percentage changes are computed here from the endpoints.
properties.parameter: fall enrolment, by school district

blocks.text: Fall enrolment in every school district holding ground in Allen County, annually for fourteen years. [verified] — [the school finance survey](../../catalog/census-school-system-finances.md).

**The schools are emptying about twice as fast as the county.** The twelve lost 1,872 pupils, 10.4 per cent, over a span in which Allen County's population fell 3.9 per cent to the 2020 census and 5.1 per cent to the 2024 estimate. [verified] — same source, and [the county](../place/allen-county.yml).

**Three districts lost a fifth and one grew.** Lima at −20.7 per cent, Waynesfield-Goshen at −20.0 and Delphos at −20.2; Bluffton is up 8.8 per cent and Allen East has not moved. [verified] — same source. The loss is as concentrated inside the school geography as [the population loss is inside the county](../period/depopulation.yml). [inference]

This is not a measurement of Allen County. Five of these districts hold ground in Putnam, Auglaize, Van Wert or Hancock counties, and the twelve together held 117,057 people in 2023 against the county's 101,685. [verified] — [the poverty file](allen-county-school-district-poverty-2023.yml). A school geography is the first one in this corpus that does not close against the county.

nodes.label: What Allen County's school districts spend and where it comes from, 2023

properties.method: `PPCSTOT` for spending, `PCTLTOT`/`PCTSTOT`/`PCTFTOT` for the shares, and `LOCRPROP` divided by `ENROLL` for property tax per pupil, which the file does not publish and the corpus computes. [verified] Dollars are nominal and this is one year, so nothing here needs a deflator; a level quoted against another year would.
properties.parameter: current spending per pupil, revenue by source, and property tax per pupil
properties.unit: dollars of current spending per pupil, Lima City Schools

blocks.text: Current spending per pupil and the source of every revenue dollar, for the twelve districts holding ground in Allen County, fiscal 2023. [verified] — [the school finance survey](../../catalog/census-school-system-finances.md).

**The district that spends the most per pupil raises the least of it.** Lima City is the county's largest district and its highest spender at $19,321, and 18.4 per cent of its revenue is local where every other district here is between 37.0 and 65.8: 59.2 per cent comes from the state and 22.4 from the federal government. [verified] — same source. That is compensatory aid working the way it is designed to, and it is worth saying plainly rather than as a surprise. [inference]

**Under it is the property tax, and under that is the housing.** Lima raises $3,098 a pupil in property tax where Shawnee raises $7,727 — a ratio of 2.49. The median house in Lima is worth $95,900 and in Shawnee Township $210,200, a ratio of 2.19. [verified] — [the housing stock](allen-county-housing-stock-2023.yml). The two ratios are not the same number and they are close, and a district's tax base is what its houses are worth. [inference]

**High spending per pupil has two different causes here and only one of them is poverty.** The three smallest districts — Waynesfield-Goshen at 472 pupils, Pandora-Gilboa at 521 and Columbus Grove at 756 — are the second, third and fourth highest spenders in the county, on child poverty rates between 6.6 and 10.2 per cent against Lima's 31.7. [verified] — [the poverty file](allen-county-school-district-poverty-2023.yml). A school has costs that do not divide, and a district of five hundred divides them by five hundred. [inference]

refusals: This does not establish that any district is spending well or badly.

nodes.label: Allen County survey sections, 2026

properties.method: Layer 55 returned in one request under the service's 1000-record cap; three zero-area duplicate polygons removed, leaving 404. Areas are the layer's own `SHAPE.area` in square feet. Points were projected onto EPSG:3734 in `crates/ground` and located by crossing-number test; the projection was checked against the county's server, which was asked to project the same seven points itself and named the same seven sections. [verified]
properties.parameter: sections of the rectangular survey, and their area

blocks.text: The rectangular survey grid the county is drawn on: **404 sections across fifteen township-range cells**, T1S–T4S by R4E–R8E, numbered 1 to 36 within each. [verified] — [Allen County GIS REST](../../catalog/allen-county-gis-rest.md), layer 55.

**It closes against the county to within five hundredths of a square mile.** The sections total **406.805 square miles**; the county's own gazetteer record is 402.545 land plus 4.306 water, **406.851**. [verified] — same layer and [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md). Two sources that share no method — the Census Bureau computing from a boundary file, the county from its own survey — and a mean section of 639.7 acres against a nominal 640. This is the corpus's first measurement of the county as *land* rather than as population or jurisdiction. [inference]

**Why the corpus wanted it.** Every question this corpus has failed to close in the last two phases was a question about ground rather than about jurisdiction: where the county jail stood in 1933, where the Lima Tank Depot stood in 1943, whether the Depot is the ground the tank plant occupies now, when the Ford engine plant was built. Land through time is indexed by the survey, because that is how the Recorder's tract books are organized. [inference]
**The ground each of the corpus's own sites stands on**, computed from its coordinates. [verified] — same layer, cross-checked against layer 51 parcel numbers:
The volume names come from the Recorder's own book list. [verified] — [Section Ground book list](../../catalog/allen-county-recorder-section-ground.md).

**The code is written two ways and the two are different strings.** Layer 55 writes the section as the county writes it and a parcel number pads it to two digits, so T4S R6E §1 is `461` in one place and `4601` in the other. **Ninety-six of the 404 sections have a single-digit number**, so a string join between the forms silently drops 24 per cent of the county. [verified] — same layer, checked against every parcel prefix on that ground.

**Two witnesses, twenty-seven agreements.** All 29 nodes in this corpus that carry a point were located twice: by polygon against layer 55, and by the leading digits of the parcel containing the same point. [verified] — same sources.

**One polygon in the layer is two sections.** T3S R8E §5 is 1,282.2 acres on a footprint 1.04 by 2.01 miles, where its thirty-five neighbours average 641 and none is missing. [verified] — same layer. It is one section's number drawn over two sections' ground.

**The Recorder's thirty volumes nearly partition the same grid.** Their section runs expand to 416 slots: 402 sections in exactly one book, T4S R5E §8 in two, T4S R5E §18 in none, and thirteen in a book but not in the county's grid. [verified] — [the book list](../../catalog/allen-county-recorder-section-ground.md).

refusals: The corpus does not assert Bluffton's section.

properties.method: BEA CAEMP25S line 10 for 1969–2000 and CAEMP25N line 10 for 2001–2022, Ohio county files at GeoFIPS 39003. Counts jobs rather than people, so a person holding two jobs is counted twice, and includes farm, government and proprietors. Not comparable with [County Business Patterns](allen-county-manufacturing-employment-1986-2022.yml), which counts private employees only. The comparison with population is a comparison of two programmes. [inference]
properties.parameter: total employment, all jobs, Allen County

blocks.text: Every job in the county, counted the same way for fifty-four years. [verified] — [BEA Regional Economic Accounts](../../catalog/bea-county-employment.md), total employment including proprietors, part-time work, farm and government.

**The county's jobs rose for thirty-one years while its people fell.** Employment went from 56,562 in 1969 to 72,973 in 2000 — a gain of 16,411, or 29 per cent. [verified] — same source. Over the same span the county's population fell from 111,144 to 108,464. [verified] — [the county series](../place/allen-county.yml).

**Jobs peaked twenty years after people did.** The county's population peaked in 1980 and its employment in 2000. [inference] — the two peaks are read from different sources and compared here. Whatever this county lost between 1980 and 2000, it was not work.

**Employment has fallen since, and by less than manufacturing did.** From 69,825 in 2001 to 64,238 in 2022, a loss of 5,587 or 8 per cent, against [manufacturing's](allen-county-manufacturing-employment-1969-2022.yml) fall of 3,182 over the same years. So manufacturing accounts for more than half the county's total job loss since 2001 while being about a seventh of its jobs. [inference] — computed here.

properties.method: Read from a rendered image of a 400-dpi scan; the volume's OCR text layer was used to find the page and not to read the columns. Checked against three arithmetic closures the table supplies and against two columns, 1900 and 1890, that this corpus already held from an unrelated county history. The `value` above is the county total for 1910, the figure this table was fetched for. [verified]
properties.parameter: total resident population by minor civil division, decennial

blocks.text: The county's thirteen minor civil divisions at three censuses — twelve townships and Ottawa, which was Lima. [verified] — [Abstract of the Thirteenth Census, Supplement for Ohio](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md), minor civil divisions table.

Written out: **Allen County held 56,580 people in 1910**, and the twelve townships outside Lima held 26,072 of them. [verified] — same source. That 1910 count was the last gap in the county's decennial record, which now runs unbroken from 1830.

**Three columns and every one closes.** The thirteen divisions sum to the printed county total in 1910, 1900 and 1890 alike, with no residual, and Lima's four wards — 5,150, 8,010, 7,830 and 9,518 — sum to its 30,508. [verified] — computed here from the printed figures.

**Ottawa Township is measured here, by name, and the coextension is datable.** The row reads "Ottawa township, coextensive with Lima city" and gives 15,987 for 1890 against the city's 15,981. Six people, and they are real rather than a misprint: without them the 1890 column does not sum to 40,644. [verified] — same source and the arithmetic above. So Ottawa held six residents outside Lima in 1890 and none at either census after. **The township and the city became exactly the same ground between 1890 and 1900.** [inference] See [what became of German and Ottawa townships](../question/what-became-of-german-and-ottawa-townships.yml).

**German Township is still German**, at all three censuses; it became [American](../place/american-township.yml) in 1918. And Cairo is still **West Cairo**, which is a third source for the older name and the first federal one. [verified] — same source.

**The countryside was shrinking while the county grew.** Five of the twelve townships outside Lima held fewer people in 1910 than in 1890, and eight of them reached their lowest recorded count somewhere between 1900 and 1940. [inference] — computed from this table and [the 1930–1950 series](allen-county-townships-1930-1950.yml). Allen County outside Lima went from 24,663 in 1890 to 28,592 in 1940, a rise of 16 per cent, while the county rose 80 per cent and the city 180. [inference] Everything that happened to this county between 1890 and 1940 happened in one municipality.

properties.method: Read from rendered images of a 300-dpi scan; the volume's own OCR text layer was used as a second reader and its column association across a three-up table was not trusted. Checked against three arithmetic closures the table itself supplies. The 1940 and 1930 columns are on 1950 boundaries where the source could put them there and exclude Lima entirely; the `value` above is the twelve-township sum for 1930, which is the county less the city. [verified]
properties.parameter: total resident population by minor civil division, decennial

blocks.text: Every one of the county's twelve townships at three censuses, and the villages inside them. [verified] — [1950 Census, Number of Inhabitants, Ohio](../../catalog/census-1950-number-of-inhabitants-ohio.md), Table 6, *Population of counties by minor civil divisions: 1930 to 1950*.

Written out, because a table is not prose: in 1930 **Marion Township was the county's largest outside Lima, with 4,959 people, and Perry its smallest at 1,515**; by 1950 Perry held 14,207 and American 25,151, because the city had crossed into both. [verified] — same source.

**Every figure sits inside an arithmetic closure.** The twelve 1950 counts sum to 88,183, which is the county total, and Lima's four parts inside them — 19,270 in American, 17,469 in Bath, 10,895 in Perry, 2,612 in Shawnee — sum to 50,246, which is Lima's own. The 1940 and 1930 columns exclude Lima, as the table's head warns they may, and they miss the county by exactly Lima: 28,592 + 44,711 = 73,303, and 27,132 + 42,287 = 69,419. [verified] — computed here from the printed figures. Three closures, no residual, and every number in the block participates in one.

**The 1940 column is a figure this corpus had already computed and published as an inference.** A phase ago it derived "the county outside Lima in 1940" as 73,303 − 44,711 = 28,592. The twelve townships sum to 28,592. [verified] — same source. A derived figure and a measured one meeting to the person is the best evidence this corpus has yet had that its subtraction is doing what it says.
**So the county outside Lima now begins in 1930, at 27,132**, and rose to 28,592 by 1940 and 37,937 by 1950. [inference] — see [the balance series](allen-county-outside-lima-1890-2020.yml).

**The city is what moved, and the townships mostly did not.** Between 1930 and 1940 seven of the twelve gained and five lost, and the whole balance moved by 1,460 people on a base of 27,132 — five per cent across a decade. [inference] — computed above. Lima gained 2,424 in the same decade. Whatever was happening to this county in the 1930s was happening in one municipality.

**Every one of the twelve is larger now than it was in 1930, and the comparison is sound.** The 1930 and 1940 columns exclude Lima, and so do today's township figures, because the Census treats the city as its own county subdivision — which is why the modern twelve sum to 66,686, exactly the 2020 estimates base less Lima. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), sub-county file, and arithmetic here. Against 1930:

The whole balance is two and a half times its 1930 size while the county is below its 1980 peak and the city has lost a third of itself. [inference] The two that grew sixfold, Shawnee and American, are the two Lima borders on its south and west.

**But 1930 was near the bottom, and the second column is why that matters.** Eight of the twelve reached their lowest recorded count somewhere between 1900 and 1940, and five held fewer people in 1910 than in 1890. [inference] — see [the 1890–1910 divisions](allen-county-townships-1890-1910.yml). Measured from 1890 the twelve still all grew, and six of them grew *less*: Monroe by three per cent rather than by a third, and Amanda by a half rather than by double. A baseline is a choice, and this one was made by which volume happened to arrive first.

**In 1950 the four townships Lima had reached still net out correctly.** Taking the city's parts back off them gives American 5,881, Bath 5,450, Perry 3,312 and Shawnee 3,796, and all twelve then sum to 37,937 — the county less Lima. [verified] — computed here. That is the fourth closure this one table supports, and it is what makes the four affected townships comparable across the century rather than only from 1950.

Also recorded here because no node yet holds it: **Westwood**, an unincorporated place of 2,296 people in 1950, split 1,968 in American and 328 in Shawnee. [verified] — same source. It is not in the corpus's places and this is the only figure it has for it.

nodes.label: Allen County facilities reporting to the Toxics Release Inventory, 1987–2024

properties.method: The Envirofacts facility register for Allen County joined to `tri_reporting_form`, paged at 1,000 rows — 5,372 forms across 49 facility identifiers, reporting years 1987 to 2024. A facility is counted as filing in a year if any form carries that year. One register entry, Heat Treating Tech Inc, has no forms at all. [verified]
properties.parameter: facilities filing a TRI reporting form, Allen County

blocks.text: Every facility in the county that filed for 2024, with the years it has filed and the parent company named against it now. [verified] — [EPA TRI](../../catalog/epa-tri.md).

**Twenty facilities filed for 2024, and the register holds forty-nine.** Twenty-eight of the forty-eight that have ever filed did not file for 2024, and only three of those twenty-eight carry the register's closure flag. [verified] The flag is not a currency test; a filing is. See [a register is not a census](../../decisions/a-register-is-not-a-census.yml).

**Six have filed in all thirty-eight years** — the refinery, Dana, Ford, INEOS, FXI and Chemtrade at Cairo. [verified] Sixteen of the twenty have filed in twenty-seven years or more, and sixteen have no gap between their first year and their last, so the county's reporting industry is old and it has stayed. [verified] The column above is first year and last, not every year between: Procter & Gamble's span is thirty-eight years and its filings are thirty. [verified]

Every parent above is a parent **now** — the register's attributes are current-state and say nothing about who owned any of these facilities earlier. And this is not a list of the county's employers: TRI covers facilities over a size threshold that handle listed chemicals, so it sees a foundry and not a hospital. No employment figure here rests on it. [verified]

properties.method: Sum of the `ballots_cast` field over the 88 Allen County precincts, from a volunteer transcription of the certified returns. Registered voters summed the same way: 67,374. [verified]
properties.parameter: ballots cast, general election

blocks.text: 48,353 ballots cast against 67,374 registered voters at the general election of 3 November 2020 — **71.8 per cent**, summed over the county's 88 precincts. [verified] — [OpenElections](../../catalog/openelections-ohio.md).

**The county figure hides a fifty-two point spread.** Turnout ran from 35.4 per cent in `LIMA 3B` to 87.8 per cent in `DELPHOS 1B`. No other quantity this corpus holds varies that far across the county: population per housing unit runs 2.19 to 2.57, and land area per subdivision by a factor of four. [verified] — same source, precinct by precinct.

Registration itself varies as much and is the more interesting number. Across the 88 precincts registered voters run from 0.28 to 0.84 per resident, and the low end of that range is where the county's [group quarters](../question/who-lives-in-the-county-without-housing.yml) are. [verified] — same source against [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md) block population.

properties.method: Distinct values in the VTD assignment file over the 3,552 blocks whose GEOID begins 39003, cross-checked against the 88 features TIGERweb returns for the county. [verified]
properties.parameter: voting districts

blocks.text: The 88 voting districts into which Allen County's 3,552 census blocks are divided in the 2020 geography, named. [verified] — [2020 Census Block Assignment Files](../../catalog/census-block-assignment-2020.md) for the assignment and [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md), layer 58, for the names, populations, housing units and areas.

**The precinct grid nests inside the civil geography exactly.** Not one of the 88 crosses a county-subdivision line. [verified] — the assignment files crossed with TIGERweb block geography, block by block — the sharp contrast with [the school districts](../jurisdiction/), which cross county and township lines freely. [Lima](../place/lima.yml) holds 23 and [Sugar Creek Township](../place/sugar-creek-township.yml) holds [one](../division/voting-district-sugar-creek-2020.yml); their populations sum to 102,206, which is [the county's own enumeration](allen-county-population-2020-census.yml).

**A second, unrelated pipeline confirms the names.** The 88 the county board of elections used on its certified returns are identical, string for string, to the 88 the Census Bureau publishes. [verified] — [OpenElections](../../catalog/openelections-ohio.md) against TIGERweb. That joins [turnout](allen-county-turnout-2020.yml) and [the vote](allen-county-presidential-vote-2020.yml) to census geography with no crosswalk, and those show the 88 are far from interchangeable.

properties.method: Computed by the Census Bureau from the 2020 TIGER geography, reflecting the corporate boundary as of that geography. [verified]
properties.parameter: land area

blocks.text: Land area of Lima city in the 2020 geography. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), Ohio place file.

This figure is the one in this corpus most exposed to the boundary problem, and it is seeded partly to make that visible. A municipality's land area changes by annexation, so comparing it to a figure from another year without checking the annexations between them compares two different pieces of ground. That check is [boundary-comparability](../../skills/boundary-comparability.md), and the corpus holds no annexation events yet for it to read. This figure describes the **corporation's territory**, not the settlement in the ordinary sense: the Census Bureau tabulates Lima at the corporate boundary of the date, so what the number counts is whatever ground the [City of Lima](../jurisdiction/city-of-lima.yml) had annexed by then. [inference] The node therefore carries a `describes` edge to the jurisdiction as well as to the place. Both are true and they are not the same claim — the place is what the name denotes, and the jurisdiction is what the boundary encloses.

properties.method: Census of Manufactures, taken for the calendar years 1909, 1904 and 1899. Read from rendered images of a 400-dpi scan and checked two ways: the two tables in the volume that report Lima independently agree on 3,607, and the 1909 detail row's components sum to its stated totals both for persons engaged and for wage earners on December 15. Establishments inside the corporate limits only. [verified]
properties.parameter: manufacturing wage earners and value of products, city of Lima

blocks.text: The first measurement of work this corpus has ever held. [verified] — [Abstract of the Thirteenth Census, Supplement for Ohio](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md), statistics of manufactures.

Written out: **Lima had 85 manufacturing establishments in 1909 employing 3,607 wage earners on average, against 2,733 in 1904 and 1,980 in 1899.** [verified] — same source, the comparative city table and the detail table for cities of 10,000 to 50,000 inhabitants, which agree on 3,607.

**The city's workforce grew 82 per cent in a decade and its output grew 25.** [inference] — computed here. Value per wage earner fell from $3,143 in 1899 to $1,766 in 1904 and recovered only to $2,150 by 1909. Something in Lima's industry became much less productive per head between 1899 and 1904 and had not recovered by 1909.

**Thirty per cent of the wage earners were women** — 1,082 of 3,607 — and 51 were under sixteen. [verified] — same source. The two industries the volume names as Lima's leading ones are **"tobacco manufactures and locomotives"**, which is a workforce of cigar makers and a workforce of machinists in one city. [verified] — same source. See [the locomotive works](../site/lima-locomotive-works-plant.yml).
**Lima was in the group of Ohio cities with products valued between $5,000,000 and $10,000,000**, of thirty-seven cities over 10,000 people. [verified] — same source.

properties.method: Read from Table 5 of a 300-dpi bitonal scan with no text layer, by rendering the page and reading the block directly rather than by trusting optical character recognition, which misread it. Checked against the eleven differences and eleven percentages the table prints beside the counts, and against two figures the corpus already held from county histories. The `value` above is this series' last and largest term, not the city's peak, which is 1970. [verified]
properties.parameter: total resident population, decennial

blocks.text: Every decennial count for [Lima](../place/lima.yml) from the city's first appearance in the census to 1960. [verified] — [1960 Census, Number of Inhabitants, Ohio](../../catalog/census-1960-number-of-inhabitants-ohio.md), Table 5, *Population of incorporated places of 10,000 or more from earliest census to 1960*.

Written out, because a table is not prose and this corpus publishes prose: **Lima held 7,567 people in 1880, 21,723 in 1900, 41,326 in 1920, 42,287 in 1930, 44,711 in 1940, 50,246 in 1950 and 51,037 in 1960.** [verified] — same source. The four counts before those, 757 in 1850 through 15,981 in 1890, are in the same block of the same table.

**Lima peaked at the 1970 census.** The city rose at every one of the twelve counts above and reached [53,734 in 1970](lima-population-1970-1990.yml), then fell at every count since. The corpus has carried the caveat that 1970 was the earliest federal figure it held and therefore a lower bound rather than a peak, and has said so on the public site and in two tests. It was the peak. [verified] — this source for 1850–1960 and [the 1990 Census volume](../../catalog/census-cph-2-37-ohio.md) for 1970. The claim is about census years: a city can rise and fall inside a decade unobserved, and decennial data cannot speak to that for Lima or anywhere else.

**The last decade before the peak is the flattest.** Lima gained 791 people in the 1950s, 1.6% — its smallest decennial gain in a hundred and ten years, and a tenth of the 1940s' rate. The city did not turn at 1970 so much as arrive there slowing. [inference] — computed from the series above. What happened between 1960 and 1970 to produce a further 2,697 is not established here.

**It corrects the 1920 figure this corpus has published since the oil phase.** The corpus held 41,306, from [Rusler's 1921 history](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md), which prints it twice. The Census gives **41,326**, and both neighbouring rows of Table 5 require that value. Twenty people, and the difference matters less than which of the two sources was believed: the 1921 figure was marked here as [a single witness read once](../../decisions/a-single-witness-read-once.yml), and it is the one that broke. The two figures the same three histories supplied that this table can also test — 7,567 in 1880 and 21,723 in 1900 — match the Census to the person. [verified] — both sources.

properties.method: Three county histories' compilations of published census returns, one figure from each. The 1900 and 1920 figures are for Ottawa Township, which both sources state was coextensive with the city. [verified] The value above is **superseded**: the Census gives 41,326 for the same date and this node keeps 41,306 because its subject is what the histories printed. For Lima's 1920 population, cite [the federal series](lima-population-1850-1960.yml). [verified]
properties.parameter: total resident population, decennial, as three county histories printed it

blocks.text: The city's counts across the oil boom and the forty years after it. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md) for 1880, [History of Allen County, 1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md) for 1900, and [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md) for 1920.

Written out, because a table is not prose and this corpus publishes prose: these three histories put **7,567 people in 1880, 21,723 in 1900 and 41,306 in 1920** in Lima. [verified] — the three sources above, one figure each. **The Census Bureau confirms the first two to the person and contradicts the third**, giving 41,326 for 1920. [verified] — [1960 Census, Number of Inhabitants, Ohio](../../catalog/census-1960-number-of-inhabitants-ohio.md), Table 5; see [the federal series](lima-population-1850-1960.yml), which supersedes this node as a measure and leaves it standing as the record of what the histories printed.

**The corpus believed the wrong one of the two, and had already said which it would be.** The 1920 figure was marked here as [a single witness read once](../../decisions/a-single-witness-read-once.yml) — Rusler's is the only scan of that book the corpus holds, and no second source could be brought against it. The Census table settles it not by being federal but by showing its work: each count is printed beside its increase over the preceding census, and 30,508 + 10,818 = 41,326 while 41,326 + 961 = 42,287. Rusler's 41,306 fails both, and the same passage of Rusler subtracts its own list of incorporated places from the county total and lands a thousand out. [verified] — same sources. No third witness was consulted, and none is needed for arithmetic. [inference]

**These are the corpus's first Lima figures earlier than 2000.** Lima nearly tripled between 1880 and 1900 and nearly doubled again by 1920 — **a fivefold rise in forty years**, which is the demographic shape of [the oil strike](../event/lima-oil-strike.yml). [inference]

**The 1900 and 1920 figures are township figures and that is not an error here.** [Ottawa Township](../question/what-became-of-german-and-ottawa-townships.yml) was coextensive with the city — the 1906 table says so in the row label, twenty-one years before the 1921 volume says it in prose. [verified] — same sources. So the township count is the city count, and the corpus can now date that coextension to 1900 or earlier rather than to 1921.

**All three are compilations, not census publications**, and this node asked for the thing that would test them: "a place-level decennial series from the Census Bureau would replace all three." It arrived, and it replaced one. Two of the three compilations were right to the person across eighty years, which is a better result for county histories than this corpus expected and is worth recording as such. [inference] The 1880 figure comes from a table whose county total the corpus has already found to disagree with the 1906 volume by sixteen people at 1850 — see [the county series](allen-county-population-1830-1900.yml), where the same question is open and no federal series has yet reached it.

properties.method: Read from the places table of the 1990 Ohio CPH-2 volume. The `value` above is the series maximum and also its first term, which made it a lower bound on the city's peak until the 1960 volume supplied the twelve counts before it. It is the peak. [verified]
properties.parameter: total resident population, decennial

blocks.text: **53,734 in 1970, 47,827 in 1980 and 45,549 in 1990.** [verified] — [1990 Census, Population and Housing Unit Counts, Ohio](../../catalog/census-cph-2-37-ohio.md), which marks the 1980 figure `r` for revised. Housing units ran 18,443, 19,096 and 18,666 across the same three counts.

**This locates a peak the corpus said one phase ago it could not see.** Reading only [7,567 in 1880, 21,723 in 1900 and 41,306 in 1920](lima-population-1880-1920.yml) against 40,307 in 2000 — the 1920 figure has since been corrected to 41,326 — the corpus concluded that "eighty years net to roughly nothing" and the peak was somewhere inside them. It is: **the city was 53,734 in 1970**, thirty per cent above its 1920 count and half again what it is today. The rise and the fall were both real and the corpus had a chord across them. [inference]

**And 1970 is the peak, not a lower bound on it.** The four counts this node could not see are 42,287 (1930), 44,711 (1940), 50,246 (1950) and 51,037 (1960), every one of them below 53,734 and each above the one before. [verified] — [1960 Census, Number of Inhabitants, Ohio](../../catalog/census-1960-number-of-inhabitants-ohio.md); see [the federal series](lima-population-1850-1960.yml). The caveat this node wrote against its own figure is answered by evidence rather than dropped.

So Lima's series, at the census years the corpus holds: 7,567 (1880) · 21,723 (1900) · 41,326 (1920) · 51,037 (1960) · **53,734 (1970)** · 47,827 (1980) · 45,549 (1990) · 40,307 (2000) · 35,579 (2020). Between 1970 and 2020 the city lost 18,155 people, **33.8 per cent of itself**, while [the county](allen-county-population-1940-1990.yml) lost 8,927, or 8.0 per cent. Lima's loss is twice the county's, which means the rest of Allen County **gained 9,228** over the same fifty years. [inference] — computed from the two series. That is a different story from the one the corpus has been telling from four years of recent data, where the ring shrinks too: over the long run the ring grew while the city emptied, and only lately have both been falling.

**And the boundary moved underneath these counts.** Between 1980 and 1990 Lima annexed ground from American, Bath and Shawnee townships. [verified] — same source, Geographic Change Notes. So the fall from 47,827 to 45,549 happened while the corporation was getting larger, which makes it an understatement of the decline inside the old boundary. [inference] This is the first annexation event this corpus has ever held, against a [comparability caveat](../../skills/boundary-comparability.md) it has carried since genesis.

nodes.label: Lima refinery operator and crude capacity, 1994–2026

properties.method: Thirty-one annual reports, `SITE` LIMA and `STATE_NAME` Ohio, taking the `TOTAL OPERABLE CAPACITY` row for barrels per calendar day. Every report from 1994 to 2026 except 1996 and 1998, which are not archived. Twelve are shown; every figure above is from all thirty-one. [verified]
properties.parameter: Atmospheric Crude Distillation Capacity (barrels per calendar day), Total Operable

blocks.text: Who filed for [the refinery](../site/lima-refinery.yml) and how much crude it could run, as of 1 January of each report year. [verified] — [EIA Refinery Capacity Report](../../catalog/eia-refinery-capacity.md).

**The refinery is larger than it has ever been in this series, and by a quarter.** 145,000 barrels per calendar day in 1994 against 183,000 in 2026 — up 38,000, or 26 per cent — across the decades in which the county's [manufacturing employment](allen-county-manufacturing-employment-1969-2022.yml) fell by more than half. [verified] — [EIA Refinery Capacity Report](../../catalog/eia-refinery-capacity.md). The low is the first year and the high is the last four.

**It is the largest refinery in Ohio.** 183,000 against 172,800 and 150,800 at Toledo and 100,000 at Canton — 30 per cent of the state's 606,600 barrels per calendar day, and 36th of the 124 refineries in the United States. [verified] — [EIA Refinery Capacity Report](../../catalog/eia-refinery-capacity.md), the 2026 report.

**The trough is 146,120 in 2007, the last Premcor year, and the recovery is the Husky years.** Capacity fell 15,380 from the 161,500 it held through 2003, and has risen 36,880 since. [verified] — [EIA Refinery Capacity Report](../../catalog/eia-refinery-capacity.md).

This series dates changes of filing entity and not changes of ownership, and the corporation column does not exist before the 2010 report. [verified] The 1996 and 1998 reports are not published, and the BP-to-Clark change falls in the second gap.

nodes.label: Ohio House District 4 land area, 2020 geography

properties.method: Computed by the Census Bureau from the 2020 TIGER geography. [verified]
properties.parameter: land area

blocks.text: Land area of [Ohio House District 4](../division/ohio-house-district-4-2020.yml) in the 2020 geography. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), state legislative lower chamber file.

properties.mouth: 41.2875489, -84.3557802, in Defiance County. Joins the Maumee River. [inference]

blocks.text: The river that collects Allen County's drainage and carries it north to the Maumee at Defiance. [inference] It rises at 40.6669957, -83.8938286 and discharges at 41.2875489, -84.3557802 in Defiance County. [verified] — [USGS GNIS](../../catalog/gnis-domestic-names-ohio.md), feature 1065901. It gives its name to Auglaize Township in the county's south — one of the twelve townships recorded in the [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md). [verified]

Its significance to this corpus is directional. Allen County drains north to Lake Erie rather than south to the Ohio, and the Auglaize is the channel by which it does so. That single fact organizes a great deal: the county's swamp history, its canal, and the basin its water quality is accounted for in are all consequences of being on the Lake Erie side of the divide. [inference]

**It rises in this county**, at 40.6669957, -83.8938286 in Auglaize township — the township named after it. [verified] — [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md), point-in-polygon. So Allen County is not merely drained by the Auglaize; it is the ground the river starts on. See [where the Auglaize rises](../question/where-the-auglaize-rises.yml). Its whole subbasin, `04100007`, is one of the seven that make up the Maumee's drainage; the four blocks of that township on [the Scioto side](scioto-river-basin.yml) drain the opposite way, so the divide and this river's source are in the same township. [verified] — [USGS Watershed Boundary Dataset](../../catalog/usgs-watershed-boundary.md).

The glacially-formed wetland that covered much of northwest Ohio until it was drained in the second half of the nineteenth century. Allen County lies at its southern margin, and its northern townships were within it. [inference]

It belongs in this corpus because it is the negative space in the county's settlement history: the swamp is why this part of Ohio was settled late relative to the south of the state, why the drainage tile and ditch systems are as extensive as they are, and why the land is as productive as it is now that they exist. [inference] It is also a feature that no longer exists as such, which is a thing this class must be able to hold — a natural-feature node is not required to describe present ground.

**It has no GNIS record.** No feature named "Great Black Swamp" appears anywhere in the 17,921 rows of the Ohio file. [verified] — [USGS GNIS](../../catalog/gnis-domestic-names-ohio.md). That is not because the gazetteer omits vanished features: it carries 56 `Swamp` features in Ohio and marks the drained ones "(historical)" in the name itself. The likelier reason is that GNIS names features with a locatable point, and a wetland that covered much of northwest Ohio across a dozen counties does not have one. [inference] So this node keeps no identifier, and the absence is a fact about how gazetteers work rather than a gap in the retrieval.

nodes.label: Hog Creek

properties.mouth: 40.7708852, -83.9557761 — the head of the Ottawa River.

blocks.text: The stream that, joining Little Hog Creek, forms the Ottawa River. Its mouth is at 40.7708852, -83.9557761 and it rises at 40.7139417, -83.7221552 in the county's east. [verified] — [USGS GNIS](../../catalog/gnis-domestic-names-ohio.md), feature 1066038.

That mouth coordinate is the whole point of this node. It is identical, to seven decimal places, to the source coordinate GNIS gives for [the Ottawa River](ottawa-river.yml) and to the mouth GNIS gives for [Little Hog Creek](little-hog-creek.yml). Three records written by one authority place the same point at the end of two creeks and the head of a river, which is what a confluence looks like in a names file. [verified] — same source. Every `flows-into` edge in this corpus before this one was asserted from general knowledge.

Hog Creek is also the older name of the whole watercourse, and the corpus's [Ottawa River](ottawa-river.yml) node records the name surviving in local usage. GNIS is consistent with that and does not establish it: what the file shows is that the name attaches today to the upper tributary only. [inference]
Ohio has a second Hog Creek, in Champaign County — feature 1041646, and unrelated. [verified] — same source.

refusals: GNIS is consistent with that and does not establish it: what the file shows is that the name attaches today to the upper tributary only.

properties.mouth: 40.7708852, -83.9557761 — the head of the Ottawa River, shared with Hog Creek.

blocks.text: The second of the two creeks that meet to form the Ottawa River. Its mouth is at 40.7708852, -83.9557761 and it rises at 40.722274, -83.8979957. [verified] — [USGS GNIS](../../catalog/gnis-domestic-names-ohio.md), feature 1042627.
Its mouth coordinate is byte-identical to [Hog Creek](hog-creek.yml)'s mouth and to [the Ottawa River](ottawa-river.yml)'s source. [verified] — same source.

nodes.label: Maumee River Basin

blocks.text: The drainage basin that **almost all** of Allen County lies within — the largest watershed draining to the Great Lakes, discharging to Lake Erie at Toledo. 3,548 of the county's 3,552 census blocks and 102,107 of its 102,206 people are in the Great Lakes Region, across three subbasins: Auglaize `04100007` holds 3,200 blocks and Blanchard `04100008` holds 348. [verified] — [USGS Watershed Boundary Dataset](../../catalog/usgs-watershed-boundary.md), by block composition.

**This basin is not a hydrologic unit, which is why no code is recorded here.** The Maumee's drainage is seven subbasins — `04100003` St. Joseph through `04100009` Lower Maumee — and the next unit up that contains them, `041000` Western Lake Erie, also contains six that are nothing to do with the Maumee: Raisin, Sandusky, Huron and three more. [verified] — [USGS Watershed Boundary Dataset](../../catalog/usgs-watershed-boundary.md). So the honest answer to this node's genesis question about its own HUC is that it does not have one, and writing `0410` here would have named a basin four times too large.

**Its other genesis question is answered against it.** Part of Allen County does drain to the Ohio River: four blocks in [Auglaize Township](../place/auglaize-township.yml), 99 people, sit in [the Scioto basin](scioto-river-basin.yml). [verified] — same source. The corpus asserted the Lake Erie side for the whole county from genesis and flagged the southern townships as unchecked; checking them cost one query and moved 99 people to the Gulf of Mexico.

refusals: It is included at genesis for that reason: without it the trace from the Ottawa River runs to the Auglaize and stops in mid-air, and the corpus cannot say where its water goes.

properties.source: 41.0828261, -85.1321928 — the St. Joseph and St. Marys confluence, Fort Wayne.

blocks.text: The river Allen County's water reaches last before Lake Erie. It rises at 41.0828261, -85.1321928 — the confluence of the St. Joseph and St. Marys at Fort Wayne, Indiana — and discharges at 41.6994922, -83.4599325 at Toledo. [verified] — [USGS GNIS](../../catalog/gnis-domestic-names-ohio.md), feature 1084017.

The discharge coordinate is what makes the corpus's Lake Erie claim more than an assertion. Allen County's water leaves the county by the Auglaize, and the river the Auglaize joins ends at Toledo on Lake Erie rather than anywhere on the Ohio. [inference] — the coordinate is verified; that the Auglaize joins *this* river at Defiance is not established by a names file.

nodes.label: Ottawa River

properties.huc_code: 0410000703 Upper Ottawa River, 0410000705 Lower Ottawa River
properties.mouth: 40.9950509, -84.2413355, in Putnam County. Joins the Auglaize River. [inference]
properties.source: 40.7708852, -83.9557761 — the Hog Creek / Little Hog Creek confluence.

blocks.text: The stream that runs through Lima, and the county's principal watercourse. It begins at 40.7708852, -83.9557761 and discharges at 40.9950509, -84.2413355 in Putnam County. [verified] — [USGS GNIS](../../catalog/gnis-domestic-names-ohio.md), feature 1070882. That the discharge point is on the Auglaize remains [inference]: a names file gives a coordinate and never says what is at it.

**It does not begin east of the city; it begins at a confluence.** Its source coordinate is identical to the mouths GNIS records for [Hog Creek](hog-creek.yml) and [Little Hog Creek](little-hog-creek.yml), so the river's head is where those two creeks meet. [verified] — same source. The older name of the whole watercourse was Hog Creek, and the name now attaches to the upper tributary; GNIS is consistent with that and does not establish it. [inference]

**Allen County's own rows do not contain it.** GNIS files a stream under the county of its mouth, so the county's principal river is filed under Putnam and is absent from the 113 features listed for Allen. [verified] — same source.

The present name is shared with a larger, unrelated Ottawa River near Toledo — feature 1066879 in Lucas County against this one's 1070882. [verified] — same source. The collision is now resolvable by identifier rather than by care.

**Where its water goes is now sourced rather than assumed.** The river has two watersheds of its own — `0410000703` Upper Ottawa River and `0410000705` Lower Ottawa River — and both sit inside subbasin `04100007`, which is named for and drains to the [Auglaize](auglaize-river.yml). [verified] — [USGS Watershed Boundary Dataset](../../catalog/usgs-watershed-boundary.md). That settles the basin and not the confluence: the WBD says this water reaches the Auglaize and never says which stream it joins first. Those two Ottawa watersheds hold 47,578 of the county's people between them, 47 per cent, which is what it means to call this the county's principal watercourse.

Being the watercourse Lima grew on, it was also the receiving water for the refinery and the works — the environmental history of this stream and the industrial history of the city are the same subject. [inference]

refusals: The older name of the whole watercourse was Hog Creek, and the name now attaches to the upper tributary; GNIS is consistent with that and does not establish it.

blocks.text: The drainage basin of the Scioto River, which discharges to the Ohio River at Portsmouth and through it to the Gulf of Mexico. **Ninety-nine people in Allen County live in it.** [verified] — [USGS Watershed Boundary Dataset](../../catalog/usgs-watershed-boundary.md).

Four census blocks in [Auglaize Township](../place/auglaize-township.yml), at the county's south-east corner between 40.6487 and 40.7104 north, fall in hydrologic unit `05060001` — the Upper Scioto subbasin of the Ohio Region. Every other block in the county, 3,548 of 3,552, is in the Great Lakes Region and drains to [the Maumee basin](maumee-river-basin.yml). [verified] — same source, by block composition; all 3,552 blocks land in exactly one subbasin and their populations sum to the county's own enumeration of 102,206.

The subwatershed those four blocks sit in is `050600010101`, **Cottonwood Ditch** — a headwater of the Scioto rising in Auglaize Township. [verified] — same source. It is the only named feature on the Ohio River side of the divide in this county.

The county's chief fiscal officer and its assessor of real property. The auditor is chosen "quadrennially in each county" and holds office "for four years", and the term begins "on the second Monday in March next after his election". [verified] — [Ohio Revised Code §319.01](../../catalog/ohio-revised-code.md).

**It is the only county office here whose term does not begin in January**, and the roster bears the statute out: the present term runs 13 March 2023 to 7 March 2027, and 13 March 2023 was the second Monday of that month. [verified] — [Ohio county elected officials lookup](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md).

The office keeps the real-property records and financial statements, licenses dogs, regulates weights and measures, administers unclaimed funds and runs the county land bank. It also administers **current agricultural use valuation**, which taxes farmland on what it yields rather than what it would sell for. [verified] — [the county's site](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md). That last function is a live one here: the county was 92.5 per cent farmland in 1910 and the corpus has no later measurement of how much it is now. See [the county's farms](../measure/allen-county-farms-1900-1910.yml).

properties.selection_method: countywide election, terms staggered by statute

blocks.text: The county's governing body, and the first multi-seat office in this corpus. Three commissioners hold it at once, elected countywide to four-year terms. [verified] — [Ohio Revised Code §305.01](../../catalog/ohio-revised-code.md): "The board of county commissioners shall consist of three persons."

**The three seats are distinguished by the day their terms begin, one day apart.** One seat runs from the first day of January after its election; of the two elected together, one begins on "the second day of January next after his election" and the other on "the third day". [verified] — same source. Allen County's roster shows exactly that: 1 January 2023, 2 January 2025 and 3 January 2025. [verified] — [Ohio county elected officials lookup](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md). The dates were read before the statute was, and the statute predicted them.
The board meets in general session every Tuesday and Thursday. [verified] — [the county's site](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md).

nodes.label: Clerk of Courts of Allen County

blocks.text: The custodian of the record for the county's courts. The office handles the "filing, preservation, retrieval and public dissemination of all documents and records" for the Court of Common Pleas, its Domestic Relations Division, and the Third District Court of Appeals. [verified] — [the clerk of courts' site](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md).

**It serves a court that is not the county's own.** The [Third District Court of Appeals](../jurisdiction/third-district-court-of-appeals.yml) hears appeals from seventeen Ohio counties, and its records are kept here — so the office is the point where a county officer does work for a regional court. [verified] — [the court's own site](../../catalog/third-district-court-of-appeals.md), which names the seventeen. That count was an [inference] on this node for one phase and is now read from the source.

The office also runs an Auto Title Division, which is where a motor vehicle title is issued in this county. [verified] — same source. That is the office's highest-volume public function and has nothing to do with courts. [inference]

The present term runs 6 January 2025 to 31 December 2028, four years. [verified] — [Ohio county elected officials lookup](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md). The holder of this office is barred by statute from also being [county engineer](allen-county-engineer.yml). [verified] — [Ohio Revised Code §315.02](../../catalog/ohio-revised-code.md).

The courts this office serves now have nodes: [the Court of Common Pleas](../jurisdiction/allen-county-court-of-common-pleas.yml), [the Lima Municipal Court](../jurisdiction/lima-municipal-court.yml) — whose territory is the whole county despite its name — and [the Third District](../jurisdiction/third-district-court-of-appeals.yml). [verified] — the sources named above.

The office that determines cause of death where a death is violent, suspicious, or otherwise not plainly natural. Ohio requires its holder to be a physician: "a physician who is licensed under Chapter 4731. of the Revised Code to practice medicine and surgery or osteopathic medicine and surgery, and who is in good standing in the person's profession", and to have held that licence for at least two years before election. [verified] — [Ohio Revised Code §313.02](../../catalog/ohio-revised-code.md).

That requirement makes the coroner the only county office here whose candidate pool is fixed by a profession rather than by residence, and in a county of about a hundred thousand people the pool is small. [inference]

The office investigates deaths from crime, violence, suicide or suspicious circumstances, performs autopsies and toxicology, determines blood alcohol in fatal crashes, and testifies as an expert witness. [verified] — [the county's site](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md).
The present term runs 6 January 2025 to 31 December 2028, four years. [verified] — [Ohio county elected officials lookup](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md).

The office responsible for the county's roads and bridges, and the only county office whose holder must be qualified twice over. Ohio requires the county engineer to be "a registered professional engineer and a registered surveyor, licensed to practice in this state". [verified] — [Ohio Revised Code §315.02](../../catalog/ohio-revised-code.md).

**The same section bars four of this county's other elected officers from holding it**: "No person holding the office of clerk of the court of common pleas, sheriff, county treasurer, or county recorder is eligible to hold the office of county engineer." [verified] — same source. Every one of those four offices exists in this corpus, which is what makes the clause readable as a graph constraint rather than a sentence.

**What the office maintains, in its own numbers:** 353 miles of county road, 550 miles of township road, 371 bridges and over 1,400 culverts. [verified] — [the county engineer's site](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md). Nine hundred miles of road is the physical form of a county that is mostly not city; see [the townships](../place/allen-county.yml).

The present term runs 6 January 2025 to 31 December 2028, four years. [verified] — [Ohio county elected officials lookup](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md); the length is arithmetic on those dates and not a statute this corpus has read. [inference]

The county's prosecutor, and also its lawyer. The office runs five divisions: Criminal, which prosecutes "hundreds of felony cases annually"; Juvenile; Civil, which "provides legal representation to county officials, townships, and agencies"; Children Services; and Victim Assistance. [verified] — [the county prosecutor's site](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md).

**The civil division is the part that makes this office structural rather than adversarial.** It is counsel to the other eight elected county offices and to all twelve [township governments](../jurisdiction/amanda-township.yml), which means one elected officer advises every other one. [inference]
The present term runs 6 January 2025 to 31 December 2028, four years. [verified] — [Ohio county elected officials lookup](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md).

The office that keeps the county's record of who owns what. It maintains deeds, mortgages and liens, and also records property lines, maps, plats, powers of attorney and military discharges, indexing them so that a chain of ownership and any encumbrance on it can be established. [verified] — [the county recorder's site](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md).

**It is the office that would answer several of this corpus's open questions.** The 151 acres of [the Hover farm](../person/james-a-hover.yml) contracted to [the Solar Refining Company](../organization/solar-refining-company.yml) in 1886, and the ownership chain from Solar to [the refinery's](../site/lima-refinery.yml) present operator, are both recorded here and in no source this corpus holds. [inference]

The present term runs 6 January 2025 to 31 December 2028, four years, and the present holder's service began in January 2005. [verified] — [Ohio county elected officials lookup](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md) and [the recorder's site](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md).
The holder of this office is barred by statute from also being [county engineer](allen-county-engineer.yml). [verified] — [Ohio Revised Code §315.02](../../catalog/ohio-revised-code.md).

The county's elected chief law enforcement officer, one of the separately elected county offices Ohio law establishes for every county. [inference] The sheriff runs the county jail and serves process in addition to policing the unincorporated area.

**Its line of holders is complete.** Thirty-nine tenures run from Henry Lippencott in 1831 to the present holder, with every term's end year equal to the next term's start year and no holder recorded twice in succession. [verified] — [Allen County Sheriff's Office past-sheriffs roster](../../catalog/acso-past-sheriffs.md); the continuity was checked across all thirty-nine entries rather than assumed, and is now checked by [`crates/succession`](../../../crates/succession/) on every test run rather than by hand.

Two features of the line are worth knowing before computing on it. John Keller held the office in 1835–1839 and again in 1843–1845, so the corpus carries one person and two tenures with `term_number` set. [verified] And the roster's ranges are year-only, so consecutive tenures share a boundary year; read as day-precision intervals every adjacent pair overlaps, and none of those overlaps is real.

**A second source now confirms the present holder and dates his term to the day.** Matthew B. Treglia holds a term running 6 January 2025 to 31 December 2028 — four years, which is what fixes `term_length` on this office. [verified] — [Ohio county elected officials lookup](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md). The sheriff's own roster and the elections roster agree on the name and answer different questions: the first gives the start of service in 2017, the second the bounds of the current term.

This office is one of nine elected county offices, and the only one whose line of holders this corpus can trace. For the other eight it holds the present term and nothing before it. [verified] — same source; see [the county government](../jurisdiction/allen-county-government.yml).

The office that collects the county's taxes and holds its money. It collects real estate and manufactured home taxes, bills the county's sanitary sewers, administers delinquent accounts, and invests county funds.
