[verified] — [the county treasurer's site](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md).

**It collects what [the auditor](allen-county-auditor.yml) assesses**, which is why the two offices are separate and separately elected: the body that values property does not receive the money. [inference]

**Its term dates are the only irregular ones on the county roster**, running 1 September 2025 to 2 September 2029 where the other seven single-seat offices run 6 January 2025 to 31 December 2028. [verified] — [Ohio county elected officials lookup](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md).

**The treasurer's own site does not print the holder's name in text**, only in an image. The name in this corpus comes from the elections roster. [verified] — same source. That is worth saying because it is the one county office whose own publication would not have answered the question.
The holder of this office is barred by statute from also being [county engineer](allen-county-engineer.yml). [verified] — [Ohio Revised Code §315.02](../../catalog/ohio-revised-code.md).

nodes.label: Judge of the Court of Common Pleas, Domestic Relations Division

blocks.text: The single-seat bench for divorce, dissolution, custody and support in Allen County. [inference] — the division's subject-matter is not established by any source this corpus holds; the name is.

One judge holds it, on a six-year term running 1 January 2023 to 31 December 2028. [verified] — [Ohio county elected officials lookup](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md); the length is arithmetic on those dates. [inference]

The [court's rules](../../catalog/allen-county-common-pleas-local-rules.md) name a Domestic Relations Division among the five divisions they govern, and the county maintains a separate site for it. [verified] — same rules and [the county's court-system page](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md).

nodes.label: Judge of the Court of Common Pleas, General Division

blocks.text: **Two judges hold it at once**, which makes it the second multi-seat office in this corpus after [the board of commissioners](allen-county-board-of-commissioners.yml). [verified] — [Ohio county elected officials lookup](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md), which assigns two of the county's four common pleas judges to the General Division.

**Its terms run six years and the two seats are offset by two.** One runs 1 January 2025 to 31 December 2030 and the other 9 February 2023 to 8 February 2029. [verified] — same source; the length is arithmetic on those dates. [inference] So the two seats never fall vacant together, the same effect the [commissioners'](allen-county-board-of-commissioners.yml) statute achieves by staggering, reached here by a different means. [inference]

The [court's own rules](../../catalog/allen-county-common-pleas-local-rules.md) call this the "General Trial Division" and name a separate Criminal Division beside it, which has no elected judge of its own. [verified]

nodes.label: Judge of the Court of Common Pleas, Probate Division

blocks.text: The single-seat bench for wills, estates, guardianships and — on the county's own arrangement of its courts — juvenile matters, which are administered together here. [verified] — [the county's court-system page](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md), which lists Probate Court and Juvenile Court as separate sites; [inference] that one elected judge covers both follows from the roster naming only a Probate Division seat among the four.
One judge holds it, on a six-year term running 9 February 2021 to 8 February 2027. [verified] — [Ohio county elected officials lookup](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md).

**Its term expires second-soonest of any seat in this corpus**, on 8 February 2027, behind only [the offset commissioner's](allen-county-board-of-commissioners.yml) 31 December 2026. [inference] — computed here across the seventeen seats whose current term dates the corpus holds.

The [court's rules](../../catalog/allen-county-common-pleas-local-rules.md) govern practice in the Probate Division and the Juvenile Division "where applicable", treating them as two divisions where the ballot treats them as one seat. [verified]

nodes.label: Judge of the Lima Municipal Court

blocks.text: Two judges hold this office at once, elected by the whole county rather than by the city the court is named for. [verified] — [Ohio county elected officials lookup](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md), which lists them among Allen County's elected officials; and [Ohio Revised Code §1901.02](../../catalog/ohio-revised-code.md): "The Lima municipal court has jurisdiction within Allen county."

**Its terms run six years and the two seats are offset by two.** One runs 1 January 2022 to 31 December 2027 and the other 1 January 2024 to 31 December 2029. [verified] — same roster; the length is arithmetic on those dates. [inference] Both begin in January, unlike the [common pleas general division](judge-of-the-common-pleas-general-division.yml), whose two seats begin in different months.

A municipal judge here serves six years and an [administrative county officer](allen-county-auditor.yml) four. That holds across every office in this corpus that states a term length — four judicial offices at six years and nine elected administrative ones at four, thirteen offices and seventeen seats. [inference] — computed here. It rests on one county's roster and is a pattern in the data, not a rule this corpus has read anywhere. The [mayor of Lima](mayor-of-lima.yml) is the one office node with no term length at all, and is excluded from the count for that reason.

nodes.label: Judge of the Third District Court of Appeals

blocks.text: The appellate bench that hears Allen County's appeals, and the office this corpus declined to write one phase ago. Four judges hold it, on six-year terms. [verified] — [Ohio county elected officials lookup](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md).

**All four terms begin in February and no two expire in the same year**, running to 8 February 2027, 8 February 2029, 10 February 2029 and 8 February 2031. [verified] — same source. Two expire two days apart in 2029, which is the same device the [board of commissioners](allen-county-board-of-commissioners.yml) uses to keep seats distinguishable. [inference]
It is a judicial office at six years, like every other judicial office here, against four for the county's elected administrators. [inference] — computed across this corpus.

The elected chief executive of the [City of Lima](../jurisdiction/city-of-lima.yml), a single seat filled at a citywide election for a four-year term. [verified] — [the elected officials roster](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md).

It was seeded with no holders, on the reasoning that an office node is meaningful without its tenures — it records that the position exists, on what terms, and within which jurisdiction — while a tenure without an office would have nothing to attach to. It stayed empty for a hundred commits, and not because the source was missing: the roster names this mayor, and the corpus had read one precinct's page of it. **It now has a holder**, and that holder is [Sharetta T. Smith](../tenure/mayor-2025-sharetta-t-smith.yml), 2025 to 2029. [verified]

**The term dates are now evidence where there was none.** This office's year begins 1 December, the city council's on 2 and 5 January, and every office of Delphos on 1 January. [verified] — same source. One city keeping three calendars at once is what a charter looks like from outside it. [inference]

nodes.label: Member of the Ohio House of Representatives, 78th District

blocks.text: Allen County's seat in the lower chamber of the Ohio General Assembly, under the map adopted 29 September 2023. [verified] — [Ohio county elected officials lookup](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md).

**Its term is two years — the shortest of any office in this corpus.** The present term runs 1 January 2025 to 31 December 2026. [verified] — same source; the length is arithmetic on those dates. [inference] Every other office here runs four years or six, so this is the one seat whose holder faces the voters in every even year.

nodes.label: Member of the Ohio Senate, 12th District

blocks.text: Allen County's seat in the upper chamber of the Ohio General Assembly, under the map adopted 29 September 2023. [verified] — [Ohio county elected officials lookup](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md).

Its term is four years, running 1 January 2025 to 31 December 2028. [verified] — same source; the length is arithmetic on those dates. [inference] So this county's two legislators serve terms of different lengths, and its senator outlasts two of its representative's.

**This is not a seat Allen County fills by itself.** Under the 2020 map the county was roughly a seventh of Senate District 12 by land area, and while the corpus cannot say what fraction it is now, a Senate district covering one county is not a shape Ohio draws. [inference] See [the district](../division/ohio-senate-district-12-2023.yml).

refusals: **This is not a seat Allen County fills by itself.** Under the 2020 map the county was roughly a seventh of Senate District 12 by land area, and while the corpus cannot say what fraction it is now, a Senate district covering one county is not a shape Ohio draws.

blocks.text: The seat Allen County's present member of the United States House of Representatives holds. [verified] — [Ohio county elected officials lookup](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md).
Its term is two years, running 3 January 2025 to 2 January 2027. [verified] — same source.

nodes.label: Bluffton Hospital

blocks.text: A twenty-five-bed critical access hospital at 139 Garau Street in [Bluffton](../place/bluffton.yml), with an emergency department. [verified] — [CMS Hospital General Information](../../catalog/cms-hospital-general-information.md), CCN 361322. It is the only one of the county's five hospitals outside Lima and its edge, and the only one in a village.

Its municipality was checked and not assumed: the county's address file reads `MUNI` BLUFFTON and `USPS_CITY` BLUFFTON, and TIGERweb puts the point in Bluffton village within [Richland Township](../place/richland-township.yml). [verified] — [Allen County GIS](../../catalog/allen-county-gis-downloads.md) and [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md).

**It is owned in the next county.** Blanchard Valley Health System of Findlay, in Hancock County, holds 100 per cent of it, with association dates of 27 January 1983 and 1 July 1995. [verified] — [CMS provider enrollment](../../catalog/cms-provider-enrollment.md).

**The body is not the name.** It enrolls as **Blanchard Valley Regional Health Center**, incorporated in Ohio on 6 July 1982 — a name that belongs to a river valley in Hancock County and says nothing about Bluffton. [verified] — same source. Its 101 individual owners are the largest such list of the county's five hospitals, and are not recorded here.

**It is the smallest employer of the four calendar-year filers and it has shrunk.** 108.25 full-time equivalents in 2011 and 89.19 in 2023, with a spike to 183.25 in 2016 and 146 in 2017 that the corpus cannot explain. [verified] — [CMS hospital cost reports](../../catalog/cms-hospital-cost-reports.md); see [the series](../measure/allen-county-hospital-employment-2011-2023.yml). Twenty-five beds in every one of the thirteen years, unmoved. See [the beds](../measure/allen-county-hospital-beds-2011-2023.yml).

**It is the only Allen County hospital to report a loss in 2020.** Its net patient revenue fell from $22.9 million in 2019 to $8.8 million in 2020 and its net income was **negative $5,799,086**, against positive figures at all four of the others. [verified] — same source. Both recovered the following year.

refusals: This corpus does not establish that the pandemic caused that year.

blocks.text: A private liberal arts university at [Bluffton](../place/bluffton.yml), with a Mennonite affiliation reflecting the Swiss Mennonite settlement of that part of the county. [inference]

**Its residential population is now a measured number.** Census block `390030101001002` holds 398 people in 2 housing units — a population living almost entirely outside housing, which is what a campus looks like in the block file. The county's address file puts Ropp Hall 0.02 miles from that block's internal point, with Bren Dell Hall, College Hall and Musselman Library inside 0.15. [verified] — [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md) block layer and [Allen County GIS](../../catalog/allen-county-gis-downloads.md). The 398 are students in residence on census day; they are not the university's enrolment, and the campus is not necessarily one block. [inference]

That block is in [Bluffton](../place/bluffton.yml) village, which settles by assignment rather than by inference where the university sits. [verified] — [2020 Census Block Assignment Files](../../catalog/census-block-assignment-2020.md).

The parent company named against [the Lima engine plant](../site/ford-lima-engine-plant.yml), which has reported to the Toxics Release Inventory in all thirty-eight years from 1987 to 2024 — as long as the inventory has existed, and on four chemicals for 2024. [verified] — [EPA TRI](../../catalog/epa-tri.md); see [the reporters](../measure/allen-county-tri-reporters-1987-2024.yml). The facility files under the name `FORD MOTOR CO LIMA ENGINE PLANT` with its mailing address at the plant itself.

**It carries no `seated-in` edge, and the absence is the claim.** `seated-in` means where an organization is headquartered, and this one is not headquartered in Allen County. Pointing it at the township its plant stands in would state something false in a structured field to avoid an empty one. The node therefore carries `instance-of` alone, which is the same shape as the seven district officers who represent this county and do not live in it. [inference]

That leaves the corpus without any edge for *the parent of a body operating here*, which is the second time this gap has been named — the first was [Mercy Health–St. Rita's](mercy-health-st-ritas-medical-center.yml) and its owner in Cincinnati. Two phases, two classes, one missing relationship. [inference]

properties.also_known_as: West Central Ohio Group Ltd.; Orthopedic Institute of Ohio (county address file)

blocks.text: A proprietary acute care hospital at 801 Medical Drive, twelve beds, with **no emergency department** — the only one of the county's five without one. [verified] — [CMS Hospital General Information](../../catalog/cms-hospital-general-information.md), CCN 360263.

**It is not in Lima, and this is the fourth time this corpus has had to say that about a Lima address.** Its postal address is Lima; the county's own address file leaves `MUNI` blank for both units at 801 Medical Drive while `USPS_CITY` reads LIMA; and TIGERweb puts the point in [Perry Township](../place/perry-township.yml) and in no incorporated place. [verified] — [Allen County GIS](../../catalog/allen-county-gis-downloads.md) and [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md). Two authorities, agreeing, checked before the claim was written rather than after. See [a postal address is not a municipality](../../decisions/a-postal-address-is-not-a-municipality.yml), whose first three instances were the refinery, the tank plant and the county's heavy industry generally.
So the county's only for-profit hospital stands on unincorporated ground, as its refinery and its tank plant do. No municipality levies on any of the three. [inference]

**It is majority-owned by the hospital across town.** Mercy Health–St. Rita's holds 51 per cent of it directly, from 1 April 2004; West Central Ohio Physicians Group Ltd. holds the other 49 and the operational and managerial control; and Bon Secours Mercy Health Inc appears above St. Rita's as the indirect 51 per cent holder from 1 September 2018. [verified] — [CMS provider enrollment](../../catalog/cms-provider-enrollment.md). So a physician-owned specialty hospital is majority-owned by a general one — see [St. Rita's](mercy-health-st-ritas-medical-center.yml) — which is a particular arrangement, and this node records it without characterising it.

**The body is not the name.** It enrolls as **West Central Ohio Group Ltd.**, incorporated in Ohio on 10 March 1997. [verified] — same source. The county's address file knows the two units at this address as the "Orthopedic Institute of Ohio" and the "Institute for Orthopedic Surgery Physical Therapy" — a third and fourth spelling of the thing, neither of them the name Medicare enrolls. [verified] — the address file.

**It is the county's smallest hospital and the only one that has grown in almost every year.** 101.01 full-time equivalents in 2011 rising to 175.06 in 2023, up 73 per cent, with a single dip in 2016. [verified] — [CMS hospital cost reports](../../catalog/cms-hospital-cost-reports.md); see [the series](../measure/allen-county-hospital-employment-2011-2023.yml). Twelve beds in every one of the thirteen years. See [the beds](../measure/allen-county-hospital-beds-2011-2023.yml), where the three small hospitals hold their bed counts flat and the two large ones do not.

A twenty-six-bed long-term acute care hospital enrolled at 730 West Market Street in [Lima](../place/lima.yml) — the address of [Mercy Health–St. Rita's](mercy-health-st-ritas-medical-center.yml). [verified] — [CMS provider enrollment](../../catalog/cms-provider-enrollment.md), CCN 362020. A long-term acute care hospital operating inside a host hospital is an ordinary arrangement; this node records the shared address and makes no claim about the arrangement. [inference]

**It is the hospital that the roster of hospitals does not have.** Care Compare's Hospital General Information file lists 193 Ohio hospitals in six types and has no long-term care category, so this one is absent from it — no CCN 362020 anywhere in the file, and the only row at this address is St. Rita's. [verified] — [CMS Hospital General Information](../../catalog/cms-hospital-general-information.md). Allen County has four hospitals or five depending on which federal file is asked, and neither file is wrong about the thing it counts.

**Its owners run thirteen deep and all of them are in Louisville, Kentucky.** One direct owner, SCCI Health Services LLC, holding 100 per cent from 13 July 1998; twelve indirect ones, the three most recent attached on 23 December 2021 and named for Knight rather than Kindred. [verified] — [CMS provider enrollment](../../catalog/cms-provider-enrollment.md).

**The body is not the name.** It enrolls as **SCCI Hospitals of America LLC**, with no incorporation date stated — the only one of the county's five whose enrollment record leaves that field empty. [verified] — same source.

**It is the only Allen County hospital that does not file on the calendar year.** It filed 1 January to 31 December through FY2013 and 1 September to 31 August ever since, which puts two of its rows in the FY2014 file — a stub from 1 January to 31 August 2014 and a full year from 1 September. [verified] — [CMS hospital cost reports](../../catalog/cms-hospital-cost-reports.md). Its 64 to 94 full-time equivalents are therefore held outside every county total this corpus computes, and stated separately. See [the series](../measure/allen-county-hospital-employment-2011-2023.yml).
79.2 full-time equivalents in 2011 and 64.1 in the year beginning September 2023, on twenty-six beds throughout. [verified] — same source.

The locomotive builder that made Lima's name in railroading. It began as a machine shop building the geared Shay locomotive under Ephraim Shay's patent — a design for logging and industrial railways that could work steep, rough, temporary track that a conventional rod locomotive could not. [inference]

It later became one of the three major American builders of mainline steam, and is associated with the "Super Power" concept — a design direction emphasising boiler capacity and free steaming that the company introduced in the mid-1920s. [inference]

**Two years of its books are now sourced, and they are the two years the war turned.** The company booked orders for 51 locomotives in 1940 against 14 in 1939, closed 1940 with a backlog of 32 engines and 19 delivered in the year, and turned a net profit of $87,007 after a net loss of $134,326 in 1939. Eighteen more locomotives were ordered in the first seven weeks of 1941. [verified] — [Chronicling America](../../catalog/chronicling-america.md), *The Bluffton News*, 20 February 1941, page 3, reporting an Associated Press dispatch from New York, where the company's main offices were.

Its main offices were in New York and its works were in Lima, which is worth stating because this corpus's other large employers are described by where they build and this one was not run from there. [inference] — same source.

**It took a tank contract in the same month.** See [the plant](../site/lima-locomotive-works-plant.yml) for the $290,000 building and the medium tank programme; the company itself is the party that contracted. [verified] — same archive, *Evening Star*, 24 August 1941.

nodes.label: Lima Memorial Health System

blocks.text: An acute care hospital at 1001 Bellefontaine Avenue in [Lima](../place/lima.yml), with an emergency department and an overall Medicare rating of 3. [verified] — [CMS Hospital General Information](../../catalog/cms-hospital-general-information.md), CCN 360009.

**It is the only hospital in this county that answers to nobody outside it.** The federal owners file lists no organizational owner for it at all — 22 owners, every one of them a person, being fifteen corporate directors, four managing employees and three officers. [verified] — [CMS provider enrollment](../../catalog/cms-provider-enrollment.md). The other four all have a corporate parent, three of them outside Allen County. See [Mercy Health–St. Rita's](mercy-health-st-ritas-medical-center.yml), [Bluffton Hospital](bluffton-hospital.yml), [the Institute for Orthopaedic Surgery](institute-for-orthopaedic-surgery.yml) and [Kindred Hospital Lima](kindred-hospital-lima.yml).

**The body is not the name.** It enrolls as the **Lima Memorial Joint Operating Company**, incorporated in Ohio on 12 May 1999, and trades as Lima Memorial Health System. [verified] — same source. `founded` here dates the corporation and not the hospital.

**It is the county's second-largest hospital employer and the only large one that has grown.** 982.94 full-time equivalents in 2011 and 1,261.83 in 2023, up 28 per cent. [verified] — [CMS hospital cost reports](../../catalog/cms-hospital-cost-reports.md); see [the series](../measure/allen-county-hospital-employment-2011-2023.yml). Over the same thirteen years its bed count fell from 195 to 110, and stood as low as 95 in 2019. See [the beds](../measure/allen-county-hospital-beds-2011-2023.yml). More staff and half the beds is the shape of hospital work moving out of the ward, and this corpus has measured the shape and not the cause. [inference]
It has one further Medicare enrollment, 36T009, flagged as its rehabilitation unit. [verified] — the enrollment file.

refusals: Whether that society is an ancestor of this hospital, of [St. Rita's](mercy-health-st-ritas-medical-center.yml), or of neither, the corpus does not know.

nodes.label: Lima Refining Company

properties.also_known_as: LIMA REFINING CO (EPA); Valero Lima Refinery (county address file, stale)

blocks.text: The company that has operated [the Lima refinery](../site/lima-refinery.yml) since the 2008 report, and the fourth name in the operator column since 1994. [verified] — [EIA Refinery Capacity Report](../../catalog/eia-refinery-capacity.md).

**It runs the largest refinery in Ohio.** 183,000 barrels per calendar day of atmospheric crude distillation, against 172,800 at Toledo, 150,800 at the other Toledo refinery and 100,000 at Canton — 30 per cent of the state's 606,600, and 36th of the 124 refineries in the United States. [verified] — same source, the 2026 report. Its parent operates two of Ohio's four. [verified]

**It is also the county's oldest continuously reporting industrial facility to the EPA**, filing under the Toxics Release Inventory in all thirty-eight years from 1987 to 2024, and filing on twenty-five chemicals for 2024 — more than any other facility in the county except one. [verified] — [EPA TRI](../../catalog/epa-tri.md); see [the reporters](../measure/allen-county-tri-reporters-1987-2024.yml). The inventory's register carries those thirty-eight years under this company's name and today's parent, which is an artifact of how the register is built and not a claim that this company was there in 1987. [verified] — see [a register is not a census](../../decisions/a-register-is-not-a-census.yml).

refusals: The `CORPORATION` column does not exist in reports before 2010, so this node cannot say who owned the works in the two years it operated them before that.

nodes.label: Mercy Health–St. Rita's Medical Center

properties.also_known_as: Mercy Health-St Ritas Medical Center LLC; St. Ritas Medical Center (cost reports through FY2013)

blocks.text: An acute care hospital at 730 West Market Street in [Lima](../place/lima.yml), with an emergency department and an overall Medicare rating of 4 — the higher of the county's two rated hospitals. [verified] — [CMS Hospital General Information](../../catalog/cms-hospital-general-information.md), CCN 360066. Its enrollment carries five subgroup flags where the others carry one or none: acute care, psychiatric, rehabilitation, and psychiatric and rehabilitation units. [verified] — [CMS provider enrollment](../../catalog/cms-provider-enrollment.md).

**It is the county's largest hospital by every measure this corpus holds, and it is owned in Cincinnati.** Bon Secours Mercy Health Inc holds 100 per cent of it, recorded from 1 January 2020, and the same body appears as the indirect 51 per cent owner of [the Institute for Orthopaedic Surgery](institute-for-orthopaedic-surgery.yml). [verified] — [CMS provider enrollment](../../catalog/cms-provider-enrollment.md). Two of Allen County's five hospitals therefore answer to one non-profit corporation in another county.

**Its legal name is not its trading name, and the change of legal name is visible in the accounts.** It enrolls as Mercy Health-St Ritas Medical Center LLC, incorporated in Ohio on 5 May 1970. [verified] — same source. It filed cost reports as "St. Ritas Medical Center" through FY2013 and as "St. Ritas Medical Center LLC" from FY2014, and across that boundary its reported full-time equivalents fell from 2,303 to 1,678 and its salaries from $145.5 million to $94.6 million. [verified] — [CMS hospital cost reports](../../catalog/cms-hospital-cost-reports.md).

**Its employment fell by more than the county's whole hospital decline.** 2,406 full-time equivalents in 2011 against 1,386.92 in 2023 — a fall of 1,019, where the four calendar-year filers together fell by 685. [verified] — same source; see [the series](../measure/allen-county-hospital-employment-2011-2023.yml). Its beds did not follow: 322 in 2011 and 329 in 2023, the steadiest bed count of the five. See [the beds](../measure/allen-county-hospital-beds-2011-2023.yml).

**A second hospital operates inside it.** [Kindred Hospital Lima](kindred-hospital-lima.yml) enrolls at this same street address. [verified] — the enrollment file. It is a separate body with a separate CCN and an owner in Kentucky, and this node makes no claim about the arrangement between them.

refusals: Whether a quarter of this hospital's workforce left the county or moved to another employer inside the same system, the corpus cannot say.

blocks.text: The Standard Oil subsidiary that built and operated [the Lima refinery](../site/lima-refinery.yml) — the corporate name attached to the county's longest-running industrial installation, and the first link in an ownership chain the refinery node has asked for since genesis. [verified] — [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md).

**It appears in the record as the buyer, not as Standard.** When Standard Oil resolved in 1886 to put a refinery in north-west Ohio, the committee that toured the candidate sites was Frank Rockefeller, the director F. B. Squiers, and **Keith, "an attorney for the Solar Refining Company"** — and the 151 acres of the Hover farm were contracted "to the Solar Refining Company". So the entity that dealt with the landowner, took the deed and took possession was Solar, with Standard's officers making the decision. [verified] — same source. That distinction is why [Standard Oil](standard-oil.yml) and this node are separate: one chose, the other bought.

Thirty-five years later the 1921 historian's summary of what the boom left is one clause: "About all that is left is the Solar refinery and the different companies dealing in oil commodities." [verified] — same source. The refinery had already outlasted the field that justified it, which is the fact [the boom's](../period/lima-oil-boom.yml) end bound is really about.

In 1918 it was one of nine Lima industrial firms that agreed to meet half the cost of equipping a machine shop at South High School, alongside Lima Locomotive Works and the Ohio Steel Foundry. [verified] — same source. It is also a corporate life member of the Lima Hospital Society, with the Buckeye Pipe Line Company, the Ohio Oil Company, the Lima Natural Gas Company and the Manhattan Oil Company. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md).

**The far end of the chain it starts is now held.** BP Oil Corp. operated [the refinery](../site/lima-refinery.yml) in 1994, and [Lima Refining Company](lima-refining-company.yml) operates it now under Cenovus. [verified] — [EIA Refinery Capacity Report](../../catalog/eia-refinery-capacity.md). So the question this node has carried since genesis is no longer *who has it now*; it is the hundred and eight years in between.

The company that industrialized the Lima oil field after the 1885 strike. Standard Oil bought into the field, built refining capacity at Lima, and solved the problem that had made Lima crude nearly worthless — its high sulphur content, which fouled refining and gave the product the name "sour crude" — by acquiring a desulphurization process. [inference]

It matters to this corpus as the mechanism by which a local discovery became a national one. The strike made oil available; Standard made it saleable, and in doing so attached this county to a national industrial economy in a way its agriculture never had. [inference] That clause is a claim about reach, and the corpus can now say what it is not a claim about. In 1909 the county's crops were worth $2,425,973 and its farms took $1,402,878 for animals sold, against $7,753,877 of products from Lima's factories; the county's farm property stood at $25,992,184 in April 1910. [verified] — [Abstract of the Thirteenth Census, Supplement for Ohio](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md); see [the farms](../measure/allen-county-farms-1900-1910.yml), [what they produced](../measure/allen-county-farm-output-1909.yml) and [Lima manufactures](../measure/lima-manufactures-1899-1909.yml).

Those numbers do not settle which sector was larger, and this node does not claim they do. The farm figure that can be compared with manufactured output is a flow and the farm figure that is impressive is a stock, and the corpus holds no capital figure for Lima's factories to set against $25,992,184. What "in a way its agriculture never had" asserts is that the oil went to a national market and the corn did not — and even that is an inference, because the corpus has not measured where either went. [inference]

**The Standard entity at Lima was the [Solar Refining Company](solar-refining-company.yml)**, and the corpus can now date its arrival: in 1886 a Standard committee — Frank Rockefeller, the director F. B. Squiers and Solar's attorney Keith — chose 151 acres in [Shawnee Township](../place/shawnee-township.yml) for [the refinery](../site/lima-refinery.yml) over Findlay and Toledo. [verified] — [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md). Standard "at once established headquarters" at Lima and was still operating there in 1921. [verified] — same source. It "cornered the Lima oil fields and went into the producing business, building the Chicago pipe line and becoming master of the oil supply of the world" — the 1921 historian's phrasing, and this corpus records it as his. [verified] — same source.

Two more of its Lima entities are named in the record: the **Buckeye Pipe Line Company** and the **Ohio Oil Company**, which with Solar and the independent Manhattan Oil Company appear together as corporate subscribers to the Lima Hospital Society. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md).

**The refinery's present operator is established and the chain to it is not.** [Lima Refining Company](lima-refining-company.yml) has filed for the works since the 2008 federal report, under Husky Energy from 2010 and Cenovus from 2022, and BP Oil Corp. held it in 1994. [verified] — [EIA Refinery Capacity Report](../../catalog/eia-refinery-capacity.md). What the corpus still lacks is everything between 1886 and 1994.

The largest home lender in Allen County by a distance. It originated **646 of the 1,932 mortgages made in this county in 2023 — a third of them** — where the second-largest lender made 113. [verified] — [the HMDA register](../../catalog/hmda-loan-application-register.md), and [the county's lending](../measure/allen-county-home-lending-2023.yml).

**It is the reason this county's mortgage market is a local one.** A hundred and ninety-one institutions lent here in 2023, including Rocket Mortgage and loanDepot, and neither reached seventy originations. The three largest after this one are the Union Bank Company of Columbus Grove, the Citizens National Bank of Bluffton and Huntington National Bank; the first two are seated in or beside this county. [verified] — same source.

**It denied less often than the county did**: 133 of 795 applications it acted on, 16.7 per cent, against 23.4 per cent countywide. [verified] Nothing here explains that. A lender with a third of a market is not comparable to the market it dominates, because most of the market's applications are its own. [inference]

**The register names it by Legal Entity Identifier and never in words.** `254900ARL5FDX2OOH702` resolves to this name, previously *Superior Financial Credit Union, Inc.*, active, registered in Ohio, LEI issued 16 January 2018. [verified] — [GLEIF](../../catalog/hmda-loan-application-register.md).

**Two addresses, and one of them is shared.** Its legal address is 540 W. Market Street, Lima 45801; its headquarters address is 4230 Elida Road, Lima 45807 — which is also the address given by *Superior Financial Solutions, LLC*, the eighth-largest lender in the county at 55 originations. [verified]

properties.character: Water transport as the organizing fact of the county's west, and a divided county economy. [inference]

blocks.text: The span in which [the Miami and Erie Canal](../site/miami-and-erie-canal.yml) was the organizing transport fact of western Allen County — roughly the 1840s to the end of the nineteenth century, when rail had comprehensively displaced it. [inference]

Its character is a geographic asymmetry rather than a countywide condition, and that is the reason it is worth naming as a period at all. The canal ran through the county's western edge and made [Delphos](../place/delphos.yml) and Spencerville into places; it did not touch Lima, which grew instead around a railway junction. So for several decades the county had two economies oriented to two different transport systems, and its later concentration on Lima is partly the story of one of them winning. [inference]

**The opening bound is now sourced and the corpus's guess was right.** The Miami extension was formally opened in June 1845, and traffic was moving at Spencerville by 1844. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md). 1845 was written here as "the corpus's rough placement" and is the date the state used.

**The closing bound now has an argument, and it moves.** The railways reached this county while the canal was still young: the Ohio & Indiana opened Crestline to Fort Wayne in 1854 and was consolidated into the Pennsylvania system in 1856; the Dayton & Michigan was chartered in 1856-57 and **completed through Allen County in 1858**. [verified] — same source. A canal whose parallel railway is finished thirteen years after it opens did not organize the county's west until 1900. [inference] The end bound is left at 1900 for now because "displaced" and "abandoned" are different dates and this corpus has argued neither.

nodes.label: Deindustrialization in Allen County

properties.boundary_basis: The start is the last year manufacturing employment stood within one per cent of its all-time peak — 18,389 in 1979 against 18,400 in 1973 — after which the series never returns to that level. [verified] The peak years 1973, 1974 and 1979 are all within one per cent of each other, so the plateau rather than the peak fixes the start. The end is the trough, 7,775 in 2009, with thirteen subsequent years all higher. [verified] Both bounds are computed from one series and would move if a second series with a different frame were preferred; County Business Patterns puts the trough one year later, in 2010. [inference]
properties.character: Contraction of manufacturing employment across the county, from a plateau at the 1973 peak to a trough in 2009, with a recession trough and recovery in the middle of it. It is not a period of falling employment generally: the county's total jobs rose through the first twenty-one years of it. [verified]

blocks.text: The span in which Allen County's manufacturing employment fell from a peak of 18,400 to a trough of 7,775 — fifty-eight per cent, across thirty years. [verified] — [the employment series](../measure/allen-county-manufacturing-employment-1969-2022.yml).

**The refusal that stood on this node from genesis is answered.** It said the corpus established nothing about manufacturing employment inside this period — first in the form "does not measure it at all", then narrowed to "inside this period" when the 1909 figures arrived. The corpus now holds fifty-four years of it: **Allen County manufacturing employment fell from a peak of 18,400 in 1973 to 7,775 in 2009, a fall of 58 per cent.** [verified] — [the long series](../measure/allen-county-manufacturing-employment-1969-2022.yml), corroborated in shape by [County Business Patterns](../measure/allen-county-manufacturing-employment-1986-2022.yml). The period's named mechanism is measured, and it happened.

**What happened after the trough is why this period can be closed.** Manufacturing employment rose to 8,917 in 2020 and stood at 8,573 in 2022 on the County Business Patterns count, up a fifth from its bottom. Private employment fell 3,709 between 2010 and 2022 while manufacturing rose 1,446, so the losses of those twelve years were entirely outside manufacturing — the largest of them in health care, which fell from 11,744 to 9,151. [verified] — [County Business Patterns](../measure/allen-county-manufacturing-employment-1986-2022.yml) and [the sector composition](../measure/allen-county-employment-by-sector-1986-2022.yml). Whatever has been emptying this county since 2010, it is not its factories. [inference]

It does not establish that the county's population decline was caused by its manufacturing decline. That was unlicensed while manufacturing employment was unmeasured, and it is now contradicted for the recent past: between 2010 and 2022 the county's private employment fell by 3,709 while its manufacturing employment *rose* by 1,446. [verified] — [the series](../measure/allen-county-manufacturing-employment-1986-2022.yml). For the last twelve years of this period the proposed cause moves opposite to the effect.

**The years this node called open one phase ago are measured, and they do not contain a decline.** Allen County manufacturing employment was 17,623 in 1969, rose to a peak of **18,400 in 1973**, and stood at 18,389 as late as 1979. [verified] — [the long series](../measure/allen-county-manufacturing-employment-1969-2022.yml). The county's factories were still adding workers through the decade this period says the decline began in.

**That is why this period no longer starts in 1970.** The old start was fixed from population and applied to manufacturing, and manufacturing did not turn until 1973 at the earliest and did not fall durably until after 1979. [verified] — same source. The node now begins at 1979, the last year within one per cent of the peak, and the population start it used to carry has gone with the population to [depopulation](depopulation.yml). [inference]

**The order is the part that matters.** [Lima](../place/lima.yml) peaked in 1970. Manufacturing peaked in 1973 and held near its peak until 1979. The county peaked in 1980. Employment of every kind peaked in 2000. [verified] — the long series, [total employment](../measure/allen-county-total-employment-1969-2022.yml) and the county's own population series. The city began emptying while the factories were still filling. [inference]

refusals: It does not establish that the county's population decline was caused by its manufacturing decline.

nodes.label: The depopulation of Lima and Allen County

properties.boundary_basis: The start is measured on both subjects and they differ by ten years. Lima peaked at 53,734 in 1970 with twelve rising counts behind it; the county peaked at 112,241 in 1980 with fifteen. [verified] 1970 is taken as the period's start because it is the earlier of the two and because the city is where the loss is concentrated. [inference] No end: every measure the corpus holds through 2024 continues it.
properties.character: Sustained population loss, beginning in the county seat and reaching the county a decade later, and continuing after the manufacturing contraction that is usually named as its cause had ended. [verified]

blocks.text: The span from 1970 in which [Lima](../place/lima.yml) lost a third of its people and the county, from 1980, lost a tenth of its own. It continues. [verified] — [the county series](../place/allen-county.yml) and the measures below.

**This node exists because a period was doing two jobs.** Until this phase the corpus held one period, [deindustrialization](deindustrialization.yml), covering both the county's manufacturing contraction and its population loss, on one start date of "roughly 1970". The two are now measured separately and they are not the same span: manufacturing peaked in 1973, fell from 1979 and bottomed in 2009, where the population turned in 1970 for the city and 1980 for the county and has not stopped. [verified] — [the employment series](../measure/allen-county-manufacturing-employment-1969-2022.yml). One process has ended and one has not. See [one period was doing two jobs](../../decisions/one-period-was-doing-two-jobs.yml).

**There was a reversal, and this node said there was none.** Between 1970 and 1980 the county *grew*, from 111,144 to **112,241** — its highest count ever — before falling to 109,755 in 1990 and 108,464 in 2000. [verified] — [1990 Census, Population and Housing Unit Counts, Ohio](../../catalog/census-cph-2-37-ohio.md), Table 3. This node has said since genesis that there was "no reversal at any measured point", and that was true of the corpus's data and false of the county: every figure it held began at 1970 or later, so the one decade that rose was the one decade outside the window. **The county's peak is 1980.** See [the 1940–1990 series](../measure/allen-county-population-1940-1990.yml).

The period keeps its name and its subject and its start moves to what the record shows: the county's population turned in the 1970s and fell from 1980. [inference] Whether manufacturing employment turned earlier is still unmeasured here, and it is the thing the period is named for.

**The decline itself is demonstrated rather than asserted.** Allen County counted 111,144 at the 1970 census and 100,866 at the 2024 estimate — a loss of 10,278 people, or 9.2%, across five decades: 111,144 (1970), 108,464 (2000), 106,331 (2010), 102,217 (2020), 100,866 (2024). [verified] — see [1970](../measure/allen-county-population-1970.yml), [2000](../measure/allen-county-population-2000.yml), [2010](../measure/allen-county-population-2010.yml), [2020](../measure/allen-county-population-2020.yml) and [2024](../measure/allen-county-population-2024.yml), which rest on [the 1970s county estimates](../../catalog/census-county-estimates-1970s.md), [the 2000-2010 intercensals](../../catalog/census-intercensal-2000-2010.md) and [Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md). The arithmetic is this corpus's; every input is a Census figure.

**The concentration is now evidenced too, over one decade.** This node carries a `concentrated-in` edge to Lima, and between 2000 and 2010 Lima fell 3.8% while the balance of Allen County — everything outside every incorporated place — fell 1.5%, from 50,809 to 50,048. [verified] — [Census Intercensal Estimates, 2000–2010](../../catalog/census-intercensal-2000-2010.md). Lima declined about two and a half times as fast as the rest of the county. [inference]

**The county's 1970 peak is no longer an artefact of where the data began.** The series now runs 578 in 1830 through 47,976 in 1900 and 68,203 in 1920 to 111,144 in 1970, and every decade of it rises. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md) and [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md); see [the county series](../measure/allen-county-population-1830-1900.yml). Four counts are still missing, 1930 to 1960, and nothing in ninety years of ascent suggests a reversal inside them. [inference] For the county, this node's start date is now argued rather than assumed.

**For Lima the 1970 date is supported after all, and by a wide margin.** The city was **53,734 in 1970**, 47,827 in 1980, 45,549 in 1990 and 40,307 in 2000. [verified] — [Lima 1970–1990](../measure/lima-population-1970-1990.yml). Two phases ago this node reasoned from 41,306 in 1920 — since corrected to 41,326 — against 40,307 in 2000 that "eighty years net to roughly nothing" and the peak was unlocatable. There was a peak and the corpus had drawn a chord across it. The city rose thirty per cent above its 1920 count by 1970 and has fallen at every count since.

**And the long run is a different story from the short one.** Between 1970 and 2020 Lima lost 18,155 people while the county lost 8,927 — so the rest of Allen County **gained 9,228** over the same fifty years. [inference] This node's finding from four recent years, that the suburban ring is shrinking too, stands for 2020–2024 and does not describe the half-century: over the long run the ring grew while the city emptied, and only lately have both been falling.

**The ring turned between 2000 and 2010, and this node asked when.** The county outside Lima held 28,592 people in 1940, 68,157 in 2000, and 66,627 at the 2020 census — growth at every count for sixty years, and a fall at both counts since. [inference] — [the balance series](../measure/allen-county-outside-lima-1890-2020.yml), computed from Census counts on both sides. **So the county has three peaks and they are thirty years apart**: Lima in 1970, the county in 1980, the county outside Lima in 2000. [inference] This period is named for a process that reached the three of them in that order, and a single line labelled "Allen County" shows none of it.

**The corporation's boundary moved underneath the city's counts.** Between 1980 and 1990 Lima annexed ground from American, Bath and Shawnee townships. [verified] — [1990 Census, Population and Housing Unit Counts, Ohio](../../catalog/census-cph-2-37-ohio.md), Geographic Change Notes. So the fall from 47,827 to 45,549 happened while the corporation was growing, and understates the decline inside the old line. [inference] This is the first annexation event the corpus has held against a caveat it has carried since genesis.

**Lima peaked in 1970, and this node's own caveat is what got answered.** It said 1970 was the first of three federal counts, and that a series beginning at its own first observation is no evidence that the observation was a peak — the city might have been larger in 1960. It was not: 51,037 in 1960, 50,246 in 1950, 44,711 in 1940, 42,287 in 1930, and every count below that lower again. [verified] — [1960 Census, Number of Inhabitants, Ohio](../../catalog/census-1960-number-of-inhabitants-ohio.md); see [the federal series](../measure/lima-population-1850-1960.yml). Twice now a refusal in this node has been retired by retrieval rather than by argument, and both times the refusal was about where the corpus's window began.

**The mechanism, for the first time.** Across the four full years 2021 to 2024 the county lost 1,271 people: **506 to natural decrease and 793 to net migration**, with a residual of 28. [verified] — [natural change](../measure/allen-county-natural-change-2021-2024.yml) and [net migration](../measure/allen-county-net-migration-2021-2024.yml), both from the same Population Estimates file this node has cited since its second phase. More people leave than arrive, and more die than are born, and the first is the larger of the two.

**The decline is broad and uneven.** Between the 2020 estimates base and 2024, eleven of the county's thirteen civil subdivisions lost population. Lima lost most in absolute terms — 841 of a county loss of 1,351 — and the only two that grew were Auglaize township, by 55, and Marion township, by 102, at the county's south-eastern and Delphos ends. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), sub-county file. So this is not a city emptying into its own suburbs: the suburban ring is shrinking too, slower. [inference]

**What the concentration is made of.** This node has said since it was split off that the loss is concentrated in Lima, and it can now say what Lima is. The city holds 34.7 per cent of the county's people, 64.1 per cent of those below the poverty line and 76.7 per cent of its Black residents, on a median household income 48 per cent of the township across its southern line. [verified] — [American Community Survey](../../catalog/census-acs-summary-file.md); see [income and poverty](../measure/allen-county-income-and-poverty-2023.yml) and [race](../measure/allen-county-race-2023.yml).

That is a description of the county as it stands and not of how it got there. The sorting could be the residue of a process this period covers or of one that finished before it opened, and nothing here dates it. [inference]

**The ground it sits on is dated, and the date is this period's own opening.** The three townships that ring Lima have median build years of 1973, 1973 and 1975 against the city's 1953, and the county's largest building decade was the 1970s — 8,298 units, 6,333 of them outside Lima, in the decade the city reached its peak and still held 48.4 per cent of the county. [verified] — [when the housing was built](../measure/allen-county-housing-age-2023.yml). A sorting into an old cheap city and a new dear ring cannot be older than the ring, and the ring went up while the city was full. [inference] That bounds the sorting from below without saying when people moved.

**What it is sorted into is now measured as well.** The county is 68.3 per cent owner-occupied, which is an ordinary American figure made of Lima at 46.4 and twelve townships between 72.0 and 91.0; the city holds 35.4 per cent of the housing and 48.2 per cent of the empty housing. [verified] — [the stock](../measure/allen-county-housing-stock-2023.yml).

**And the city is younger than almost all of the ground around it.** Median age 35.4 against the county's 39.7 and 15.6 per cent over 65 against 18.7, with eleven of the twelve townships older. [verified] — [age structure](../measure/allen-county-age-structure-2023.yml).

This corpus does not establish that Lima is emptying because it is aging. It carries natural decrease as a component of the county's loss and it carries the concentration in Lima, and those two facts invite that conclusion; the age measure contradicts it. Whatever natural decrease this county has, it is not principally the city's. [verified] — same source.

It does not establish that the county's population decline was caused by its manufacturing decline. The two spans overlap and do not coincide — the city began emptying three years before manufacturing peaked, and manufacturing has risen since 2009 while the population has not. [verified] — [the employment series](../measure/allen-county-manufacturing-employment-1969-2022.yml). A population series cannot establish a cause however many other series sit beside it, and that was true before this corpus had the other series. [inference]

refusals: It does not establish that either mechanism reaches back before 2020.

It does not establish that the decline has ended: fifteen people on 100,851 is far inside what a modelled estimate can resolve, one year is not a direction, and the same programme revises its own earlier years with every vintage.
This corpus does not establish that Lima is emptying because it is aging.
It does not establish that the county's population decline was caused by its manufacturing decline.

properties.character: A local discovery converted into national industry, added on top of a farming county that kept farming. This field said "the county's shift from agriculture to manufacturing" until the agriculture was measured and had not shifted. [inference]

blocks.text: The span opened by [the 1885 strike](../event/lima-oil-strike.yml), in which the Lima–Indiana field made this county a centre of national petroleum production and Lima an industrial city. [inference]

Its character is the attachment of a local agricultural economy to national capital. The refinery, the growth of Lima's population, and much of the built fabric of the city date from it. [inference] *Attachment* is the right word and *replacement* is not: the agriculture was still there at the end of the period, on 92.5 per cent of the county's land. [verified] — [Abstract of the Thirteenth Census, Supplement for Ohio](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md); see [the county's farms](../measure/allen-county-farms-1900-1910.yml). The field's dominance was relatively brief — it was displaced as new fields opened elsewhere — but the refining capacity it justified is still operating, which is why the period's most durable legacy is [a site](../site/lima-refinery.yml) rather than an industry. [inference]

**The start bound is now supported from the other side.** The 1885 county history, printed as the boom began, treats the county's petroleum as prospective — "a subject for the enterprise of the future" — while cataloguing everything else in Lima to the dollar. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md). A source that would have reported the field and does not is a lower bound on the field. [inference]

**The start bound is now a date: May 9, 1885.** [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md). It is also, on the same source, a slightly later date in substance — the first *persistent* production came from the second well that autumn, the pioneer having broken. [inference]

**The boom is now measurable and the measure is large.** Allen County gained 9,330 people between 1880 and 1890 — **29.7 per cent, the largest decennial gain in its history** — and Lima "doubled her population" in the same decade, going from 7,567 to 21,723 by 1900. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md); see [the county series](../measure/allen-county-population-1830-1900.yml) and [Lima's](../measure/lima-population-1880-1920.yml). The 1906 compilers attribute the increase to the discovery without qualification, and they were living in the town when it happened.

**And the end bound has a shape at last, though not a date.** By 1920 Lima had reached 41,326 — the Census figure; the 1921 history says 41,306 and see [the federal series](../measure/lima-population-1850-1960.yml) — and by 1921 the whole residue of the field was, in the later historian's words, "the Solar refinery and the different companies dealing in oil commodities", with "little oil now being pumped in Allen County". [verified] — [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md). So the *field* was substantially finished before 1921 while the *city* kept growing — which is why this period's legacy is a site rather than an industry, and why 1910 as a placeholder is defensible for production and wrong for consequence. [inference]

The Lima businessman whose drilling produced the 1885 strike that opened the Lima oil field. [inference] He was drilling for natural gas, on the pattern of the Findlay gas boom to the north, and struck oil instead. [inference]

**His other business interests are now on record, and they are most of industrial Lima.** [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md), printed the year of the strike and therefore describing him entirely as he was before it:

**The paper mill matters to the received account.** A straw-board works is a fuel-hungry industry; his daughter Carrie married the secretary of the Lima Gaslight Company on January 7, 1885; and the same volume records gas shows across the county as an undeveloped prospect. [verified] — same source. That is the setting the drilling story requires, established independently of the story.

**The well is now on record and so is why he drilled it.** It was completed May 9, 1885 on the grounds of his own Lima Straw Board Works, by the contractors Brownyear and Martin, for a double purpose: better process water, and the natural gas that Findlay and Bowling Green had just found. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md). The corpus's `[inference]` that he was drilling for gas is verified, and gains a first motive nobody retells — he wanted water.

A second historian adds that he had "acquired the ownership of the city's first street railway — then a horse-car line — and secured the exclusive control of the Lima Strawboard Company", and was president of the Strawboard Association of the United States. [verified] — same source. And of the strike itself: "It was not a great success in itself but it was the pioneer stake in an industry that has produced millions for Allen County." [verified] — same source. The well that carries his name broke; [the second one](../event/lima-oil-strike.yml) made the field.

**He was leasing ground in the county four months after the strike.** An oil lease over part of the north-west quarter of section 17 in Bath Township ran to "B. C. Faurot et al", dated 29 September 1885 and recorded 30 April 1886; it was later released. [verified] — [Section Ground book list](../../catalog/allen-county-recorder-section-ground.md), volume 0028A page 164. It is the only record this corpus holds of him acting outside the city, and the only one of his dealings it has from a land record rather than from a county history.

**He is in the corpus because of what he explains.** This corpus established by coordinate, two phases before it had any history, that [the refinery](../site/lima-refinery.yml) stands on unincorporated ground in [Shawnee Township](../place/shawnee-township.yml) with a Lima postal address — and recorded that as a fact about tax base and authority without being able to say why. The engineer who located the Miami and Erie Canal, and who spent the last forty years of his life in the county it runs through. Died at [Delphos](../place/delphos.yml) in 1874. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md).

He surveyed the Shelby Canal in 1824, was connected with the canal surveys from July 1825 to 1831 and **located the Miami & Erie**, was appointed canal commissioner in 1832, and was elected to the newly organized Board of Public Works in 1835. In 1871, at seventy-eight, he still held the post of consulting engineer for the canal he had laid out. [verified] — same source.

**He is also a pioneer of [Marion Township](../place/marion-township.yml)**, which the 1885 compiler says of him plainly: he purchased land on Sections 20 and 18 in 1834 and ultimately settled there, making Delphos his home. [verified] — same source. The man who chose where the canal would run then lived on it.

**His board is the county's other canal name.** The State Board of Public Works he joined in 1835 is the body Col. Spencer sat on in 1848 — the man [Spencer Township](../place/spencer-township.yml) and, at one remove, [Spencerville](../place/spencerville.yml) are named for. [verified] — same source. Two of the four things in this county named or placed by the canal trace to one board.
