The county itself, as ground rather than as government: 402.545 square miles of land and 4.306 square miles of water in the northwest quarter of Ohio, with an internal point at 40.771627, -84.106103. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md).

The land is glacial till plain, flat and poorly drained, and its northern reach lay within the Great Black Swamp until nineteenth-century drainage. [inference] That flatness is the reason the county's transport history runs through a canal and then a railway junction rather than through a river port: its streams drain north and west to the Auglaize and the Maumee and were never navigable here.

**It is three places.** Lima holds 35,531 people; the three townships wrapped around it — [American](american-township.yml) 14,571, [Shawnee](shawnee-township.yml) 12,509 and [Bath](bath-township.yml) 9,399 — hold 36,479 between them, more than the city; and the other nine townships hold about thirty thousand across roughly five hundred square miles. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), sub-county file. That suburban middle is largely outside any municipality: Shawnee Township contains no incorporated place at all. [verified] — same source.

**Its whole population history, with no gaps.** The county has a count at every decennial census from 1830 to 2020 and an estimate for 2024: **578 (1830), 9,079 (1840), 12,100 (1850), 19,185 (1860), 23,623 (1870), 31,314 (1880), 40,644 (1890), 47,976 (1900), 56,580 (1910), 68,203 (1920), 69,419 (1930), 73,303 (1940), 88,183 (1950), 103,691 (1960), 111,144 (1970), 112,241 (1980), 109,755 (1990), 108,464 (2000), 106,331 (2010), 102,217 (2020) and 100,866 (2024).** [verified] — assembled from [1830–1900](../measure/allen-county-population-1830-1900.yml), [1890–1910](../measure/allen-county-townships-1890-1910.yml), [1940–1990](../measure/allen-county-population-1940-1990.yml) and the four modern measures — which rest between them on [Leeson 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md), [the 1910 Ohio supplement](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md), [the 1950 volume](../../catalog/census-1950-number-of-inhabitants-ohio.md), [CPH-2-37](../../catalog/census-cph-2-37-ohio.md), [the 1970s county estimates](../../catalog/census-county-estimates-1970s.md), [the intercensals](../../catalog/census-intercensal-2000-2010.md) and [Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md). Every figure is from a published table. Twenty-one observations, and until this phase two of them were missing.

**Once, nine-tenths of it was farms.** In 1910 the county held 2,939 farms covering 240,472 of its 259,840 acres — 92.5 per cent of the land area — with 203,222 acres improved and $25,992,184 of farm property standing on them. [verified] — [Abstract of the Thirteenth Census, Supplement for Ohio](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md); see [the county's farms](../measure/allen-county-farms-1900-1910.yml), [what they produced](../measure/allen-county-farm-output-1909.yml) and [its animals](../measure/allen-county-domestic-animals-1910.yml). That is the same census that counts 30,508 people in Lima, so the county was already more than half city by population while still being nine-tenths farm by ground. [inference]

**It is two-thirds farms now, and it is a hog county.** 178,921 acres in 2022 — 69.4 per cent of the land area — on 897 operations, of which 268 part-owners farm 78.4 per cent of the ground and more than half of all farmland is rented from somebody else. [verified] — [the Census of Agriculture](../../catalog/usda-census-of-agriculture.md); see [the modern farms](../measure/allen-county-farms-2002-2022.yml), [the livestock](../measure/allen-county-livestock-2002-2022.yml) and [the crops](../measure/allen-county-crops-2022.yml). The county held 31,741 hogs on 59 places in 2002 and 235,800 on 28 in 2022, and sells more of them than of anything else it raises.

So the county's other nine-tenths has an answer at both ends and none in the middle: 52,322 of the 61,551 acres that left the farms went in the ninety-two years no census in this catalog covers. [inference] — computed here from the two censuses. See [when the farmland went](../question/when-the-farmland-went.yml). The 1910 and 2022 farm counts are not subtracted anywhere in this corpus, because the two censuses define a farm differently; see [a farm count is a definition](../../decisions/a-farm-count-is-a-definition.yml).

**Who represents it, and under which map.** The county sends one member to the Ohio House from [the 78th District](../division/ohio-house-district-78-2023.yml) and one to the Ohio Senate from [the 12th](../division/ohio-senate-district-12-2023.yml), both under the legislative map adopted 29 September 2023; and it is not split between districts in either chamber. [verified] — [Ohio county elected officials lookup](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md); [inference] for the not-split, reasoned from the roster naming one of each. Its sitting member of Congress sits for the 4th District. [verified] — same source.

**It rose for a hundred and fifty years and has fallen for forty-four.** The peak is 1980 and the county is now smaller than it was in 1960. [inference] The first two figures count different ground — the [reorganization of 1848](../event/reorganization-of-1848.yml) moved 138 square miles — so the series is continuous only from 1850.

A township of 33.315 square miles about 9 miles west of the county's centre, internal point 40.734865, -84.272548. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), Ohio county subdivisions.

Its population was 2,070 at the 2020 estimates base and 2,049 in 2024. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), sub-county file. Its population fell by 21 over those four years, as all but two of the county's subdivisions did.
It contains no incorporated place; all of it is unincorporated. [verified] — same source, which lists no place within this township.

**No school district is named for it and three divide it**: 1,072 of its people are in [Spencerville Local](../jurisdiction/spencerville-local-school-district.yml), 665 in [Shawnee Local](../jurisdiction/shawnee-local-school-district.yml) and 324 in [Elida Local](../jurisdiction/elida-local-school-district.yml). [verified] — [2020 Census Block Assignment Files](../../catalog/census-block-assignment-2020.md) crossed with [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md) block geography. A township with no village and no district of its own has no institution that takes its name as a whole, which is worth knowing before reading anything into how little is written about it.

**Erected in 1830 by the commissioners of Mercer County** — the earliest township organization recorded in this county, and it happened two years before Allen County had a board of its own, while Allen was attached to Mercer for judicial purposes. Thirteen electors lived in it and twelve of them came to the organizing meeting; Samuel Baxter was chosen clerk and Daniel Hoak justice of the peace. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md).

**It is named for Fort Amanda**, built here in 1812 by Col. Poague's command and named for the colonel's wife. [verified] — same source. In the [reorganization of 1848](../event/reorganization-of-1848.yml) it lost sections 7 and 18 to [Spencer](spencer-township.yml) and was recomposed from the south half of Marion and its own north half. [verified] — same source.

**Earlier still, it was falling: 1,425 people in 1890, 1,384 in 1900 and 1,263 in 1910.** [verified] — [Abstract of the Thirteenth Census, Supplement for Ohio](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md); see [the 1890–1910 divisions](../measure/allen-county-townships-1890-1910.yml). So its low point is 975 in 1940 and its high point before the war is 1890, and the doubling below is measured from near the bottom of a fifty-year decline. [inference]

**It held 1,008 people in 1930, 975 in 1940 and 980 in 1950**, and 2,070 at the 2020 estimates base. [verified] — [1950 Census, Number of Inhabitants, Ohio](../../catalog/census-1950-number-of-inhabitants-ohio.md), Table 6; see [the township series](../measure/allen-county-townships-1930-1950.yml). So it doubled, and all of it happened after 1950 — through the 1930s and 1940s the township was flat and slightly falling. [inference] It has no incorporated place, so every one of those people was and is counted in unincorporated territory.
A township of 24.017 square miles wrapping the west and north of Lima, internal point 40.769378, -84.17822. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md).

It is the most populous township in the county outside Lima itself, and the Census Bureau's "balance of American township" figure — the township minus the incorporated villages inside it — is the larger part of that. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), sub-county file. Its population was 14,571 at the 2020 estimates base and 14,445 in 2024 — **the most populous civil subdivision in the county after Lima**, and 12,541 of the 2024 figure is the balance outside [Elida](elida.yml), the one village in it. [verified] — same source.

**Neither the refinery nor the tank plant is here.** This node claimed both stand on or near its boundary with Lima, and therefore that this township holds most of the county's heavy industry. Both are in [Shawnee Township](shawnee-township.yml), south of Lima; this township wraps Lima's west and north. [verified] — [Allen County GIS](../../catalog/allen-county-gis-downloads.md) and [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md), agreeing independently on both points. The claim is withdrawn entire rather than narrowed: it named two sites and was wrong about both.
It does hold a fifth of [census tract 39003010300](../division/census-tract-39003010300.yml) — 13,403,443 square metres and 408 people. [verified] — same source, block composition.

**This township was called German until some time after 1885.** The commissioners' act of December 6, 1831 established it "under the name German", over the territory running west from Section 3, Town 3, Range 6 to the old Amanda line. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md). That book's German Township "forms the geographical centre of the county", takes the Ottawa River in from [Shawnee](shawnee-township.yml) at Section 33, and passes it by Allentown and [Elida](elida.yml) into [Sugar Creek](sugar-creek-township.yml) — which is this township and no other, since Elida is in it and in nothing else. [inference] Its erection date therefore belongs here, and it makes this the third township the county had.

In 1848 it lost its north tier of sections to Sugar Creek and kept its name; in 1857 it gave 1,040 acres to Ottawa Township. [verified] — same source, and [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md) independently, giving the same acreage thirty-six years later.

**The name changed on August 16, 1918, and the reason was the war.** The citizens of German Township petitioned, and the Allen County commissioners acted — the same instrument that erected the county's townships and incorporated its villages. Article II of the petition says only "that good cause is shown"; the 1921 historian reads it plainly — "'good cause' means patriotism" — and sets it in its moment: "The name German had come into disfavor when the German nation changed its attitude toward the rest of the world. School books were undergoing changes at the time, and business concerns bearing the name German were eliminating the offensive designation, and the people of German Township were caught in the wave of popular sentiment." [verified] — [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md), which is a single witness read once for this date.

**The same page records the dissent**, three years after the fact: "there are residents of the township who a little later on would not have voted for the change, because of sacred associations in early history. They do not hold the German people responsible for the conduct of some of their leaders." [verified] — same source. The corpus had declined to assert the obvious motive; the motive is confirmed, and so is that it was contested at the time. **As German Township its line with Lima moved twice, and once each way.** Part of German was annexed to Lima city in 1902, and part of Lima city was annexed back to German in 1906. [verified] — [Abstract of the Thirteenth Census, Supplement for Ohio](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md), Allen County footnote. This is the earliest dated boundary event the corpus holds anywhere in the county, and the pattern it belongs to — four events into the city and two out of it, each outward one a year after an inward one — is set out at [Lima](lima.yml).

**As German Township it held 1,615 people in 1890, 1,951 in 1900 and 2,172 in 1910**, the Census using the old name at all three censuses. [verified] — [Abstract of the Thirteenth Census, Supplement for Ohio](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md); see [the 1890–1910 divisions](../measure/allen-county-townships-1890-1910.yml). It is one of only four of the county's twelve whose lowest recorded count is 1890 — it has grown at every observation the corpus holds, and ninefold since. [inference]

**It held 2,560 people in 1930 and 2,957 in 1940**, before Lima crossed into it: the 1950 return is 25,151 of which 19,270 is Lima city, leaving 5,881 outside the city. [verified] — [1950 Census, Number of Inhabitants, Ohio](../../catalog/census-1950-number-of-inhabitants-ohio.md), Table 6; see [the township series](../measure/allen-county-townships-1930-1950.yml). At 14,571 in 2020 it is **more than five and a half times its 1930 size outside the city**, the second fastest growth of the county's twelve townships. [inference] [Elida](elida.yml) ran 542, 551 and 607 across the same three censuses, so almost none of that growth is the village.

The Census returns it as American at all three of those censuses, the earliest being 1930. That is consistent with, and no more than consistent with, the [renaming of August 16, 1918](../question/what-became-of-german-and-ottawa-townships.yml): the first federal count after the change already carries the new name. [inference]

A township of 35.99 square miles about 11 miles south-east of the county's centre, internal point 40.695518, -83.928053. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), Ohio county subdivisions.

Its population was 2,764 at the 2020 estimates base and 2,819 in 2024. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), sub-county file. It is one of only two subdivisions in the county that grew over those four years, by 55.

It contains [Harrod](harrod.yml) [verified] — same source, which reports it as a place within this township — and also [Westminster](westminster.yml), a census designated place of 406 that the sub-county file does not list because it has no government. [verified] — [2020 Census Block Assignment Files](../../catalog/census-block-assignment-2020.md).

Its schools are split: 2,740 of its people are in [Allen East Local](../jurisdiction/allen-east-local-school-district.yml) and 17, on two blocks at the south-east corner, in Auglaize County's [Waynesfield-Goshen](../jurisdiction/waynesfield-goshen-local-school-district.yml). [verified] — same source, crossed with [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md) block geography.

**The continental divide runs through it.** Four of its census blocks — 99 people and 43 housing units, along the county's eastern edge between 40.6487 and 40.7104 north — are in [the Scioto basin](../natural-feature/scioto-river-basin.yml) and drain to the Ohio River and the Gulf of Mexico. They are the only ground in Allen County that does. [verified] — [USGS Watershed Boundary Dataset](../../catalog/usgs-watershed-boundary.md), by block composition.

**Established March 5, 1832 by order of the commissioners of Allen County** — the first township the county's own board created from nothing rather than inherited. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md).

**A township named Scioto was disestablished into it in December 1832** and attached to Auglaize "for judicial purposes"; until [Perry](perry-township.yml) was established in December 1833 its twelve eastern sections were part of this township. [verified] — same source. The county has carried no Scioto township since, and this township is still where [its Gulf-side ground](../natural-feature/scioto-river-basin.yml) lies — the only part of Allen County that drains to the Ohio.

**The later history says Scioto is unexplained; the earlier one explains it.** In 1921 Rusler writes that "when Allen County was organized in 1831, its four townships were Amanda, Bath, Jackson and Scioto; in 1832 there was a German but no Scioto and no explanation is offered about it." [verified] — [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md). The explanation is in the book on the shelf beside it: the commissioners disestablished Scioto in December 1832 and attached its district to this township for judicial purposes. The corpus's older source answers its newer source's stated gap — which is the argument for holding both.

**Its 1,929 people in 1890 stood as its highest count for the next sixty years**, against 1,909 in 1900 and 1,883 in 1910. [verified] — [Abstract of the Thirteenth Census, Supplement for Ohio](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md); see [the 1890–1910 divisions](../measure/allen-county-townships-1890-1910.yml). [Harrod](harrod.yml) ran 269, 370 and 474 across the same three censuses, so the village nearly doubled while the township slipped — the growth below is a recovery before it is an expansion. [inference]

**It held 1,675 people in 1930, 1,719 in 1940 and 1,912 in 1950**, and 2,764 at the 2020 estimates base. [verified] — [1950 Census, Number of Inhabitants, Ohio](../../catalog/census-1950-number-of-inhabitants-ohio.md), Table 6; see [the township series](../measure/allen-county-townships-1930-1950.yml). It has grown at every observation the corpus holds, which no other township here has done, and it is also one of only two subdivisions in the county that gained population between 2020 and 2024. [inference] [Harrod](harrod.yml) ran 421, 422 and 482, so the village has been about a quarter of the township throughout and is now a sixth.

A township of 30.698 square miles about 3 miles east of the county's centre, internal point 40.781965, -84.042618. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), Ohio county subdivisions.

Its population was 9,399 at the 2020 estimates base and 9,263 in 2024. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), sub-county file. Its population fell by 136 over those four years, as all but two of the county's subdivisions did. That makes it the third most populous of the county's thirteen civil subdivisions.
It contains no incorporated place; all of it is unincorporated. [verified] — same source, which lists no place within this township.

**It is older than the county's own government and no record of its erection survives.** The 1885 compiler, working from the commissioners' books, found the name and organization of Bath in use before Allen County was organized and "no record of its establishment either in the records of Allen or Mercer County"; he concedes that by 1831 it was a regularly organized township with Lima at its centre, with Chris. Wood, John Schrouf and James Daniels as justices. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md). This is the one township in the county whose erection is not on record anywhere the corpus has looked.

**Its boundary with Lima moved twice in four years, and once each way.** Part of Bath was annexed to Lima city in 1905, and part of Lima city was annexed back to Bath in 1903. [verified] — [Abstract of the Thirteenth Census, Supplement for Ohio](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md), Allen County footnote. Together with the annexation from Bath between 1980 and 1990, that is three dated boundary changes on this township's line with the city, spread across eighty-five years.

**It held 1,448 people in 1890, 1,517 in 1900 and 1,501 in 1910**, before the city arrived. [verified] — [Abstract of the Thirteenth Census, Supplement for Ohio](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md); see [the 1890–1910 divisions](../measure/allen-county-townships-1890-1910.yml). Its lowest recorded count is 1890 and it has grown six and a half times since, which is the third largest growth of the county's twelve townships. [inference]

**It held 2,875 people in 1930 and 3,438 in 1940**, before Lima crossed into it: the 1950 return is 22,919 of which 17,469 is Lima city, leaving 5,450 outside the city. [verified] — [1950 Census, Number of Inhabitants, Ohio](../../catalog/census-1950-number-of-inhabitants-ohio.md), Table 6; see [the township series](../measure/allen-county-townships-1930-1950.yml). At 9,399 in 2020 it is more than three times its 1930 size outside the city. [inference] The [refinery](../site/lima-refinery.yml) sits in [Shawnee](shawnee-township.yml) rather than here, but the annexations that took Lima's corporation into Bath are the same process, and one of them is dated: the city annexed from Bath between 1980 and 1990.

A village of 0.63 square miles in [Richland Township](richland-township.yml), about 8 miles north-east of the county's centre, internal point 40.832487, -83.973383. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), Ohio places.

Its population was 321 at the 2020 estimates base and 314 in 2024. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), sub-county file. It lost 7 people over those four years.

**All of it is in Allen County.** The same file marks a place that crosses a county line with `(pt.)` and marks this one plainly, which is what separates it from [Bluffton](bluffton.yml) and [Delphos](delphos.yml). [verified] — same source.

**The village is one voting precinct, exactly.** Precinct `BEAVERDAM` holds 319 people and 151 housing units, and every block in it is in the village and every block of the village is in it. [verified] — [2020 Census Block Assignment Files](../../catalog/census-block-assignment-2020.md) crossed with [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md) block geography. Four of the county's nine municipalities are single precincts on these terms; the other five are split, and [Lima](lima.yml) is cut into 23. [verified] — [the county's voting districts](../measure/allen-county-voting-districts-2020.yml).

**The Census spelt it as two words until at least 1940.** "Beaverdam village returned in 1940 as Beaver Dam." [verified] — [1950 Census, Number of Inhabitants, Ohio](../../catalog/census-1950-number-of-inhabitants-ohio.md), Table 6, Allen County footnote. So the one-word form is the later one and the change is datable to between 1940 and 1950 in federal usage. [inference] The 1885 history agrees: it spells the place "Beaver Dam" throughout — scores of times in each of the two scans the corpus holds — and never as one word in either. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md), both scans. The two disagree on the tally, because they break lines differently; they do not disagree on the form. Which is what the etymology below would lead one to expect, and is the kind of agreement that makes the etymology likelier rather than merely repeated.

**Established in 1853, and named for the beaver dams** that were abundant near the original town site. [verified] — [Allen County](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md), cities and villages page. The [Village of Beaverdam](../jurisdiction/village-of-beaverdam.yml) was incorporated twenty-five years later, in 1878.

**Frederick Shull established it**, laying it out on Sections 29, 30, 31 and 32 of [Richland Township](richland-township.yml) — the original town bounded by North Street, Lima Street and Church Street. He was the village's postmaster when the office moved here about 1849, four years before the plat. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md). The county's page gives 1853 and no name; this source gives the name, and the two agree on the year against an OCR reading of 1858 in the other scan — see [two scans of one book](../../decisions/two-scans-of-one-book.yml), where an unrelated source settling a scanning dispute is the case the rule was written for.

**Its ground is the one piece of this county the survey grid cannot name.** Beaverdam's internal point falls inside the county's polygon for T3S R8E §5, and that polygon is 1,282 acres on a footprint 1.04 by 2.01 miles — one section's number drawn over two sections' ground. No parcel contains the point either, so there is no second witness. [verified] — [the survey sections](../measure/allen-county-survey-sections.yml).

nodes.label: Bluffton

properties.area_sq_mi: 3.652 land, 0.069 water (2020) — whole village, both counties

blocks.text: A village of 3.652 square miles in the county's north, internal point 40.892048, -83.887793. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md).

Like [Delphos](delphos.yml), Bluffton straddles a county line — here the Allen–Hancock line — and appears in Allen County tables as `Bluffton village (pt.)`, with 3,762 in the 2020 estimates base against a village total that is larger. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md). So its edge to the county is `partially-within`, not `within`.

It is the seat of Bluffton University and has a Swiss Mennonite settlement history that distinguishes it from the rest of the county. [inference] **It was originally known as Shannon.** [verified] — [Allen County](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md), cities and villages page, which also names [Bluffton University](../organization/bluffton-university.yml) here and its Mennonite affiliation.

**Platted in 1837 as Shannon, by Joseph Deford**, on Sections 1 and 12 of [Richland Township](richland-township.yml) — four blocks bounded by Jackson, Monroe, Jefferson and Riley streets. **The name was changed to Bluffton in 1872-73**, "although long prior to this the latter name was bestowed upon it". [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md), both scans agreeing. At 1837 it is the county's second-oldest platted town after [Lima](lima.yml), and it was called something else for the first thirty-five years of that.

**Its bank is why John Dillinger was in the Allen County jail.** He was brought up from Dayton in the autumn of 1933 charged with robbing "the Bluffton, O., Commercial Bank of $2200", and was awaiting trial at Lima when three men shot the sheriff and took him out of the cell. [verified] — [Chronicling America](../../catalog/chronicling-america.md), *The Washington Daily News*, 13 October 1933; see [the raid on the Allen County jail](../event/allen-county-jail-raid-1933.yml).

**Its two witnesses to its own ground disagree, and the county line is why.** The section grid puts Bluffton's internal point in T2S R8E §1; the parcel containing the same point is numbered into §12, directly south. [verified] — [the survey sections](../measure/allen-county-survey-sections.yml). The point is the *whole* village's, Hancock County included, so it sits near that section line rather than inside either section with a margin — which is the same straddle that makes this village `Bluffton village (pt.)` in every census table. [inference]

refusals: The corpus does not assert its section.

blocks.text: A village of 0.277 square miles in [Monroe Township](monroe-township.yml), about 4 miles north of the county's centre, internal point 40.830753, -84.084489. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), Ohio places.

Its population was 519 at the 2020 estimates base and 508 in 2024. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), sub-county file. It lost 11 people over those four years.

**All of it is in Allen County.** The same file marks a place that crosses a county line with `(pt.)` and marks this one plainly, which is what separates it from [Bluffton](bluffton.yml) and [Delphos](delphos.yml). [verified] — same source.

[verified] — [2020 Census Block Assignment Files](../../catalog/census-block-assignment-2020.md) crossed with [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md) block geography. Four of the county's nine municipalities are single precincts on these terms; the other five are split, and [Lima](lima.yml) is cut into 23. [verified] — [the county's voting districts](../measure/allen-county-voting-districts-2020.yml).

**Established in 1848 as West Cairo**, and renamed Cairo in 1922. [verified] — [Allen County](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md), cities and villages page. Main Street here was part of the Lincoln Highway, the country's first coast-to-coast road. [verified] — same source.

**It was platted in 1848 by Jacob Miller**, on Sections 29, 30, 31 and 32 of [Monroe Township](monroe-township.yml), running east from the Brenneman farm and lying mainly west of the Perrysburg Road at its crossing with the Bucyrus Road. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md). The county's own page gives 1848 without a founder; this is a second source arriving at the same year by a different route, seventy years earlier.

**The corporation dates from April 12, 1875**, twenty-seven years after the plat: "the village lay dormant awaiting developments until April 12, 1875, when it was organized and it still maintains a corporate existence." [verified] — [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md). A single witness read once, and the only incorporation date the corpus has for this village.

**A third witness for the older name, and the first federal one.** The 1910 census returns it as *West Cairo village*, at 386 in 1910, 338 in 1900 and 325 in 1890. [verified] — [Abstract of the Thirteenth Census, Supplement for Ohio](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md). So the name was in federal use as West Cairo as late as 1913, which sits inside the window the two county histories already gave and narrows nothing — but it does mean the 1922 renaming changed a name the Census Bureau was using, not only a local one. [inference]

properties.area_sq_mi: 3.322 land, 0.045 water (2020) — whole city, both counties

blocks.text: A city of 3.322 square miles on the county's western edge, internal point 40.846581, -84.336474. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md).

Delphos straddles the Allen–Van Wert county line, and the Census Bureau's Allen County rows record it as `Delphos city (pt.)` for exactly that reason: the 3,941 counted there in the 2020 estimates base is the Allen County portion, not the city. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md). Any figure for Delphos taken from an Allen County table and reported as the city's population understates it. Its edge to the county is `partially-within` for the same reason, matching the qualification [the Village of Bluffton](../jurisdiction/village-of-bluffton.yml) already carries.

The city grew as a port on the Miami and Erie Canal, which is why it sits on the county edge rather than on any natural centre. [inference] See [the Miami and Erie Canal](../site/miami-and-erie-canal.yml). **It was four towns before it was one.** The county records Delphos as originally Howard, Section Ten, West Bredeick and East Bredeick, merged into a single town in 1851. [verified] — [Allen County](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md), cities and villages page. That is the only municipality in the county the source describes as made rather than founded, and it is a different kind of origin from a platted town site: four settlements with four names, none of which survives on the map.

**The merged town was incorporated by an act of February 7, 1851**, and held its first election on March 3, returning Lester Bliss as mayor and Smith Talbott as recorder. The corporation spent $80.67 in its first year. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md), both scans agreeing on the act's date. That puts a day on the year [the county's own page](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md) gives for the merger, from a source that had never seen it.

**Section Ten was a place before it was a name.** The tract was the Ten-Mile Woods: in 1834 William Brady and William Scott cut a road from the Auglaize River through it to Van Wert and "not even one cabin was to be seen in all that distance". [verified] — same source. The town's first newspaper, in 1848, was still called the *Section Ten Budget*.

A village of 1.102 square miles in [American Township](american-township.yml), about 5 miles west of the county's centre, internal point 40.78699, -84.199651. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), Ohio places.

Its population was 1,924 at the 2020 estimates base and 1,904 in 2024. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), sub-county file. It lost 20 people over those four years.

**All of it is in Allen County.** The same file marks a place that crosses a county line with `(pt.)` and marks this one plainly, which is what separates it from [Bluffton](bluffton.yml) and [Delphos](delphos.yml). [verified] — same source.

**Established in 1852**, and the [Village of Elida](../jurisdiction/village-of-elida.yml) incorporated in 1878. [verified] — [Allen County](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md), cities and villages page.

**It was platted in 1852 by Griffith John**, on Sections 7, 8, 17 and 18 of what was then German Township — now [American](american-township.yml). [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md). Griffith John is the same man who petitioned the commissioners in March 1833 to enlarge German Township and who assessed its district in 1846: the village was laid out by the township's own long-standing figure, on ground he had spent twenty years enlarging. [verified] — same source.

**It is named for the founder's brother.** "Griffith John was its founder, and it bears the name of his brother Elida John who never lived in the community." [verified] — [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md), which also confirms 1852 and the 1878 incorporation. That is a single witness read once, and it is the only etymology the corpus has for this village; the commonly repeated alternative — that Elida is a contraction of two women's names — appears in no source held here.

properties.former_names: Listed as "Fort Shawnee village" in Census files through the 2010 census, and as "Fort Shawnee CDP" in the 2020 geography. [verified]

blocks.text: A community of 9.51 square miles south of Lima, internal point 40.681287, -84.149835. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), where it is listed as `Fort Shawnee CDP`.

It was an incorporated village through at least 2010: the intercensal file lists `Fort Shawnee village` with 3,866 at the 2000 base and 3,726 at the 2010 census. [verified] — [Census Intercensal Estimates, 2000–2010](../../catalog/census-intercensal-2000-2010.md). In the 2020 geography it is a census designated place, and the Vintage 2024 sub-county file does not list it at all. [verified]

It lies within [Shawnee Township](shawnee-township.yml): all 120 of its census blocks do, and its 6,263 people at the 2020 census are half the township's 12,482. [verified] — [2020 Census Block Assignment Files](../../catalog/census-block-assignment-2020.md) crossed with [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md) block geography. That 6,263 is **not** to be read against the 3,726 the village recorded in 2010: the CDP outline is drawn by the Census Bureau and the village boundary was drawn by annexation, so the two figures count different ground. [inference] As a CDP it is a statistical outline and not a boundary anyone is governed by, and it does not reach the tank plant a mile and a half north of its internal point — the plant is in Shawnee Township and in no place at all. [verified] — [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md), point-in-polygon against the 2020 CDP layer.

An unincorporated community of 2.286 square miles in the north-west of the county, internal point 40.845448, -84.182796, with 345 people at the 2020 census. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), where it is listed as `Gomer CDP`, and [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md) for the count.

It lies wholly within [Sugar Creek Township](sugar-creek-township.yml) — all twelve of its census blocks do, and it is the only settlement in the county's least populous township. [verified] — [2020 Census Block Assignment Files](../../catalog/census-block-assignment-2020.md) crossed with TIGERweb block geography. Its 345 people are 28 per cent of that township's 1,231.

**It was laid out in 1850 by Samuel Ramsay and James Nicholas**, on Sections 20, 21, 28 and 29, with the first and second additions made by D. D. Nicholas. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md), which also records it as the only post office in the township — as it is still the township's only settlement.

**The Welsh settlement is on record.** The Welsh Congregationalists built a house of worship just south of the village in 1873 at a cost of over $16,000 — an enormous sum for a hamlet in a township of a thousand people — and the Welsh had already put up another two and a half miles east. [verified] — same source, which names Welsh families among the township's farmers. The local account of a Welsh settlement here is therefore not folklore.

Four of the county's nine municipalities are single precincts on these terms; the other five are split, and [Lima](lima.yml) is cut into 23. [verified] — [the county's voting districts](../measure/allen-county-voting-districts-2020.yml).

**Named for the Harrod family**, who settled the ground in 1841; the village was established in 1884, forty-three years later. [verified] — [Allen County](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md), cities and villages page. It is the only municipality in the county the source names a family for.

**The Harrod was William Harrod**, born in Knox County, Ohio on October 4, 1819, of Pennsylvania stock and from a family among Knox County's early pioneers. He settled on the land in 1841 and still occupied it in 1885; his son J. M. Harrod was born in [Auglaize Township](auglaize-township.yml) on March 7, 1852 and farmed there, with the post office already carrying the family name. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md). The county's page gives 1841 with no name; this is the same year from an unrelated source, with a person attached to it.

A township of 35.719 square miles about 10 miles east of the county's centre, internal point 40.781058, -83.920597. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), Ohio county subdivisions.

Its population was 3,144 at the 2020 estimates base and 3,071 in 2024. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), sub-county file. Its population fell by 73 over those four years, as all but two of the county's subdivisions did.
It contains [Lafayette](lafayette.yml). [verified] — same source, which reports it as a place within this township.

Wood and Samuel Stewart first sat. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md), which records the petition twice, in this township's chapter and in [Bath's](bath-township.yml). The board also authorized a township of Sciota that day. That makes this township's erection the earliest dated act of the county's own government anywhere in this corpus — see [when the county was organized](../question/when-allen-county-was-organized.yml).
Its bounds were altered in December 1834 and the original Township 3 south, Range 8 east was set off again under the same name. [verified] — same source.

**It held 1,818 people in 1890, 1,931 in 1900 and 1,810 in 1910**, and that 1900 figure was its highest until sometime after 1950. [verified] — [Abstract of the Thirteenth Census, Supplement for Ohio](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md); see [the 1890–1910 divisions](../measure/allen-county-townships-1890-1910.yml). [Lafayette](lafayette.yml) was 316 in 1900 and 418 in 1910; the 1890 figure is not returned separately. [verified] — same source.

[verified] — [1950 Census, Number of Inhabitants, Ohio](../../catalog/census-1950-number-of-inhabitants-ohio.md), Table 6; see [the township series](../measure/allen-county-townships-1930-1950.yml). It has roughly doubled, and [Lafayette](lafayette.yml) — 382, 411 and 444 across the same censuses — has not, so the growth is outside the village.

A village of 0.233 square miles in [Jackson Township](jackson-township.yml), about 8 miles east of the county's centre, internal point 40.758911, -83.949922. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), Ohio places.

Its population was 402 at the 2020 estimates base and 395 in 2024. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), sub-county file. It lost 7 people over those four years.

**All of it is in Allen County.** The same file marks a place that crosses a county line with `(pt.)` and marks this one plainly, which is what separates it from [Bluffton](bluffton.yml) and [Delphos](delphos.yml). [verified] — same source.

[verified] — [2020 Census Block Assignment Files](../../catalog/census-block-assignment-2020.md) crossed with [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md) block geography. Four of the county's nine municipalities are single precincts on these terms; the other five are split, and [Lima](lima.yml) is cut into 23. [verified] — [the county's voting districts](../measure/allen-county-voting-districts-2020.yml).

The [Village of Lafayette](../jurisdiction/village-of-lafayette.yml) was **incorporated in 1868**, the earliest incorporation this corpus holds for any municipality in the county. [verified] — [Allen County](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md), cities and villages page.

**It was platted by William B. Weyer**, in Section 28 of [Jackson Township](jackson-township.yml), laid out in regular blocks north of Sugar Street with Weyer's own western and southern additions around it. **The commissioners granted authority to organize the village on September 3, 1867**, on M. C. Murnagh's petition, and the first election was held March 13, 1868. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md). That is the county's own record behind the bare "incorporated in 1868" on its website, and it shows the two dates the website collapses: the authority and the election fall in different years.

nodes.label: Lima

blocks.text: The county seat and largest settlement, 13.617 square miles of land with an internal point at 40.740679, -84.112091. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md). It is the only place in Allen County that the Census Bureau treats as its own county subdivision rather than as a village inside a township, which is the tabular trace of its having been separated from the townships around it. [verified] — same source, county subdivision file.

**Ten phases of counting this city and this is the first that says who is in it.** 35,304 people in the 2023 survey: 64.0 per cent white, 23.5 per cent Black, 4.8 per cent Hispanic. Median household income $43,370 ± $2,298; 24.8 per cent below the poverty line; median age 35.4. [verified] — [American Community Survey](../../catalog/census-acs-summary-file.md); see [income and poverty](../measure/allen-county-income-and-poverty-2023.yml), [race](../measure/allen-county-race-2023.yml) and [age](../measure/allen-county-age-structure-2023.yml).

**It is a third of the county's people, two thirds of its poor, and three quarters of its Black residents.** 34.7 per cent of the population, 8,214 of the county's 12,815 people below poverty, and 8,290 of its 10,805 Black residents. [verified] — same source. The twelve townships hold the remainder and all three sums close exactly on the county's own rows.

**Its household income is 48 per cent of the township across its southern line.** $43,370 against Shawnee Township's $91,134 — a gap of $47,764 against a combined margin of $6,359 — and 55 per cent of the national figure. [verified] — same source.

This does not establish that Lima is the poorest subdivision in the county. Perry Township's median household income is higher by $9,902 against a combined margin of $11,142, and two figures that close cannot be ordered from this source. [verified] — see [a survey is not a count](../../decisions/a-survey-is-not-a-count.yml).

**And it is the young end of this county, not the old one.** Median age 35.4 against the county's 39.7, 15.6 per cent over 65 against 18.7, and a higher share under 18. Eleven of the twelve townships are older. [verified] — same source. A city losing a third of its people over fifty years is not, on this evidence, losing them to age.

**It is where the county rents, and where the county's empty houses are.** 46.4 per cent of its occupied units are owner-occupied, against 72.0 to 91.0 per cent in every township; it holds 35.4 per cent of the county's housing and 48.2 per cent of its vacant housing. Its median house is worth $95,900 where Shawnee Township's, across the southern line, is $210,200. [verified] — [the housing stock](../measure/allen-county-housing-stock-2023.yml).

**The median house standing in Lima was built in 1953**, twenty years before the median house in the three townships that ring it, and 34.9 per cent of the city's housing predates 1940 against 6.4 to 7.1 per cent in those three. [verified] — [when the housing was built](../measure/allen-county-housing-age-2023.yml).

**Borrowing against a house here is the hard thing, and buying one is a little harder too.** Across 2018–2024, mortgages to purchase in the city's census tracts were denied at 13.3 per cent against 10.8 elsewhere in Allen County, and every other purpose at 37.7 against 21.5. [verified] — [seven years of the register](../measure/allen-county-home-lending-2018-2024.yml). Twenty-one per cent of the 2023 denials here cite collateral against 13 per cent elsewhere. [verified] — [the single year](../measure/allen-county-home-lending-2023.yml). Collateral is the house. [inference]

This node said until now that buying a house here was no harder than buying one anywhere in the county. That was 2023, the only year of seven in which Lima's purchase rate is the lower one, and it is withdrawn. [verified] — see [a rule is not a habit](../../decisions/a-rule-is-not-a-habit.yml).

**It tripled after the oil, peaked at the 1970 census and has lost a third of itself since.** 757 in 1850, 7,567 in 1880, 21,723 in 1900, 41,326 in 1920, 42,287 in 1930, 44,711 in 1940, 50,246 in 1950, 51,037 in 1960, **53,734 in 1970**, 47,827 in 1980, 45,549 in 1990, 40,307 in 2000, 38,771 in 2010, 35,579 in 2020. [verified] — [1850–1960](../measure/lima-population-1850-1960.yml) and [1970–1990](../measure/lima-population-1970-1990.yml). **Every count rises to 1970 and every count falls after it**, so the peak is a census year and not an artefact of where the corpus's data began. The 1920 figure was 41,306 here until the Census contradicted the county history that supplied it.

**It lies in four townships, and the Census has said so since 1950.** American, Bath, Perry and Shawnee held 19,270, 17,469, 10,895 and 2,612 of the city's people at that census. [verified] — [1950 Census, Number of Inhabitants, Ohio](../../catalog/census-1950-number-of-inhabitants-ohio.md), Table 6. Those are the same four [Ottawa Township](../question/what-became-of-german-and-ottawa-townships.yml) was carved out of in 1857, and the 1940 census had returned the whole city as coextensive with Ottawa, which the 1950 volume calls nonexistent. [verified] — same source.

**Its boundary has moved in both directions, and the record starts in 1902.** "Parts of German and Bath townships annexed to Lima city in 1902 and 1905, respectively; parts of Lima city annexed to Bath and German townships in 1903 and 1906, respectively." [verified] — [Abstract of the Thirteenth Census, Supplement for Ohio](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md), Allen County footnote. Then "part of Shawnee township annexed to Lima city in 1944" and annexations from American, Bath and Shawnee between 1980 and 1990. [verified] — [1950 Census, Number of Inhabitants, Ohio](../../catalog/census-1950-number-of-inhabitants-ohio.md) and [1990 Census, Population and Housing Unit Counts, Ohio](../../catalog/census-cph-2-37-ohio.md).

Six boundary events across ninety years, four into the city and **two out of it**, and the two outward ones each follow an inward one by a year. [inference] The caveat this corpus carries about the city's counts not being comparable across time now has dates attached, and it is older and less one-directional than the caveat assumed.

**Its wards are on record for 1910**: 5,150, 8,010, 7,830 and 9,518, summing to the city's 30,508. [verified] — same 1910 source. Four wards, and the corpus holds no other ward-level figure for any place in the county except Delphos in the same year and Lima's four in 1881.

Lima is the county's industrial centre: the 1885 oil strike, the locomotive works, and the tank plant are all here or on its edge. [inference] This node used to add "and the reason its history is not an agricultural one", which the county's own figures do not bear — in 1910, with Lima already holding more than half the county's people, 92.5 per cent of the county's land was still in farms. [verified] — [Abstract of the Thirteenth Census, Supplement for Ohio](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md); see [the county's farms](../measure/allen-county-farms-1900-1910.yml). Lima is why the county's history is not *only* agricultural. [inference] Its population has been falling since the 1970s and continues to fall — see [Lima population, 2020](../measure/lima-population-2020.yml) and [Lima population, 2024](../measure/lima-population-2024.yml).

**Its schools are not one system.** The city's 35,579 people at the 2020 census divide among five school districts: 27,821 in [Lima City](../jurisdiction/lima-city-school-district.yml), 4,849 in [Elida Local](../jurisdiction/elida-local-school-district.yml), 1,573 in [Bath Local](../jurisdiction/bath-local-school-district.yml), 1,033 in [Shawnee Local](../jurisdiction/shawnee-local-school-district.yml) and 303 in [Perry Local](../jurisdiction/perry-local-school-district.yml). [verified] — [2020 Census Block Assignment Files](../../catalog/census-block-assignment-2020.md) crossed with [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md) block geography, block by block. A fifth of the city is outside the district that carries its name — the shape annexation leaves when the school boundaries do not move with the corporate one.

**The most widely reported hour in its history was in the county jail.** On the night of 12 October 1933 three armed men walked in, shot Sheriff Jess L. Sarber, freed the prisoner John Dillinger and drove west out of town; the three were tried here the following spring under a National Guard detachment with machine guns at the approaches to the jail. [verified] — [Chronicling America](../../catalog/chronicling-america.md); see [the raid on the Allen County jail](../event/allen-county-jail-raid-1933.yml). It is the only thing this corpus records happening in Lima between the oil boom and the 1970s. [verified] — the corpus's own event nodes.

**Founded in 1831**, and the county seat. [verified] — [Allen County](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md), cities and villages page — which puts it on Interstate 75 about 72 miles north of Dayton and 78 south of Toledo, the county's own way of saying where it is.

**It is also where the county's minority vote lives, and where it is shrinking fastest.** Eleven of Allen County's 88 precincts went to Biden in 2020 and ten of them are here; the county as a whole went 69 to 29 the other way. [verified] — [OpenElections](../../catalog/openelections-ohio.md). The city holds a third of the county's people, most of its density, five school districts and 23 of its 88 precincts, and on every one of those measures it is the part that does not resemble the rest.

Between 2016 and 2020 its 23 precincts moved toward the Republicans by a mean of **3.2 points** while the county's other 65 moved 1.6 — the city drifting right about twice as fast as the ground around it, from a much more Democratic starting point. [verified] — same source, computed across three general elections. So the county's political division is narrowing from the city's side, which is the opposite of the direction its [population decline](../period/depopulation.yml) runs.
Pronounced LY-muh, not like the Peruvian capital. [inference]

refusals: This does not establish that Lima is the poorest subdivision in the county.

blocks.text: A township of 42.371 square miles about 10 miles west of the county's centre, internal point 40.81041, -84.292789. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), Ohio county subdivisions.

Its population was 6,629 at the 2020 estimates base and 6,731 in 2024. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), sub-county file. It is one of only two subdivisions in the county that grew over those four years, by 102.
It contains [Delphos](delphos.yml). [verified] — same source, which reports it as a place within this township.

**Set off from the north end of [Amanda](amanda-township.yml) in December 1833** by the commissioners of Allen County, on a petition from the settlers of Township 3 south, Range 5 east. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md).

**Its present shape dates from 1848, not 1833.** In the [reorganization of that February](../event/reorganization-of-1848.yml) the original township was cut in half — the south half went into Amanda — and six sections from Jennings Township were added, giving the forty-two square miles it still has. [verified] — same source. Its first trustees after the change were Christian Stukey, Michael Swisher and Thomas J. Fair.

**It held 4,723 people in 1890, 4,573 in 1900 and 4,665 in 1910** — already the county's largest township outside Lima, and already barely moving. [verified] — [Abstract of the Thirteenth Census, Supplement for Ohio](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md); see [the 1890–1910 divisions](../measure/allen-county-townships-1890-1910.yml). [Delphos](delphos.yml)'s Allen County part ran 2,331, 2,289 and 2,556, and the whole city across both counties 4,516, 4,517 and 5,038, which is the earliest figure the corpus holds for Delphos as a single place. [verified] — same source.

**It was the county's largest township outside Lima in 1930**, with 4,959 people, against 4,924 in 1940 and 5,382 in 1950. [verified] — [1950 Census, Number of Inhabitants, Ohio](../../catalog/census-1950-number-of-inhabitants-ohio.md), Table 6; see [the township series](../measure/allen-county-townships-1930-1950.yml). At 6,629 in 2020 it has grown by a third in ninety years, the fourth slowest of the twelve, and the reason is [Delphos](delphos.yml): the city's Allen County part ran 3,055, 3,086 and 3,418 across those three censuses and has barely moved since. [inference] A township that was largest because it held a city stayed middling because the city stopped growing.

A township of 36.094 square miles about 7 miles north of the county's centre, internal point 40.864357, -84.060914. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), Ohio county subdivisions.

Its population was 2,050 at the 2020 estimates base and 2,005 in 2024. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), sub-county file. Its population fell by 45 over those four years, as all but two of the county's subdivisions did. That makes it the 11th most populous of the county's thirteen civil subdivisions.
It contains [Cairo](cairo.yml). [verified] — same source, which reports it as a place within this township.

Three school districts divide it, and one of them is not an Allen County district at all: 1,129 of its people are in [Bath Local](../jurisdiction/bath-local-school-district.yml), 489 in Putnam County's [Columbus Grove Local](../jurisdiction/columbus-grove-local-school-district.yml), and 449 in [Bluffton Exempted Village](../jurisdiction/bluffton-exempted-village-school-district.yml). [verified] — [2020 Census Block Assignment Files](../../catalog/census-block-assignment-2020.md) crossed with [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md) block geography.

**Organized in 1835 as a township of Putnam County**, on a petition to that county's commissioners, with John Peters, Peter Harpster and Anthony Early as trustees, Benjamin Parker clerk and Luke Tipton justice of the peace. **It was not in Allen County until 1848**, when this portion of Putnam was attached in the [reorganization](../event/reorganization-of-1848.yml) — which let it keep both its name and its organization while every township around it was recomposed. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md).

**It was largest in 1890, at 1,995 people, then 1,875 in 1900 and 1,768 in 1910.** [verified] — [Abstract of the Thirteenth Census, Supplement for Ohio](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md); see [the 1890–1910 divisions](../measure/allen-county-townships-1890-1910.yml). It fell at every count the corpus holds from 1890 to 1930 and is 2,050 today, **three per cent above where it started** — the least changed of the county's twelve townships across a hundred and thirty years. [inference] [Cairo](cairo.yml) appears as *West Cairo village* at all three, at 325, 338 and 386, which is a federal witness for the older name. [verified] — same source.

**It held 1,591 people in 1930, 1,622 in 1940 and 1,699 in 1950**, and 2,050 at the 2020 estimates base. [verified] — [1950 Census, Number of Inhabitants, Ohio](../../catalog/census-1950-number-of-inhabitants-ohio.md), Table 6; see [the township series](../measure/allen-county-townships-1930-1950.yml). [Cairo](cairo.yml) ran 374, 440 and 505 across the same three censuses — the village grew by a third while the township grew by a fifteenth, so through the 1930s and 1940s Monroe was concentrating into its village. [inference]

A township of 32.704 square miles about 8 miles south-east of the county's centre, internal point 40.675113, -84.041425. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), Ohio county subdivisions.

Its population was 3,377 at the 2020 estimates base and 3,333 in 2024. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), sub-county file. Its population fell by 44 over those four years, as all but two of the county's subdivisions did.
It contains no incorporated place; all of it is unincorporated. [verified] — same source, which lists no place within this township.

**Established by the county board in December 1833 and organized in April 1834** at the house of Joseph Crossley, with Hugh Skilling Sr., John Ridenour and Joseph Crossley elected trustees. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md). Its twelve western sections had until then belonged to [Auglaize Township](auglaize-township.yml). [verified] — same source.

**It held 1,537 people in 1890, 1,467 in 1900 and 1,602 in 1910.** [verified] — [Abstract of the Thirteenth Census, Supplement for Ohio](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md); see [the 1890–1910 divisions](../measure/allen-county-townships-1890-1910.yml). Outside Lima it has slightly more than doubled since, to 3,377, and almost all of that had already arrived by 1950, when the township outside the city held 3,312. [inference] Seventy years of the last hundred and thirty added sixty-five people to it.

**It held 1,515 people in 1930 — the smallest of the county's twelve — and 1,944 in 1940**, before Lima crossed into it: the 1950 return is 14,207 of which 10,895 is Lima city, leaving 3,312 outside the city. [verified] — [1950 Census, Number of Inhabitants, Ohio](../../catalog/census-1950-number-of-inhabitants-ohio.md), Table 6; see [the township series](../measure/allen-county-townships-1930-1950.yml). At 3,377 in 2020 the township outside Lima has gained sixty-five people in seventy years. [inference] It is the clearest case in the county of a township that grew by being annexed rather than by being settled: the ground kept filling and the city kept taking it.

A township of 41.648 square miles about 11 miles north-east of the county's centre, internal point 40.869365, -83.936562. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), Ohio county subdivisions.

Its population was 5,889 at the 2020 estimates base and 5,775 in 2024. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), sub-county file. Its population fell by 114 over those four years, as all but two of the county's subdivisions did.
It contains [Beaverdam](beaverdam.yml) and [Bluffton](bluffton.yml). [verified] — same source, which reports them as places within this township.

**Organized in 1835 as a township of Putnam County**, on the petition of David Miller and others, with Henry Shank and Daniel Goble the first justices and Henry Carter the first constable. **It was not in Allen County until 1848**, when the [reorganization](../event/reorganization-of-1848.yml) added Riley Township's south tier to it. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md).

**It is named for Richland County, Ohio.** Henry Carter's reminiscence, recorded in 1885, credits David Miller — a shoemaker "just in from Richland County" — with pushing the new township through and giving it his former county's name. [verified] — same source. That is a settler's recollection of fifty years earlier, not a record entry, and it is the only name origin in the county that comes with the person who chose it.

**It held 3,434 people in 1890, 4,099 in 1900 and 4,214 in 1910.** [verified] — [Abstract of the Thirteenth Census, Supplement for Ohio](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md); see [the 1890–1910 divisions](../measure/allen-county-townships-1890-1910.yml). 1890 is its lowest recorded count, so unlike most of the county's townships it did not empty in the first half of the century — it only paused. [inference] [Bluffton](bluffton.yml) ran 1,290, 1,783 and 1,953 and [Beaverdam](beaverdam.yml) 397, 477 and 455, the village spelt *Beaver Dam* here as it is in the 1885 history. [verified] — same source.

**It held 3,914 people in 1930, 3,765 in 1940 and 4,179 in 1950**, and 5,889 at the 2020 estimates base. [verified] — [1950 Census, Number of Inhabitants, Ohio](../../catalog/census-1950-number-of-inhabitants-ohio.md), Table 6; see [the township series](../measure/allen-county-townships-1930-1950.yml). Its loss of 149 across the 1930s is the largest of the five townships that fell in that decade. [inference] [Bluffton](bluffton.yml) ran 2,035, 2,077 and 2,423 and [Beaverdam](beaverdam.yml) 360, 377 and 450, so the villages held their ground while the countryside around them emptied and then refilled.
A township of 28.97 square miles immediately south and west of Lima, internal point 40.691353, -84.170464. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md).

**Its name was chosen for that reason and the record says so.** The commissioners, in session December 1, 1834, granted the petition of the people of Shawnee to set Township 4, Range 6 off from the Hog Creek Reservation "under the name of its original inhabitants"; the first meeting was held on December 13 in Ezekiel Hover's log house, and the list of voters ran to twelve names. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md). The township was cut twice afterwards: its south tier went to the new county of Auglaize in 1848, and the north-east quarter of Section 1 to Ottawa Township in May 1857. [verified] — same source. The name is the clearest surviving toponymic trace in the county's civil geography of the people who were removed from it — and the book that records the naming introduces them as "sanguinary savages", which is a fact about the source and not about them. See [the Ottawa removal](../event/ottawa-removal.yml). With 12,509 people at the 2020 estimates base and 12,490 in 2024 it is the county's second most populous civil subdivision after Lima — and it **contains no incorporated place at all**. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), sub-county file, which lists no place row under this township. Twelve and a half thousand people live here under township government and no municipal one.

**It holds the county's heavy industry**, which the corpus attributed to Lima at genesis and to [American Township](american-township.yml) alongside it. Both the [refinery](../site/lima-refinery.yml) and the [tank plant](../site/lima-army-tank-plant.yml) stand on unincorporated ground in this township, with Lima postal addresses and no municipality. [verified] — [Allen County GIS](../../catalog/allen-county-gis-downloads.md) and [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md).

That is a fact about tax base and authority as much as geography: the two largest industrial installations in the county are outside every municipality that could levy on them, and the township is the government whose ground they sit on. [inference] **It held 1,279 people in 1890, 1,493 in 1900 and 1,312 in 1910**, which makes 1890 its lowest recorded count and this township **the fastest-growing in the county over the whole period — nearly ten times its 1890 size**. [verified] — [Abstract of the Thirteenth Census, Supplement for Ohio](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md); see [the 1890–1910 divisions](../measure/allen-county-townships-1890-1910.yml).

**It held 2,070 people in 1930 and 2,336 in 1940**, before Lima crossed into it: the 1950 return is 6,408 of which 2,612 is Lima city, leaving 3,796 outside the city. [verified] — [1950 Census, Number of Inhabitants, Ohio](../../catalog/census-1950-number-of-inhabitants-ohio.md), Table 6; see [the township series](../measure/allen-county-townships-1930-1950.yml). At 12,509 in 2020 it is **six times its 1930 size outside the city — the fastest growth of the county's twelve townships**. [inference]

**And the annexation into it is dated.** "Part of Shawnee township annexed to Lima city in 1944." [verified] — same source, Allen County footnote. That is forty years earlier than the earliest annexation this corpus previously held, and it is the mechanism behind the 1950 return above.

A township of 23.308 square miles about 14 miles west of the county's centre, internal point 40.732439, -84.371928. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), Ohio county subdivisions.

Its population was 3,058 at the 2020 estimates base and 2,998 in 2024. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), sub-county file. Its population fell by 60 over those four years, as all but two of the county's subdivisions did.
It contains [Spencerville](spencerville.yml). [verified] — same source, which reports it as a place within this township.

**The county's youngest township, created February 28, 1848** — it did not exist before the [reorganization](../event/reorganization-of-1848.yml), which took the north-east quarter of Salem and the east half of Jennings **from Van Wert County**, added sections 7 and 18 of [Amanda](amanda-township.yml), and set the whole off under a new name. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md).

Its two parent townships have dates of their own: Jennings was laid off June 2, 1834 and organized at Benjamin Griffin's house on June 21; Salem was established in December 1836 and organized at Michael Tippe's house in January 1837, set off from the older township of Wayne. [verified] — same source.

**It is named for Col. Spencer**, a member of the State Board of Public Works in 1848 and an ardent supporter of canal building — which is why the county's canal township carries a canal commissioner's name. [verified] — same source. See [the Miami and Erie Canal](../site/miami-and-erie-canal.yml), whose lock is in section 36 of this township. Charles C. Marshall was justice of the peace at organization.

**It held 2,444 people in 1890, 3,016 in 1900 and 2,794 in 1910**, and that 1900 count was its highest until sometime after 1950. [verified] — [Abstract of the Thirteenth Census, Supplement for Ohio](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md); see [the 1890–1910 divisions](../measure/allen-county-townships-1890-1910.yml). [Spencerville](spencerville.yml) ran 1,266, 1,874 and 1,748 across the same three censuses — the village grew by half in the 1890s and pulled the township up a quarter with it, and both then fell back. [inference]

**It held 2,405 people in 1930, 2,340 in 1940 and 2,625 in 1950**, and 3,058 at the 2020 estimates base. [verified] — [1950 Census, Number of Inhabitants, Ohio](../../catalog/census-1950-number-of-inhabitants-ohio.md), Table 6; see [the township series](../measure/allen-county-townships-1930-1950.yml). [Spencerville](spencerville.yml) ran 1,612, 1,623 and 1,826, which is two thirds of the township in 1930 and, at 2,205 of 3,058, nearly three quarters now: the village has taken a larger share of its township as both grew. This is a village with a township around it rather than the other way about. [inference]

A village of 0.965 square miles in [Spencer Township](spencer-township.yml), about 14 miles west of the county's centre, internal point 40.707965, -84.353159. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), Ohio places.

Its population was 2,205 at the 2020 estimates base and 2,164 in 2024. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), sub-county file. It lost 41 people over those four years.

**All of it is in Allen County.** The same file marks a place that crosses a county line with `(pt.)` and marks this one plainly, which is what separates it from [Bluffton](bluffton.yml) and [Delphos](delphos.yml). [verified] — same source.

**Founded in 1844 on the banks of the [Miami and Erie Canal](../site/miami-and-erie-canal.yml).** [verified] — [Allen County](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md), cities and villages page. That verifies for this village what the canal node had only inferred about the two canal towns, and it dates the settlement to the canal's own working decade.

**It was laid out about 1844-45 for Tyler, McConnell and Conover of Dayton**, who bought 350 acres and built a mill at the upper canal lock. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md), quoting Dr. Campbell's 1880 reminiscence. Speculators from Dayton buying at a lock the year the canal opened is what a canal town's founding looks like from the inside.

**The name is [Spencer Township's](spencer-township.yml), and that is Col. Spencer** of the State Board of Public Works in 1848, "an ardent supporter of canal building enterprises". [verified] — same source. The canal town is named, at one remove, for a canal commissioner.

**A village died to make it.** "The old village of Hartford ceased to exist upon the founding of Spencerville, to which location many of the Hartford people came to reside" — it had two physicians practising by 1836. [verified] — same source, though only one of the two scans carries the passage legibly; see [two scans of one book](../../decisions/two-scans-of-one-book.yml).

**[The corporation](../jurisdiction/village-of-spencerville.yml) dates from an act of 1867**, twenty-three years after the settlement. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md).

The **smallest of the county's thirteen civil subdivisions by population** and among its smallest by area — 24.094 square miles, internal point 40.824171, -84.173843. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md). Its 2020 estimates base was 1,226 and its 2024 estimate 1,197, a twelfth of American Township's on comparable ground, and it contains no incorporated place. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), sub-county file.

It contains one settlement, [Gomer](gomer.yml), whose 345 people are 28 per cent of the township — a census designated place, so the claim above that it holds no *incorporated* place still stands. [verified] — [2020 Census Block Assignment Files](../../catalog/census-block-assignment-2020.md). It is also one of only two townships in the county that a single school district covers entire; every block of it is in [Elida Local](../jurisdiction/elida-local-school-district.yml), a district named for a village three miles south of this township and not in it. [verified] — same source, crossed with [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md) block geography.

**It was Putnam County's before it was Allen's.** The township was set off in 1831 as a division of Putnam County, then Congressional Township 2, Range 6, with James Porter, Daniel Gray and William Turner as its first trustees. Its present shape dates from the [reorganization of 1848](../event/reorganization-of-1848.yml), which joined the north tier of German Township — now [American](american-township.yml) — to the south half of the old township and organized the two as Sugar Creek. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md).

**It is named for its sugar maple groves**, whose number and productiveness the 1885 compiler gives as the origin, adding that the Shawnee took their year's supply of maple sugar from this ground. [verified] — same source.

It is in the corpus as the worked example of why [division](../division/) is a separate class from place: the census tract that covers this ground is [tract 39003010300](../division/census-tract-39003010300.yml), whose internal point lies about three quarters of a mile from the township's and whose land area is roughly five square miles larger. The two units nearly coincide and are not the same ground. **It held 1,010 people in 1890, 1,038 in 1900 and 1,088 in 1910.** [verified] — [Abstract of the Thirteenth Census, Supplement for Ohio](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md); see [the 1890–1910 divisions](../measure/allen-county-townships-1890-1910.yml). A hundred and thirty years later it is 1,226, and every figure the corpus holds for this township — seven counts across that span — lies between 969 and 1,226, a range of a quarter. [inference]

**It held 1,023 people in 1930, 969 in 1940 and 990 in 1950**, and 1,226 at the 2020 estimates base. [verified] — [1950 Census, Number of Inhabitants, Ohio](../../catalog/census-1950-number-of-inhabitants-ohio.md), Table 6; see [the township series](../measure/allen-county-townships-1930-1950.yml). It is the least changed place in Allen County: a fifth larger after ninety years, the smallest growth of the twelve townships, and smaller in 1950 than it had been in 1930. [inference] It contains no incorporated place.

An unincorporated community of 1.821 square miles in the south-east of the county, internal point 40.701038, -83.975081, with 406 people at the 2020 census. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), where it is listed as `Westminster CDP`, and [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md) for the count.

It lies wholly within [Auglaize Township](auglaize-township.yml) — all fourteen of its census blocks do — and holds 15 per cent of that township's 2,757 people. [verified] — [2020 Census Block Assignment Files](../../catalog/census-block-assignment-2020.md) crossed with TIGERweb block geography. The generous test that county subdivisions merely *intersecting* it returns two townships, Auglaize and Perry; the block composition returns one. The difference is a shared boundary line, and it is why containment here is settled by counting blocks rather than by asking a spatial query.

**It is older than every village in the county but one.** The county's 1834 tax list assesses Alex. Creps $1.89 on **thirty-six lots in the village of Westminster**, at a valuation of $172. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md), both scans agreeing. A platted village with thirty-six taxable lots in 1834 predates Bluffton by three years, Spencerville by ten and Gomer by sixteen, and is beaten only by [Lima](lima.yml) in 1831. It has never been incorporated in the hundred and ninety years since, which is the difference between this place and the nine that were: they got a corporation and a boundary, and this got a plat and then nothing.

nodes.label: Which congressional district is Allen County in now?

properties.would_close_this: A county-to-congressional-district relationship file from the Census Bureau reflecting the plan adopted 31 October 2025, if one is published under a path this corpus has not found; the Ohio Secretary of State's district map, retrieved by hand rather than by an automated client; or the enacted plan itself, which names its constituent counties. An elections roster will not do it, and now the corpus knows why: a roster names the sitting member, and a sitting member is evidence about the map that elected him.

blocks.text: At the 2020 census, all 3,552 of Allen County's census blocks fell in [Ohio's 4th congressional district](../division/ohio-congressional-district-4-2020.yml). [verified] — [2020 Census Block Assignment Files](../../catalog/census-block-assignment-2020.md).

**Half of it is now answered, and the half that is answered is not the half that was asked.** Allen County's sitting member of Congress is [James D. Jordan](../person/james-d-jordan.yml) of Ohio's 4th District, serving 3 January 2025 to 2 January 2027.
