[verified] — [Ohio county elected officials lookup](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md), an elections roster that names officeholders by county and was reachable where the geography files were not.

**The county's state legislative districts did close**, because the legislative map adopted 29 September 2023 is the map still in force and is the one the same election ran on. The county is in [House District 78](../division/ohio-house-district-78-2023.yml) and [Senate District 12](../division/ohio-senate-district-12-2023.yml). [verified] — the same two sources. One roster, one election, two vintages, and the difference decided which half of this question could close.

refusals: The corpus does not know the county's current district and does not guess it.

nodes.label: Who is Allen County named for?

properties.would_close_this: The text of the 1820 act erecting the county, or contemporaneous legislative journals from the Ohio General Assembly session that passed it. A county history asserting the attribution is not sufficient on its own: local histories are the origin of both candidates and repeat each other.

blocks.text: The county's name is not securely attributed. The two candidates usually offered are [John Allen](../person/john-allen.yml), a Kentucky colonel killed at the River Raisin in 1813, and Ethan Allen of Vermont. [inference]

**The source this node named as insufficient has arrived, and it is more interesting than expected: it does not make the claim at all.** The 1885 county history's chapter on Ohio's counties opens by telling the reader that "Adams County was named in honor of John Adams, second President of the United States", and gives namesakes freely down the list. Its entry for the county the whole book is about reads, entire: "Allen County was formed from the Indian Territory April 1, 1820. Lima is its county seat." [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md), both scans identical.

A subscription history written for the county's own subscribers, which names namesakes for its neighbours, declines to name one here. That is not proof of anything, but it is evidence of a kind the node did not anticipate: the standard local history — the genre this node said was "the origin of both candidates" — did not carry the attribution in 1885. [inference] Whatever produced the John Allen and Ethan Allen stories may be later than the book usually blamed for them.

nodes.label: What was Allen County's population before 1970, and when did Lima peak?

properties.resolution: Allen County's decennial population is on record from 1830, complete but for 1930, and its peak is 1980. Lima's is on record from 1850, complete, and its peak is the 1970 census — every count before it rises and every count after falls. The question asked when Lima peaked and whether 1970 was a peak or a late point on a plateau; it was neither for the county, which went on growing to 1980, and it was the peak for the city.
properties.would_close_this: For the county, the Census publication "Population of States and Counties of the United States: 1790–1990" (a 14.9MB PDF located but not read), or the 1900 Ohio bulletin "Population of Ohio by Counties and Minor Civil Divisions" for the nineteenth-century series. For Lima, a place-level decennial series — the 1970 and 1980 Census of Population volumes for Ohio, which the county-level file used here does not cover. What actually closed it was the right family and the wrong decade: the **1960** volume, not the 1970 or 1980 ones. Each decennial "Number of Inhabitants" volume carries a table reaching back to each place's earliest census, so the volume to ask is the last one before the gap closes, not the first one after it. Worth remembering the next time this field is filled in.

blocks.text: Allen County's population is on record at 111,144 in 1970 and 100,866 in 2024, and Lima's at 40,307 in 2000. [verified] — [1970–1979 county estimates](../../catalog/census-county-estimates-1970s.md), [Vintage 2024 estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md) and [2000–2010 intercensal estimates](../../catalog/census-intercensal-2000-2010.md). No source reaching earlier than those has been retrieved, so the corpus's county series begins at 1970 and its Lima series at 2000 — see [the 1970 census count](../measure/allen-county-population-1970.yml).

Two specific things were unknown when this was opened, and they mattered differently. Both are answered now; the two paragraphs that follow are the question as it was posed, kept because the answers are only legible against them. [inference]

**The county's 1900–1960 series** would show whether 1970 was the peak or merely a late point on a plateau. The corpus asserted a decline *from* 1970 because 1970 was the earliest figure it had, which was a fact about the sources retrieved and not about the county. If the county was already falling before 1970, or still rising, the [depopulation](../period/depopulation.yml) node's start date was wrong. It was wrong, in the third of the three ways: the county was still rising. [inference]

**Lima's own peak** is the sharper gap. Every claim in this corpus that Lima's decline was steeper than the county's rested on figures from 2000 onward, and the city's industrial employment fell well before that. The corpus held no Lima figure earlier than 2000 and could not locate the city's largest year, though it named a period beginning in 1970 partly on that basis. [inference]

**Answered for the county, and the answer corrects this corpus.** The series is complete from 1830 except for 1930: 73,303 (1940), 88,183 (1950), 103,691 (1960), 111,144 (1970), **112,241 (1980)**, 109,755 (1990). [verified] — [1990 Census, Population and Housing Unit Counts, Ohio](../../catalog/census-cph-2-37-ohio.md), Table 3; see [the 1940–1990 series](../measure/allen-county-population-1940-1990.yml). **The peak is 1980.** This node was opened to ask whether 1970 was a peak or a late point on a plateau, and it was neither: the county went on growing for a decade after the date the corpus had named for the start of its decline.

**Answered for Lima to 1970, and the earlier conclusion here was wrong.** The city was 53,734 in 1970 against 40,307 in 2000. [verified] — [1990 Census, Population and Housing Unit Counts, Ohio](../../catalog/census-cph-2-37-ohio.md); see [Lima 1970–1990](../measure/lima-population-1970-1990.yml). One phase ago this node reasoned from 41,306 in 1920 and 40,307 in 2000 that eighty years netted to nothing and the peak was unlocatable. Two points that happen to be level are not a plateau, and the corpus had drawn a chord across a rise and a fall. Lima 1930–1960 was still missing when that was written, and it no longer is.

For the county, the series now runs 578 (1830) through 47,976 (1900) and 68,203 (1920) to the 111,144 of 1970 the corpus already held. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md) and [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md); see [the county series](../measure/allen-county-population-1830-1900.yml). **Every decade rises.** So the county's 1970 peak is no longer an artefact of where the corpus's data began — it is a peak with ninety years of ascent behind it and no earlier candidate. What remains missing for the county is 1930 to 1960, four counts, and nothing in the shape so far suggests a reversal inside them. [inference] (Three of the four arrived the phase after that was written, and there *was* a reversal — just later, in the 1970s. One count is missing now: 1930.)

For Lima the answer runs the other way and is sharper than the question expected. [The city](../measure/lima-population-1880-1920.yml) was 7,567 in 1880, 21,723 in 1900 and **41,306 in 1920** — against 40,307 in 2000. **Lima was already at about its 2000 size in 1920.** (Both halves of that sentence are wrong: the figure is 41,326 and the city was thirty per cent below its peak.) [inference] The gap this node called "the sharper gap" is not a gap in a rising line; it is eighty years that net to roughly nothing, inside which the peak sits somewhere the corpus still cannot see. The city's decline is real and its starting point is now known to be earlier than 1970 or later than 1970 but certainly not derivable from 1970.

**A nineteenth-century series has arrived, and it makes the problem worse before it makes it better.** The county totalled 578 in 1830 and 9,079, 12,116, 19,185, 23,623 and 31,314 at the five censuses from 1840 to 1880. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md), statistics chapter, both scans agreeing. But the same table footnotes eight of its townships as having gone to Auglaize County, and the county gained Sugar Creek, Monroe, Richland and Spencer in the same act. [verified] — same source. **The 1830 and 1840 figures count a different county**, and no amount of later data repairs that — see [the reorganization of 1848](../event/reorganization-of-1848.yml). The 1900–1960 stretch this node actually asks about is still unretrieved, and now sits between two series that are not each other's continuation.

**Closed. Both halves answered, and the second one on the last try.** The 1960 Census volume's Table 5 gives Lima twelve decennial counts from 757 in 1850 to 51,037 in 1960 — 42,287 in 1930, 44,711 in 1940, 50,246 in 1950 — every one of them rising and every one below the 53,734 of 1970. [verified] — [1960 Census, Number of Inhabitants, Ohio](../../catalog/census-1960-number-of-inhabitants-ohio.md); see [the federal series](../measure/lima-population-1850-1960.yml). **Lima peaked at the 1970 census.** The county's peak is 1980. Both dates are now argued from complete decennial series rather than placed at the edge of a retrieval.

**What this node feared did not happen, and is worth saying so.** It was opened warning that this was "the gap most likely to be filled by mistake rather than by research: a plausible peak figure for Lima is easy to find in secondary sources and easy to write down, and it would be the first unsourced number in a corpus whose population figures are otherwise all primary." Four phases and three federal publications later, every figure in both series is a Census count with a table and a page behind it. [verified] The warning did its job by being written down where the temptation would be felt.

nodes.label: What happened at the two irregular sheriff transitions?

properties.would_close_this: For 2017: the county's own record of the appointment, or Allen County commissioners' or common pleas records for that year, which record a vacancy and its filling. A federal court docket in the Northern District of Ohio would establish a prosecution and not an appointment, and the corpus wants the second. The 1933 half is closed.

blocks.text: The [past-sheriffs roster](../../catalog/acso-past-sheriffs.md) is continuous from 1831 to the present with no gaps and no overlaps. [verified] Two of its thirty-nine entries are nonetheless irregular in a way the source does not explain, and both had an obvious reading the corpus declined to write down. One of them is now answered.

**1931–1933 Jess L. Sarber, then 1933–1935 Donald F. Sarber — answered, and the obvious reading was right.** Jess L. Sarber was shot dead in the Allen County jail on the night of 12 October 1933 by three men who came to free John Dillinger, and his son Donald succeeded him. [verified] — [Chronicling America](../../catalog/chronicling-america.md); a Lima dispatch of 4 March 1934 describes the accused as awaiting trial for "the slaying of the sheriff's father" and calls the dead man "the elder Sarber, who preceded his son as sheriff". See [the raid on the Allen County jail](../event/allen-county-jail-raid-1933.yml).
**2017–2017 James K. Everett — still open.** The only entry whose range begins and ends in the same year, sitting between an eight-year holder and the current one. [verified] — the same roster.

nodes.label: What became of German and Ottawa townships?

properties.resolution: German Township was renamed American on August 16, 1918, by the county commissioners on the citizens' petition, in the anti-German sentiment of the war. Ottawa Township was never abolished within the reach of any source held here; Lima annexed until the two were coextensive and the township survived in 1921 only to elect a justice of the peace and constables. The residual — the date it formally ended — is recorded in the description rather than left standing, because it is a detail of an answer and not the absence of one.
properties.would_close_this: The Allen County commissioners' journal after 1885 for both, or the Ohio Secretary of State's record of township name changes. For Ottawa specifically, Lima's annexation record.

blocks.text: **German became American on August 16, 1918.** The citizens petitioned and the Allen County commissioners acted — the same instrument that erected every township here and incorporated every village. Article II of the petition says only "that good cause is shown why the name of said township should be changed", and stipulates that the change "shall in no wise affect the right of property, or the internal concerns of said township". [verified] — [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md), which reads the language for what it is: "'good cause' means patriotism." School books were being reset and businesses were dropping the word; the township "were caught in the wave of popular sentiment". The corpus had declined to assert the obvious motive. It was the obvious motive, and the same page records that it was contested — residents "who a little later on would not have voted for the change, because of sacred associations in early history". See [American Township](../place/american-township.yml) and, for the day itself as a happening rather than as an answer, [the renaming of German Township](../event/renaming-of-german-township-1918.yml).

**Ottawa was not abolished. Lima grew until it was the same ground.** It was erected in May 1857 because "Lima was spreading out into so many townships that Ottawa was created in order to shelter it" — 1,600 acres from [Bath](../place/bath-township.yml), 1,040 from German, 560 from [Perry](../place/perry-township.yml) and a quarter section from [Shawnee](../place/shawnee-township.yml), which is the same composition the 1885 book gives, acre for acre, thirty-six years earlier. [verified] — same source and [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md).

By 1921 it was a shell: "today it is not recognized only in the election of a justice of the peace, constables and by the county infirmary board of directors... the township a nonentity and Lima the unit of the tax duplicates. **The City of Lima is coextensive with it.**" [verified] — same source. So the answer is not an act of abolition but sixty years of annexation, ending in a township whose boundary and whose city's boundary were the same line. [inference]

**A township made to hold a city was consumed by it, which is what it was for.** Ottawa existed only because Lima was outgrowing Bath, and the 1857 commissioners called 3,360 acres a "liberal allowance for the future growth of the seat of justice". Lima passed it. [inference]

**It may never have formally ceased, and the corpus was looking for the wrong kind of event.** The Census Bureau's Ohio user note says: "the Census Bureau, in agreement with the State of Ohio, does not recognize an Ohio township that is coextensive with a village or a city, and treats such places as independent of any MCD." [verified] — [1990 Census, Population and Housing Unit Counts, Ohio](../../catalog/census-cph-2-37-ohio.md). So Ottawa's absence from every present-day federal source this corpus holds is explained by a **reporting rule**, not by an act of abolition — and the rule's condition is exactly the state the 1921 historian described, the city being coextensive with the township. [inference]

**The Census Bureau called it nonexistent, in 1952, in a footnote.** "Lima city in Bath, Perry, and Shawnee townships returned in 1940 as coextensive with nonexistent Ottawa township." [verified] — [1950 Census, Number of Inhabitants, Ohio](../../catalog/census-1950-number-of-inhabitants-ohio.md), Table 6, Allen County footnote. That is thirty years earlier than the reporting rule this node already quotes and much blunter, and it is the word "nonexistent" that has to be read carefully: it is a statement about what the Bureau would recognize as a minor civil division for the 1950 tabulation, not a finding of Ohio law. [inference] The 1885 and 1921 histories both describe Ottawa's erection in May 1857 with its acreage, so it existed; what the Bureau is saying is that by 1940 it should not have been used, and that the 1940 return which did use it was wrong.

**And the 1950 volume puts Lima back into exactly the four townships Ottawa was carved out of.** Its Table 6 splits the city across [American](../place/american-township.yml) (19,270), [Bath](../place/bath-township.yml) (17,469), [Perry](../place/perry-township.yml) (10,895) and [Shawnee](../place/shawnee-township.yml) (2,612), summing to Lima's own 50,246. [verified] — same source. Ottawa was made in 1857 from 1,600 acres of Bath, 1,040 of German — which is American — 560 of Perry and a quarter section of Shawnee. The same four, ninety-three years apart. [verified] — same sources as above. The city had long since outgrown Ottawa's 3,360 acres, so this is not the original carve reappearing; it is evidence that Lima grew outward from Ottawa without ever crossing into a fifth township. [inference]

**And Ottawa is measured, by name, in a federal table — with its own count, not the city's.** The 1910 supplement lists "Ottawa township, coextensive with Lima city" at 30,508, 21,723 and 15,987 for 1910, 1900 and 1890, and Lima city on the line beneath at 30,508, 21,723 and **15,981**. [verified] — [Abstract of the Thirteenth Census, Supplement for Ohio](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md); see [the 1890–1910 divisions](../measure/allen-county-townships-1890-1910.yml).

**Six people, and they date the coextension.** The difference at 1890 is not a misprint: without it the county's 1890 column does not sum to 40,644, and it does with it. [verified] — arithmetic on the printed figures. So Ottawa Township held six residents outside Lima city in 1890 and none at either census after. **The township and the city became exactly the same ground between the 1890 and 1900 censuses** — thirty-three years after Ottawa was erected to make room for a city that then filled it entirely. [inference] The 1921 historian's "the City of Lima is coextensive with it" was already true in 1900 and had a date to within a decade.

nodes.label: What happened to the Village of Fort Shawnee?

properties.would_close_this: Ohio Secretary of State or Allen County records of municipal dissolution, or the county's own list of political subdivisions; alternatively the Census Bureau's Boundary and Annexation Survey for the relevant year, which records why a place's status changed and would distinguish a dissolution from a reclassification directly.

blocks.text: [Fort Shawnee](../place/fort-shawnee.yml) is listed by the Census Bureau as `Fort Shawnee village` with a population of 3,866 in 2000 and 3,726 in 2010, as `Fort Shawnee CDP` in the 2020 Gazetteer, and not at all in the Vintage 2024 sub-county file. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md) and [Census Intercensal Estimates, 2000–2010](../../catalog/census-intercensal-2000-2010.md).

refusals: So something changed between the 2010 and 2020 geographies, and the corpus does not know what.

nodes.label: When was Allen County's government organized?

properties.resolution: 1831. The Allen County commissioners first sat on June 6, 1831; before that the county was attached to Shelby and then to Mercer for judicial purposes, and its first township was organized by Mercer's board in 1830. Closed on a secondary source that resumes the commissioners' record, corroborated on a named person by the sheriff's roster. The residual question — the exact organizing act — is recorded in the description rather than left as a standing question, because it is a refinement of an answer and not the absence of one.
properties.would_close_this: The Ohio General Assembly act organizing the county, or the first volume of the Allen County commissioners' or common pleas records, whose opening date bounds the answer directly.

blocks.text: **Answered: 1831, and the commissioners' first recorded sitting was June 6 of that year.** [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md), whose sixth chapter resumes the commissioners' record meeting by meeting. James Daniels, John G. Wood and Samuel Stewart sat with William G. Wood as secretary, granted the petition to organize [Jackson Township](../place/jackson-township.yml), authorized a township of Sciota, allowed the assessor $11, and ordered a road to the county seat.

**The gap between 1820 and 1831 was an attachment, and the corpus now knows to which counties.** The organic act of 1820 divided the Maumee cession into fourteen counties and provided that Allen "be attached to Shelby County for judicial purposes"; Allen was subsequently attached to **Mercer** until the organization of 1831. [verified] — same source. That is the exact shape the corpus had reasoned to from general Ohio practice and could not name — see [the erection of the county](../event/erection-of-allen-county.yml).

**Its first township was erected by another county's board.** [Amanda](../place/amanda-township.yml) was organized in 1830 under authority granted by the commissioners of Mercer County — a year before Allen had commissioners of its own. [verified] — same source. A county government's prehistory is not empty; it is somebody else's minutes.

**Two independent sources agree, and on a name as well as a year.** The Allen County Sheriff's Office's roster records Henry Lippencott as sheriff from 1831. [verified] — [past-sheriffs roster](../../catalog/acso-past-sheriffs.md). The 1885 book, working from the commissioners' book, has the board appointing Henry Lippincott in October 1831 to prepare plans for confining Uri Martin. Two records kept by different offices for different purposes put the same man in the same county in the same year. [inference]

**A second historian, working thirty-six years later, gives the same date.** "This was effected in advance of the formal local organization of Allen County June 6, 1831, from which time official business was all transacted within the bounds of the county." [verified] — [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md). It adds that Lima became the seat of government on **March 3, 1831** — three months before the board first sat, so the county had a county seat before it had a government — and that the first court proceedings on June 6 were held in James Daniels Sr.'s cabin on the bank of the Ottawa River, Daniels being one of the three commissioners who sat that day. [verified] — same source.

**That residual is now closed too, and the answer is yes.** "Allen County was erected by act of February 12, 1820, and was **organized by act of February 9, 1831**." [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md), both scans identical. So there are three dates and they are three different things: the county was created in 1820, organized by statute on February 9, 1831, and its commissioners first sat on June 6, 1831 — four months after the act and three months after Lima became the seat of government on March 3. The corpus asked whether an act named an earlier date in 1831. It did.

nodes.label: When did Allen County stop being nine-tenths farmland?

properties.would_close_this: One agricultural census at county grain between 1910 and 2002, and preferably three. The census was taken in 1920, 1925 and then every five years to 1954, every four or five to 1978, and every five to 1997; the Census Bureau conducted it through 1992 and NASS from 1997. Each printed volume carries an Ohio county table of farms, land in farms, crop acreage and livestock — the same rows this question is short of. NASS's own online publication begins at 2002 and does not reach back: the bulk Quick Stats extracts stop there, `qs.census1997.txt.gz` does not exist, and the Cornell historical archive that used to hold the scans now redirects into nass.usda.gov without them. So the volumes are the shelf and the route to them is not NASS. This names a shelf and not an answer, which is what [asking the volume just after the gap](../../decisions/ask-the-volume-just-after-the-gap.yml) says to do when the obvious source has been tried.

blocks.text: Allen County held 240,472 acres in farms in 1910, 92.5 per cent of its land, and 178,921 acres in 2022, 69.4 per cent of it. [verified] — [Abstract of the Thirteenth Census](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md) and [the Census of Agriculture](../../catalog/usda-census-of-agriculture.md); see [the 1910 farms](../measure/allen-county-farms-1900-1910.yml) and [the modern series](../measure/allen-county-farms-2002-2022.yml).

**Nine-tenths of that loss is inside a window this corpus cannot see.** By 2002, the first year of the modern series, the county was already down to 188,150 acres. So 52,322 of the 61,551 acres went between 1910 and 2002, and 9,229 in the twenty years since. [inference] — computed here.

The same window swallows every other change the two ends disagree about. The horses were 14,676 in 1910 and 618 in 2002. The sheep were 41,240 and 835. Oats took 30,156 acres and then 194. Soybeans were not a crop in this county in 1909 and were its largest in 2002. Every one of those turned somewhere in ninety-two unmeasured years. [verified] — same two sources.

refusals: This corpus cannot say whether the farmland left in one decade or in nine, and the difference matters: a county that lost fifty thousand acres to drainage failure, to the oil field, to Lima's annexations or to the interstate lost them for four different reasons, and only the last of those can be dated from anything already here.

nodes.label: Does the Auglaize River rise in Allen County?

properties.resolution: Point-in-polygon against TIGERweb's 2020 county and county-subdivision layers. The source is in Allen County, Ohio, in Auglaize township — the township named for the river.
properties.would_close_this: A county boundary polygon checked against the source coordinate. Closed by exactly that.

blocks.text: **Yes, and in the township named after it.** The river's source coordinate, 40.6669957, -83.8938286, falls inside Allen County, Ohio — GEOID `39003` — and inside Auglaize township, GEOID `3900302988`, in census tract 115. [verified] — [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md), point-in-polygon against the 2020 county and county-subdivision layers. The source coordinate is [USGS GNIS](../../catalog/gnis-domestic-names-ohio.md) feature 1065901. [verified]

So Allen County is not merely drained by the Auglaize. It is the ground the river starts on, and the township that carries the river's name is the one it rises in — which is the ordinary direction for a name to travel and is worth having checked rather than assumed. [inference]

nodes.label: Who are the 1,360 people in a Lima block with no housing units?

properties.would_close_this: The Ohio Department of Rehabilitation and Correction's facility list, which gives each institution's current name, address and population; or the Census Bureau's group-quarters tabulation from the 2020 redistricting file, which reports institutional population by type and is not served by TIGERweb.

blocks.text: Two census blocks in Allen County hold a substantial population and essentially no housing units, which by the Census Bureau's own definitions means their residents are in **group quarters** rather than households. Together they hold 1,758 people, 1.7 per cent of the county. [verified] — [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md), block layer, `POP100` against `HU100`.

**One is settled.** Block `390030101001002` holds 398 people in 2 housing units, and the county's address file puts [Bluffton University](../organization/bluffton-university.yml)'s Ropp Hall 0.02 miles from its internal point with five more university buildings inside 0.15. [verified] — [Allen County GIS](../../catalog/allen-county-gis-downloads.md).

**The other is not.** Block `390030112001004` holds **1,360 people in zero housing units** over 0.141 square miles, inside [Lima](../place/lima.yml) and in precinct `LIMA 1A`. Exactly one county address point falls within it and its landmark reads `BIBLE ROAD AUTO WRECKING AT 505 BIBLE RD`. [verified] — same two sources, the address points projected out of State Plane and tested against the block polygon.

The county's three state correctional institutions — `ALLEN CORRECTIONAL INSTITUTE` and `LIMA CORRECTIONAL INSTITUTE` at 2338 and 2350 N West St, `OAKWOOD CORRECTIONAL FACILITY` at 3200 N West St — are in the same precinct and in adjacent blocks, about half a mile west. [verified] — same source. That an institution's single address point sits at its gate while its residents are counted in the block holding the buildings would explain the whole discrepancy. [inference] It is an inference and not a finding: nothing retrieved here names what stands on those ninety acres.

**A third source now agrees with the first two and still does not answer them.** The precinct containing that block, [`LIMA 1A`](../division/voting-district-lima-1a-2020.yml), has 908 registered voters against 3,240 residents — 0.28 per resident, the lowest of the county's 88 against a median of 0.68 and a next-lowest of 0.54. Take the 1,360 out and the ratio is 0.48, inside the range the rest of the county occupies. [verified] — [OpenElections](../../catalog/openelections-ohio.md) against [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md).

A census count, a housing count and a registration roll therefore agree that these residents are present without households and without registering. Three measurements of the same absence is not a name. [inference]

nodes.label: Why do Allen County's mortgage outcomes differ by race and by purpose?

properties.would_close_this: Both routes this question named are spent. Loan-to-value, debt-to-income and the years 2018-2024 were read and the gap survived all of them; property value and rate spread remain, and would test the collateral hypothesis rather than the race one. What is left for the race gap is an underwriting record, a matched-pair test, or a supervisory examination, and none of the three is public. This question may not be closeable from outside a lender.

blocks.text: **By race.** Pooled across 2018–2024, applications from Black applicants were denied at 32.4 per cent and from white applicants at 17.8, in all seven years and inside all twenty-three strata of the four controls the file carries. [verified] — [seven years of the gap](../measure/allen-county-lending-denial-gap-2018-2024.yml).

**By purpose.** Borrowing against a house already owned in Lima's tracts is denied at 37.7 per cent against 21.5 elsewhere; buying one is 13.3 against 10.8. [verified] — [seven years of the register](../measure/allen-county-home-lending-2018-2024.yml).

**Half of what this question asked for has been done, and it narrowed the question rather than closing it.** Both routes it named — the register's unread columns and six more years — were taken. The years turned 174 applications into 1,334 and the gap did not move. The columns turned a raw comparison into a controlled one: within 311 cells of purpose, income, debt-to-income and loan-to-value, 955 applications from Black applicants drew 223 denials against 132.5 expected at the white rate in the same cells. [verified] — same source. Composition explains fifteen per cent of the gap.

**The purpose gap still has a candidate in the file.** Twenty-one per cent of denials in Lima's tracts cite collateral against 13 per cent elsewhere, and collateral is the house: a loan against a $95,900 house built in 1953 is a different proposition from the same loan against a $210,200 house built in 1973. [inference] The register's property-value column would test that and has not been read.

refusals: The corpus does not know why either.

nodes.label: Why are Allen County's village seats filled by appointment where its township seats are not?

properties.would_close_this: Candidate filings or the official canvass for a village race in this county — either would say whether a seat drew anyone, which is the fact that separates "nobody stood" from "someone left". The village council minutes recording an appointment would give the date and the vacancy it filled. Neither is the state-level election file this corpus already holds: [the returns](../../catalog/openelections-ohio.md) are precinct-level for federal and state offices and have never been checked for a village line.

blocks.text: **It is not size.** The two forms sit on the same ground and are staffed opposite ways. [Spencer Township](../jurisdiction/spencer-township.yml) elected all four of its officers while [Spencerville](../jurisdiction/village-of-spencerville.yml) inside it, holding most of its people, appointed four of seven. [Monroe Township](../jurisdiction/monroe-township.yml) elected four while [Cairo](../jurisdiction/village-of-cairo.yml) seated five appointees and left a seat empty. [Jackson Township](../jurisdiction/jackson-township.yml) and [Lafayette](../jurisdiction/village-of-lafayette.yml) do it out of the same building. [verified] — same source.

**Nor is it simply the smallest places failing.** Beaverdam is the smallest village in the county and appointed two of seven; Bluffton is the largest and appointed one — the two extremes of size are the two lightest users of it. The heaviest are Cairo and Harrod, third and fourth smallest of the seven. So the emptiest government is not the smallest one and the ranking does not run with population. [verified] — same source and [the estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md).

**One structural difference is on the table and is not an answer.** A village fills seven elective seats — a mayor and six council — where a township fills four, and Harrod fills ten. So the village form asks more people of a smaller population, and a place of four hundred is asked for ten officers. [inference] That is arithmetic about the form, not evidence about why a particular seat went unfilled, and this corpus has read no candidate filing, no canvass and no village minute book.

refusals: The corpus does not know why, and will not guess.

nodes.label: Where are the children who live in these districts and are not enrolled in them?

properties.would_close_this: Ohio's nonpublic school enrolment reports, which give private and parochial enrolment by county and would name the schools this corpus has never recorded. The state's community school directory. Open-enrolment and scholarship counts by district, which the state publishes for the funding formula. Any one of the four would turn a share of the 4,331 into a number; all four would close it.

blocks.text: **The two numbers do not measure quite the same thing, and that accounts for some of it.** The first is a modelled resident population aged 5 to 17; the second is fall membership, which includes a district's eighteen-year-old seniors and excludes five-year-olds who have not started. [inference] Neither is a count, and the gap of 21.2 per cent is a difference between two instruments before it is a difference about children.

**It matters because of what the corpus has just published.** A district's spending per pupil is computed on its enrolment, and a district's child poverty rate on its resident children. If the two populations differ by a fifth, and differ by more in one district than another, then the two measures are not describing the same set of families — and this corpus has set them side by side in twelve nodes. [inference] Nothing here says the difference is uneven. Nothing says it is not.

refusals: The corpus does not know where the other 4,331 are.

blocks.text: The seat of county government at Lima — the building the [county government](../jurisdiction/allen-county-government.yml) occupies and the physical expression of Lima's status as county seat. [inference]

It stands at 301 N Main Street, 40.7430708, -84.1051751, and the county records its `MUNI` as Lima. [verified] — [Allen County GIS](../../catalog/allen-county-gis-downloads.md). The Census Bureau puts the same point in Lima city, GEOID `3943554`. [verified] — [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md). This is the one site of the three checked whose `located-in` edge was right all along, and it was checked anyway — a corpus that only tests the claims it doubts learns nothing about the ones it trusts.

**It is the county's third courthouse, and the caution written into this node was right.** The node refused to assume the building was original, on the general ground that Ohio courthouses are usually the third or fourth on their site. It is the third. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md).

**The architect was G. H. Maetzel of Columbus**, whose plans were adopted September 20 and who was appointed October 27, 1881. The county issued $142,500 in bonds, let eleven contracts on November 10, 1881 — $39,000 of Berea cut stone, $35,600 of iron work — and the total came to about $160,000 with $10,000 of stained cherry furniture. [verified] — same source. The corner-stone was placed on the Fourth of July "without ceremony".

**The vote that authorised it is also a census of the county's civil geography in 1881**, returned in fifteen units: twelve townships by name — German and Ottawa among them — Lima City with its four wards itemised, and [Richland](../place/richland-township.yml) appearing not by name but as its two precincts, Bluffton and Beaver Dam. Thirteen townships, fifteen returns. [verified] — same source. See [what became of German and Ottawa townships](../question/what-became-of-german-and-ottawa-townships.yml).

**The canvass adds up, and that is the point of transcribing it.** The fifteen returns sum to exactly the 1,014 dissenting and 3,333 consenting the book states, for its stated majority of 2,319, and Lima's four wards sum to exactly its city total of 31 and 1,250. [verified] — computed from the printed figures. A compiler inventing a canvass does not make it balance to the vote.

**The building committee corroborates a sheriff.** It included "John Franks, Sheriff" in 1881, and [the roster](../person/john-franks.yml) kept by the sheriff's own office gives his term as 1877-1881. Two records with no common source agree on the man and the year. [verified] — same source and [past-sheriffs roster](../../catalog/acso-past-sheriffs.md).

properties.address: 1155 Bible Road, Lima OH 45801 — a postal address, not a municipality.

blocks.text: An engine plant at 1155 Bible Road, operated by [Ford Motor Company](../organization/ford-motor-company.yml). [verified] — [EPA TRI](../../catalog/epa-tri.md), which names the facility `FORD MOTOR CO LIMA ENGINE PLANT` with Ford Motor Co as its parent and the plant itself as its mailing address.

**It has a Lima address and is not in Lima.** The county's address file records it at 1155 Bible Road with `USPS_CITY` LIMA and `MUNI` **blank**, at 40.774253, -84.084246; TIGERweb, asked that point, puts it in [Bath Township](../place/bath-township.yml) and in no incorporated place. [verified] — [Allen County GIS](../../catalog/allen-county-gis-downloads.md) and [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md).

**So all three of the county's large industrial installations stand outside every municipality.** This plant in Bath Township, [the refinery](lima-refinery.yml) and [the tank plant](lima-army-tank-plant.yml) in [Shawnee](../place/shawnee-township.yml). [verified] — [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md), point-in-polygon on all three against the 2020 county-subdivision and incorporated-place layers.
Three townships' ground and no city's, which is a fact about who may levy on them before it is a fact about geography. [inference]

**It is one of six Allen County facilities that have reported to the EPA in every one of the inventory's thirty-eight years.** The others are [the refinery](lima-refinery.yml), Dana Driveshaft Manufacturing, INEOS Nitriles, FXI at Spencerville, and Chemtrade's sulphur works at Cairo. [verified] — [the reporters](../measure/allen-county-tri-reporters-1987-2024.yml). Six of forty-eight, in a register where twenty-eight facilities have stopped filing.

**It stands on T3S R7E section 17**, which the Recorder abstracts in **Section Ground volume 28A**. [verified] — [Allen County GIS REST](../../catalog/allen-county-gis-rest.md) layer 55, cross-checked against the parcel number on the same point, and [the Recorder's book list](../../catalog/allen-county-recorder-section-ground.md).

That matters more here than anywhere else in the corpus, because this node's open question has no newspaper route at all — no paper in the national archive reaches 1957 for it — and a tract page records a conveyance whether or not anyone reported it. [inference]

**When Ford took this ground: 24 August 1955.** The Recorder's tract abstract for the NW quarter of section 17 records DTI Enterprises Inc conveying to Ford Motor Company by warranty deed dated 24 August 1955 and recorded 27 September 1955, at volume 332 page 529 — with a second parcel from the same grantor a fortnight later at 332/531, one from two individuals on 17 January 1956 at 350/184, and two more from DTI on 17 August 1956 at 357/577 and 357/579. [verified] — [Section Ground book list](../../catalog/allen-county-recorder-section-ground.md), volume 0028A pages 163–166.

**It was assembled for Ford, and not by Ford.** DTI Enterprises Inc bought this ground from the National Lime & Stone Company on 2 June 1955 and from a private owner on 24 December 1955, and conveyed to Ford four times between August 1955 and August 1956. [verified] — same pages. A company buying up adjacent parcels over eighteen months and passing them to one manufacturer is the ordinary shape of a site assembly, in which an assembler exists so that the buyer's name does not appear and the price does not move. [inference]

**And it was building by September 1957.** A mechanic's lien for **$91,546.07** was filed against Ford Motor Company by Carlson Manufacturing Inc on 30 September 1957, released 17 October 1962. [verified] — same pages, mortgage side. A mechanic's lien is a claim for work done on the ground, so it dates construction the way no directory or aerial photograph the corpus holds could. [inference]

**The liens keep coming for forty years**, and they are the closest thing this corpus has to a record of the plant's growth: Vicon Supply in 1967; Strunk Maintenance four times and Durako Paint and Skyline Industrial in 1972–73; Chas A Strand in 1976; Tilton and E C Ernst/Jansen Electric in 1978; Penn Ventilator and Midwest Steel Erection in 1980; a General Electric supply division and All Phase Electric in 1984; Rent All Mart in 1990; and six notices of commencement from Tuttle Construction, Tilton and Rudolph Libbe across 1994 and 1995. [verified] — same pages.

**The ground was a quarry before it was a factory.** The chain behind DTI Enterprises runs National Lime & Stone Company, which took it from the National Quarries Company in January 1944; National Quarries had it from 1917. [verified] — same pages. A ten-year lease to the Hercules Powder Company in 1922 is consistent with that and is what the record says rather than an inference from the name. [inference]

**This is one quarter of the plant's ground and not all of it.** The plant's parcel runs the entire west half of section 17 and crosses the line between the NW and SW quarters, so a tract index organized by quarter cuts through it. [verified] — [the survey sections](../measure/allen-county-survey-sections.yml) and county parcel geometry.

nodes.label: Joint Systems Manufacturing Center (Lima Army Tank Plant)

properties.address: 1151 Buckeye Road, Lima OH 45804 — a postal address, not a municipality.

blocks.text: The government-owned tank plant south of Lima — the only facility in the United States that builds main battle tanks, producing and rebuilding the M1 Abrams under contractor operation. [inference] It stands at 40.6994478, -84.137903 and is registered as `United States Army Joint Systems Manufacturing Center Lima`, feature class Military. [verified] — [USGS GNIS](../../catalog/gnis-domestic-names-ohio.md), feature 2512481.

**It is not in Lima.** The plant stands in [Shawnee Township](../place/shawnee-township.yml), GEOID `3900371955`, and no incorporated place and no census designated place contains it — not Lima, and not the [Fort Shawnee](../place/fort-shawnee.yml) CDP a mile and a half away. [verified] — [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md), point-in-polygon against the 2020 county-subdivision, incorporated-place and CDP layers. The `located-in` edge points at the township accordingly; it named Lima from genesis until this was checked.

The county says so too, from its own data and by a different route: its address file records the plant at 1151 Buckeye Road with `USPS_CITY` "LIMA" and `MUNI` **blank**. [verified] — [Allen County GIS](../../catalog/allen-county-gis-downloads.md). Two agencies, two geometries, one answer.

Two claims here were wrong in the same direction. This node said the plant is on Lima's **northern** edge and it is 2.84 miles south of Lima's internal point, in another township entirely; and [American Township](../place/american-township.yml) said the plant stands on or near *its* boundary with Lima, which wraps Lima's west and north. The plant is south of the city and on neither. [verified] — same source.

It is government-owned and contractor-operated, which is why its `operated-by` edges point at both a jurisdiction and a company in principle; only the ownership side is asserted here, because the operating contractor is a corporate relationship this corpus has not sourced and which has changed hands. [inference]

Its presence makes Allen County's industrial base unusual in a specific way: the plant's workload is set by federal procurement rather than by any regional market, so the county has a major employer whose fortunes are decoupled from the deindustrialization that shaped the rest of its economy. [inference]

**One contractor name is attached to this plant now, for seven years thirty years ago.** The Toxics Release Inventory holds two records at this address: `U.S. ARMY JSMC GENERAL DYNAMICS LAND SYSTEMS`, parent General Dynamics Corp, filing from 1987 to 1993; and `U S ARMY JOINT SYSTEMS MANUFACTURING CENTER`, parent US Department of Defense, filing from 1994 to 2024. Same street, same coordinates. [verified] — [EPA TRI](../../catalog/epa-tri.md); see [the reporters](../measure/allen-county-tri-reporters-1987-2024.yml).

**The county's tank work began at the Locomotive Works, and it began in 1941.** Medium tank production was scheduled to start "this fall" at the Lima Locomotive Works, which had joined Chrysler, American Locomotive, Baldwin, Pullman Standard and Pressed Steel Car in the medium tank programme. [verified] — [Chronicling America](../../catalog/chronicling-america.md), *Evening Star*, 24 August 1941, page 4, and *Automotive News*, 14 April 1941, page 10. That is a private company retooling its own plant, and it is not this installation.

**There was also an Army installation, and it is a different thing again.** The [Lima Tank Depot](lima-tank-depot.yml) was under construction in January 1943, operated by a contractor, and existed to finish and dispatch vehicles built at arsenals elsewhere rather than to build them. [verified] — same archive.

**The ground now has a name and a book.** The plant stands on **T4S R6E section 14**, and the Recorder abstracts that section in **Section Ground volume 34A**. [verified] — [Allen County GIS REST](../../catalog/allen-county-gis-rest.md) layer 55, cross-checked against the parcel number on the same point, and [the Recorder's book list](../../catalog/allen-county-recorder-section-ground.md); see [the survey sections](../measure/allen-county-survey-sections.yml).

That is not an answer. It is the first time this corpus can say *where to look* for one: a tract index runs from the federal patent forward and records who conveyed this ground to whom and when, which is the shape of the question this node has been asking since genesis. [inference]

**The United States bought this ground in June 1951, and that is a different war.** Five warranty deeds from five private owners, dated 20, 20, 21, 27 and 28 June 1951 and recorded the same day or the next, conveyed parts of this quarter section to the United States of America — 60.24 acres, 5 acres, 40 acres of the west half of the east half, and two more described only as "Pt". [verified] — [Section Ground book list](../../catalog/allen-county-recorder-section-ground.md), volume 0034A pages 89–92, at volumes 320 pages 573, 574 and 577 and 321 pages 245 and 246.
Five conveyances closing inside nine days, most recorded on the day of signature, is what a government buying under deadline looks like rather than a farm changing hands. [inference]

**So this ground was in private hands throughout the Second World War.** The same abstract shows it mortgaged to Home Bank in 1940 and 1941 and to a Home Savings & Loan in 1941 and 1944, leased to the Protective Association of Lima and the Allen County Fishing & Game club in April 1940, and crossed by pipeline rights of way granted by its private owners in 1939, 1940 and 1949. [verified] — same pages. Whatever the Army was doing at Lima during that war, it was not doing it here.

**That settles the question the corpus refused to settle, and settles it the other way.** Two phases ago this node and [the Lima Tank Depot](lima-tank-depot.yml) were held as separate nodes with the identity question written on both, against the obvious reading that two government-owned tank installations at one small city forty years apart must be one place. The Depot was under construction in January 1943; this ground was a mortgaged farm until June 1951. [verified] — same pages and same archive. They are not the same ground. [inference] See [a second node is not an assertion of difference](../../decisions/a-second-node-is-not-an-assertion-of-difference.yml).

**It was called the Lima Army Modification Center in 1972.** A sewer easement to the Allen County commissioners that January runs from "(Lima Army Modification Center) Sec'y of the Army". [verified] — same pages, volume 519 page 538. It is the only name this corpus holds for the installation between its acquisition and the present one.

**General Dynamics was here in 1988 and still had an interest in 2003.** A mechanic's lien for $37,367.96 was filed by Orbit Movers & Erectors Inc against "General Dynamics Corp United States of America" on 30 September 1988; General Dynamics Land Systems granted a financing statement to General Electric Capital Corp recorded 13 January 2003. [verified] — same pages.

That bears directly on what changed in 1994. The Toxics Release Inventory shows General Dynamics filing to 1993 and the Department of Defense from 1994, and this node could not say whether the operator changed with the filer. A contractor still granting a financing statement on this ground ten years later is evidence that it did not. [inference]

refusals: Whether the operator changed with it, this corpus does not know, and the reporting entity at a government-owned plant is a compliance arrangement rather than a contract award.

So the wartime half of this node's open question is answered twice over and the plant's own half is not answered at all: the corpus now knows of two tank installations at Lima in the war and cannot say whether either of them stands on this ground.

blocks.text: The locomotive erecting shops at Lima, where the Shay geared locomotives and later the mainline steam locomotives were built. [inference]

The plant has a node distinct from [the company](../organization/lima-locomotive-works.yml) because the two ended differently: the corporate identity was merged away in the mid-twentieth century while the physical works continued under other ownership building other products. Collapsing them would make the company's disappearance look like the site's, which is not what happened. [inference]

**It built tanks, and the corpus can now date that.** In February 1941 the works had "under construction a new $290,000 factory building", which the local press read as confirmation that it was switching part of its activity to defense production; by that August medium tank production was scheduled to begin "this fall". [verified] — [Chronicling America](../../catalog/chronicling-america.md), *The Bluffton News*, 20 February 1941, page 3, and *Evening Star*, 24 August 1941, page 4.

That makes this plant, and not [the tank plant](lima-army-tank-plant.yml), the first place in Allen County where tanks were built. [inference] The two are separate undertakings two years apart; so is [the Lima Tank Depot](lima-tank-depot.yml).

properties.address: 1150 S Metcalf Street, Lima OH 45804 — a postal address, not a municipality.

blocks.text: The petroleum refinery at Lima, built to process the crude of the Lima field after the 1885 strike and still operating. [inference] It is the longest-running industrial installation in the county and has outlived every corporate arrangement that has owned it.

**It has a Lima address and is not in Lima.** The county's address file records it at 1150 S Metcalf Street with `USPS_CITY` "LIMA" and `MUNI` **blank**, at 40.7221100, -84.1134691. [verified] — [Allen County GIS](../../catalog/allen-county-gis-downloads.md). The Census Bureau, asked the same point independently, puts it in [Shawnee Township](../place/shawnee-township.yml) and in no incorporated place. [verified] — [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md). The `located-in` edge named Lima from genesis until both authorities were asked.

**It is here because a farmer paid $5,000 to keep it here, in 1886.** Standard Oil resolved to build a refinery in north-west Ohio with Findlay and Toledo leading for the site. Its location committee — **Frank Rockefeller**, the director F. B. Squiers, and Keith, attorney for [the Solar Refining Company](../organization/solar-refining-company.yml) — inspected the candidates and settled on 151 acres of [James A. Hover's](../person/james-a-hover.yml) farm in [Shawnee Township](../place/shawnee-township.yml), lying between the C. & E. and the L. E. & W. railroads. Hover contracted to sell for $17,500; the Trenton Rock Oil Company, holding a drilling lease he had granted in 1885, demanded $10,000 to release it; Rockefeller refused to see him "held up" and threatened Findlay or Toledo. Hover bought the lease out of his own pocket for $5,000, and Rockefeller later sent him a personal cheque for $2,500 to split the loss. [verified] — [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md), which has the story from Hover's son and prints it as testimony rather than record.

**So the works were built by the Solar Refining Company, a Standard Oil subsidiary, from 1886.** [verified] — same source. That is the beginning of the ownership chain this node has asked for since genesis, and it explains what the corpus had already established by coordinate and could not explain: **the refinery sits outside every municipality because it was sited on a farm.** Standard picked 151 acres of open ground between two railroads in 1886, and no annexation has taken it since. [inference]

**The chain has its recent end now, and the present capacity with it.** The operator column of the federal refinery census reads BP Oil Corp. through the 1997 report, Clark Refining & Marketing in 1999 and 2000, Premcor Refining Group Inc from 2001 through 2007, and [Lima Refining Company](../organization/lima-refining-company.yml) from 2008 to now, under Husky Energy from 2010 and Cenovus from 2022. The works can run **183,000 barrels of crude per calendar day**, the largest refinery in Ohio and 36th of the 124 in the United States. [verified] — [EIA Refinery Capacity Report](../../catalog/eia-refinery-capacity.md); see [the series](../measure/lima-refinery-capacity-1994-2026.yml).

**It is bigger than it has ever been in that series, and by a quarter.** 145,000 barrels per calendar day in 1994 against 183,000 now. [verified] — same source. This node has said since genesis that the refinery "has outlived every corporate arrangement that has owned it"; it has also outgrown them, through the decades in which the county's [manufacturing employment](../measure/allen-county-manufacturing-employment-1969-2022.yml) fell by more than half. [inference]

**Two witnesses to the fact that a name outlives its owner.** The county's own address file still labels this site `VALERO LIMA REFINERY`, and the federal census never prints the word Valero in any year of any report. [verified] — [Allen County GIS](../../catalog/allen-county-gis-downloads.md) and the same EIA source. One of the two is naming somebody who is no longer here; both cannot be current. See [a register is not a census](../../decisions/a-register-is-not-a-census.yml).

nodes.label: Lima Tank Depot

blocks.text: A United States Army installation at Lima during and after the Second World War: the place where combat vehicles built elsewhere were finished, tested and dispatched to the fighting fronts. [verified] — [Chronicling America](../../catalog/chronicling-america.md), *The Bluffton News*, 3 August 1944, page 2.

**It did not build tanks. That is the whole point of it.** Vehicles arrived "in a 'raw' state of completion to Lima from the tank arsenals throughout the United States", and it was at the Depot that the modifications for a particular theatre of operations were installed, the vehicle given a final run on the Depot's proving ground, sealed, and put on a road train for a shipping port. The officer in charge described it as "the central supply base for combat vehicles": when troops in the field needed tanks, "the officers do not order from a particular factory. The order is flashed to Washington war headquarters and in turn to Lima." [verified] — same page.

**It was operated by a contractor.** Automotive News reports the Depot in February 1944 as "operated by United Motors Service, Inc.", whose plant-protection force had just received the War Department's Guidon Award following an inspection on 3 December. [verified] — same archive, *Automotive News*, 21 February 1944, page 28. A government installation run by a private company is the same arrangement [the tank plant](lima-army-tank-plant.yml) operates under today, eighty years apart, and this is the earlier of the only two contractor names this corpus holds for either. [inference]

**It was under construction in January 1943**, which places it two years later than the Locomotive Works' tank building and makes the two separate undertakings rather than one. A construction worker at the Depot — a brick mason foreman — died in St. Rita's hospital of injuries from falling beneath the wheels of a truck. [verified] — same archive, *The Bluffton News*, 21 January 1943, page 6.

**Its workforce came from thirteen counties.** The majority of employees travelled to the Depot from within a radius of fifty miles, across an area of thirteen counties. [verified] — same page. That is a larger labour shed than anything else this corpus records for Allen County, and it is a wartime measure of the county's reach that no census gives. [inference]

**It outlived the war by at least five years.** The Depot appealed its workers' draft classifications to the local board in 1945, and was still operating and named in 1950. [verified] — same archive, *The Bluffton News*, 22 March 1945 and 9 February 1950.

If it stood where the tank plant stands, that ground is **T4S R6E section 14**, abstracted in **Section Ground volume 34A**. [verified] — [the survey sections](../measure/allen-county-survey-sections.yml). The conditional is the whole of the claim: the section is where to look, not where the Depot was. [inference]

**It is very probably not the tank plant's ground, and that is now evidence rather than caution.** The NW quarter of section 14 — where the Joint Systems Manufacturing Center stands — was a mortgaged farm through the whole of the war, leased to a fishing and game club in April 1940 and crossed by pipeline easements its private owners granted in 1939, 1940 and 1949; the United States did not buy it until June 1951. [verified] — [Section Ground book list](../../catalog/allen-county-recorder-section-ground.md), volume 0034A pages 89–92. This Depot was under construction in January 1943. Two installations cannot occupy one piece of ground eight years apart with a farm in between. [inference]

refusals: This node does not establish where the Depot stood.
It does not establish whether this is the ground the [Joint Systems Manufacturing Center](lima-army-tank-plant.yml) occupies today.

blocks.text: The state canal running between the Ohio River at Cincinnati and Lake Erie at Toledo, passing through the western edge of Allen County by way of [Delphos](../place/delphos.yml) and Spencerville. [inference]

It is a site rather than a natural feature because it was dug, and it is a site with an extent rather than a point — which is the case this class is defined to cover. Its significance here is that it gave the western townships a transport connection decades before the railways arrived. **Spencerville is verified to be one of its towns**: the county records it as founded in 1844 on the banks of this canal. [verified] — [Allen County](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md), cities and villages page. Delphos is not — the same page describes it as four towns merging in 1851 and does not mention the canal — so the claim that the canal is why *both* towns stand where they do is halved: verified for one, still an inference for the other. [inference]

The canal was superseded by rail and abandoned as a commercial route in the early twentieth century. [inference] Lima, notably, is not on it — the county's later industrial centre grew around a railway junction instead, which is part of why the canal towns and the county seat have such different nineteenth-century trajectories. [inference]

**GNIS names it and this node declines its coordinate.** The canal is feature 1057843, filed under Henry County with a primary coordinate at 41.3269935, -84.1943905 and a source of `0.0, 0.0`. [verified] — [USGS GNIS](../../catalog/gnis-domestic-names-ohio.md). That primary point is about 34 miles north of Delphos [inference], because a names file gives one coordinate per feature and this feature is a 250-mile canal. Writing it into `coordinates` would put the Delphos reach in Henry County, and writing the source into anything would put a canal in the Gulf of Guinea. The identifier is worth keeping; the coordinate is not.

**It was located by a man who then lived and died in this county.** Samuel Forrer was connected with the canal surveys from July 1825 to 1831 and located the Miami & Erie; he was appointed canal commissioner in 1832 and elected to the Board of Public Works in 1835, and was still its consulting engineer in 1871 at seventy-eight. He settled in [Marion Township](../place/marion-township.yml) and made [Delphos](../place/delphos.yml) his home until his death in 1874. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md). See [Samuel Forrer](../person/samuel-forrer.yml).

**The chronology through this county.** The route was surveyed in 1824 and Congress made a land grant to Ohio to aid construction in 1828. The Wabash & Erie opened for navigation in **July 1843**, and the Miami extension — this canal's northern reach, the one that passes through Allen County — was formally opened in **June 1845**. [verified] — same source. Locally the water came a little earlier than the formal opening: Dr. Campbell's reminiscence has "the canal was opened for traffic in 1844", which is the year [Spencerville](../place/spencerville.yml) was laid out at its upper lock. [verified] — same source.

**Delphos is verified as a canal town after all**, on the same source that halves nothing: it sits "on the Miami and Erie Canal, above the confluence of that waterway with the Wabash and Erie Canal system", and the canal opened there in 1845. [verified] — same source. Its `located-in` edge is no longer an inference.
